===== Xiao2025_Genetics_Sorghum-EMS-MaleSterility =====

GENETICS, 2025, 230(3), iyaf017 
https://doi.org/10.1093/genetics/iyaf017
Advance Access Publication Date: 30 January 2025 
Plant Genetics and Genomics
Targeted seed EMS mutagenesis reveals a basic  
helix–loop–helix transcription factor underlying male sterility 
in sorghum
Yuguo Xiao,1,† Rajdeep S. Khangura  
,2,3,† Zhonghui Wang,1 Brian P. Dilkes  
,2,3 Andrea L. Eveland  
1,*
1Donald Danforth Plant Science Center, St. Louis, MO 63132, USA
2Department of Biochemistry, Purdue University, West Lafayette, IN 47907, USA
3Center for Plant Biology, Purdue University, West Lafayette, IN 47907, USA
*Corresponding author: Donald Danforth Plant Science Center, St. Louis, MO 63132, USA. Email: AEveland@danforthcenter.org
†Y.X. and R.S.K. contributed equally to this work.
Forward genetic screens of mutant populations are fundamental for functional genomics studies. However, isolating independent mu­
tant alleles to molecularly identify causal genes is challenging in species recalcitrant to genetic manipulation. Here, we demonstrate that 
classic seed ethyl methanesulfonate (EMS) mutagenesis coupled with genome sequencing can overcome this limitation in sorghum. 
We used this method to generate new mutant alleles of sorghum MALE STERILE 8 (MS8) and identified the causal locus for the ms8 
phenotype as Sobic.004G270900, which encodes the sorghum ortholog of maize bhlh122, a basic helix–loop–helix (bHLH) transcription 
factor required for male fertility in maize. Bulked segregant analysis mapped ms8-1 to a region on chromosome 4 containing 
Sobic.004G270900. Seeds from heterozygous MS8/ms8-1 plants were mutagenized and screened for chimeric inflorescences contain­
ing sectors with white, sterile anthers resembling the ms8-1 homozygous phenotype. DNA sequencing of sterile and fertile sectors from a 
single chimeric inflorescence revealed two mutations in Sobic.004G270900 within the sterile sector, but not the fertile sector. Isolation of 
this loss-of-function allele (ms8-2) established Sobic.004G270900 as the causative locus for male sterility in the ms8 mutant. We gener­
ated additional alleles of MS8 in a different genetic background using CRISPR/Cas9-based gene editing, where deletions in 
Sobic.004G270900 also resulted in male sterility. Our work identified a gene underlying male sterility in sorghum and provides a novel 
and straightforward genetic tool for researchers who lack access to advanced transformation facilities to validate gene candidates. Unlike 
gene editing, no prior knowledge of candidate genes is required for targeted seed EMS mutagenesis to aid identification of causal loci.
Keywords: bulked segregant analysis; male sterility; chemical mutagenesis; sorghum; germinal sectors; noncomplementation

Introduction
Mutant populations are valuable resources for functional genomics, 
enabling causative mutations to be linked to phenotypes of interest 
through mapping and/or sequencing (Jiang and Ramachandran 
2010; Jiao et al. 2017; Wang et al. 2021; Gupta et al. 2023; Xiong et al. 
2023). Forward genetic screens using mutant populations often 
yield a single mutant allele for a phenotype of interest. Reverse gen­
etics resources can be used to validate gene candidates identified 
through forward genetics or other methods but the number of lines 
sequenced is often limited, and multiple loss-of-function alleles 
may not be recovered for a given gene. Due to the high rate of back­
ground mutations in experimental mutagenized populations, it is 
necessary to identify independent mutant alleles to distinguish a 
true causative mutation in a gene from linked noncausative muta­
tions. Reverse genetics tools such as TILLING (McCallum et al. 2000), 
or gene editing tools such as Cas9-guide (g)RNA approaches (van der 
Oost and Patinios 2023) can be used to isolate independent alleles in 
a candidate gene but they are resource-intensive, not available in all 
species, take at least two generations for validation, and most im­
portantly, require knowledge of candidate genes beforehand.
In this study, we present a forward genetic mutagenesis screen in 
sorghum (Sorghum bicolor) specifically designed to identify novel al­
leles of mutants with visible phenotypes. We couple a classic strat­
egy termed “targeted mutagenesis” with linkage mapping and 
genome sequencing. Targeted mutagenesis gets its name not be­
cause of specific targeting of DNA but because of the experimental 
crossing design that facilitates recovery of loss-of-function mutants 
at a particular locus. For recessive mutants, mutagenesis is carried 
out on heterozygous material in an effort to recover new alleles by 
screening for a failure to complement when the allele is mutated. 
This approach is popular in maize by mutagenizing wild-type pollen 
and using that to pollinate mutant testers, followed by screening of 
the F1 generation to recover novel mutant alleles that fail to comple­
ment (Candela and Hake 2008). We have repeatedly successfully ta­
ken this approach to recover novel alleles when only one was 
recovered in our primary genetic screen (Marla et al. 2018; Best 
et al. 2021; Sauer et al. 2023). The pollen mutagenesis approach is 
highly efficient in monoecious plants like maize where male and fe­
male inflorescences are distinct. This approach, though highly ef­
fective, suffers from few drawbacks such as recovery of false 
positives due to occasional self-pollination of the mutant tester or 
Downloaded from academic.oup.com/genetics/article/230/3/iyaf017/7990424 by guest on 06 September 2026

gynogenic haploids (Best et al. 2021). A similar targeted screen can be 
done by mutagenizing heterozygous seeds to recover new 
loss-of-function alleles visible as somatic sectors (Candela and 
Hake 2008). This technique can generate somatic leaf chimeras re­
sulting from loss of function in dominant alleles. For example, mu­
tagenesis of heterozygotes at the semidominant lesion mutant 
Rp1-D21 in maize generated derivative suppressor alleles of 
Rp1-D21 that were visible as wild-type leaf sectors on an otherwise 
lesioned Rp1-D21/+ heterozygous plant (Karre et al. 2021).
Here, we deployed a targeted genetics mutagenesis screen to 
isolate novel mutant alleles and accelerate molecular identifica­
tion of genes responsible for mutant phenotypes in sorghum. 
Male sterility is an agronomically important trait for hybrid seed 
production. In sorghum, several recessive nuclear male sterility 
mutant loci (msal, ms1, ms2, ms3, ms7, ms8, and ms9) are known 
(Pedersen and Toy 2001; Xin et al. 2017; Chen et al. 2019). Only 
male sterile9 has been molecularly identified and encodes a 
PHD-finger transcription factor (Chen et al. 2019). A mutant allele 
at the MALE STERILE8 (MS8) locus, hereafter referred to as ms8-1, 
was morphologically characterized previously (Xin et al. 2017, 
2018), but its map position and gene identity were unknown. 
This allele exhibits a recessive inheritance, and the homozygous 
ms8-1 plants produce inflorescences with florets containing bright 
white anthers at anthesis that are completely devoid of pollen due 
to disruption of tapetum development (Pedersen and Toy 2001; 
Xin et al. 2017; Chen et al. 2019). We hypothesized that loss of the 
wild-type allele in a sector of a MS8/ms8-1 heterozygous head would 
result in white anthers in an otherwise fertile inflorescence at anthe­
sis. Using this approach, we isolated a novel mutant allele, ms8-2, 
that provided evidence of the underlying gene. We further validated 
the gene by generating additional alleles using a CRISPR/Cas9-based 
gene editing approach in a different genetic background. Together 
this demonstrates that Sobic.004G270900 encodes MS8. This gene is 
orthologous to maize bhlh122 (Nan et al. 2022), which encodes a basic 
helix–loop–helix (bHLH) transcription factor required for male fertil­
ity and tapetum development in multiple plant species (Niu et al. 
2013; Ji et al. 2013; Zhu et al. 2015; Nan et al. 2022).
The targeted seed ethyl methanesulfonate (EMS) mutagenesis 
approach described here is simple, time-saving and relies on 
built-in complementation testing within the same generation as 
part of the experimental design. This offers a significant advantage 
in species such as sorghum where multiple mutagenized popula­
tions (Addo-Quaye et al. 2018; Jiao et al. 2024) enable functional gen­
omics studies to identify gene-to-phenotype relationships, but 
oftentimes lack independent mutant alleles required to validate 
candidate genes. Furthermore, this approach can be easily adapted 
to characterize mutants displaying any visible cell autonomous 
phenotype at the whole plant level in other plant species. This 
makes it particularly valuable for species or cultivars that are ei­
ther recalcitrant to transformation protocols for gene editing, 
have long generation times, or lack resources altogether.
Materials and methods
Plant materials and genetic nomenclature
The ms8-1 mutant allele was isolated from a mutagenized BTx623 
population described previously (Xin et al. 2017; Zhao and Xin 
2019). We obtained the seeds of ms8-1 genetic stock in BTx623 
background from the laboratory of Dr. Gebisa Ejeta at Purdue. 
Seeds of ms8-1 genetic stock in BTx623 are freely available from 
GRIN (Xin et al. 2018). All gene, allele, and gene product names 
are provided here in the format detailed by Meinke and 
Koornneef (1997) in their guidelines for the Arabidopsis genetics 
community as this is the most common format used in plant gen­
etics, and there is no accepted community standard for sorghum.
Bulked segregant analysis mapping of ms8
We performed bulked segregant analysis (BSA) analysis to map the 
ms8-1 mutation in sorghum, following the method described in 
Klein et al. (2018) with some adjustments. Two independent ms8-1 
F2 mapping populations were generated by crossing pollen from 
other EMS mutagenized BTx623 lines (Addo-Quay et al. 2018) onto 
ms8-1 heads, and selfing the F1 MS8/ms8-1 plants. These F2 popula­
tions were planted at the Danforth Center’s Research Field in the 
summer of 2022 and phenotyped for male sterility. DNA was ex­
tracted using a CTAB method (Gallavotti and Whipple 2015) from 
pooled leaf tissue collected from male sterile and male fertile plants, 
respectively. Each pooled sample was made by taking four leaf 
punches from each individual using a paper punch. Sequencing li­
braries were prepared using the NEBNext Ultra II FS DNA Library 
Prep Kit for Illumina (E7805) according to the manufacturer’s instruc­
tions (NEB). Sequencing of the DNA pools was performed on an 
Illumina Hi- Seq 2500 at Novogene Corporation, generating 150-bp 
paired-end reads. FastQC (v0.11.9) was used to assess the overall 
quality of the sequencing data (“Babraham Bioinformatics—FastQC 
A Quality Control tool for High Throughput Sequence Data”). 
Trimmomatic (v0.35) (Bolger et al. 2014) was used to filter and remove 
low-quality reads and adapter sequences with the following para­
meters: ILLUMINACLIP: TruSeq3:2:30:10 LEADING:25 TRAILING:25 
SLIDINGWINDOW:5:20 MINLEN:36. The trimmed reads were 
mapped to version 3 of the sorghum reference genome BTx623 
(Sbicolor_454_v3.0.1; McCormick et al. 2018), using Bowtie2 
(v2-2.2.9; Langmead and Salzberg 2012) with the following para­
meters: –maxins 2000 –dovetail. Only uniquely mapped reads with 
a mapping quality greater than 20, determined by SAMtools (v1.11), 
were used for subsequent variant calling.
SAMtools and BCFtools were used to generate pileup and vari­
ant call format (VCF) files from the indexed BAM file (Li et al. 2009). 
Pileup files were used to identify the mapping region, while VCF 
files were used to identify candidate SNPs. The pileup and VCF 
files were first filtered out to remove nonvariant positions to focus 
on variant positions with a minimum coverage of two reads. Next, 
the pileup and VCF files from the ms8-1 DNA pool were further fil­
tered to exclude homozygous variants shared with its wildtype 
sibling DNA pool and experimentally determined error-prone 
sites shared among individuals in the same genetic background 
(Addo-Quaye et al. 2018). The final filtered pileup file was split 
into 10 chromosomes and plotted against the BTx623 reference 
genome to identify chromosomal regions enriched for homozy­
gous SNPs in the mutant pool due to linkage to the causative mu­
tations. In this analysis, homozygous variants were defined as 
nucleotide positions that differed from the reference genome at 
a frequency greater than or equal to 0.99. The boundaries of the 
ms8-1 mapping intervals were defined as the chromosomal coor­
dinates where variant frequency returned to background levels.
To identify potential causative lesions within the mapping in­
tervals, SnpEff (v4.3a) was used to predict the impact of SNPs on 
gene function (Cingolani et al. 2012). We filtered out SNPs that 
were not homozygous or noncanonical EMS changes (G to A or C 
to T). Candidate SNPs were subsequently validated through 
Sanger sequencing.
Phylogenetic analysis of bHLH transcription 
factors
Phylogenetic tree construction of bHLH transcription factors followed 
the protocol outlined by Bélanger et al. (2023), with some

Downloaded from academic.oup.com/genetics/article/230/3/iyaf017/7990424 by guest on 06 September 2026

modifications. Proteome sequence files were obtained from 
Phytozome 
(https://phytozome-next.jgi.doe.gov/), 
except 
for 
Arabidopsis thaliana, which was sourced from TAIR (https://www. 
arabidopsis.org/). To label individual proteins in the phylogenetic 
tree, species names were abbreviated and combined with protein IDs.
OrthoFinder v2.5.4 (Emms and Kelly 2015) was used to identify 
orthologous protein groups among eight species using default 
parameters. Orthologous groups for the bHLH family were identi­
fied using the known bHLH protein sequences from Arabidopsis 
(A. thaliana), rice (Oryza sativa), and maize (Zea mays) obtained 
from the Plant Transcription Factor Database (PlantTFDB v5.0, 
https://planttfdb.gao-lab.org/download.php). The presence of 
the bHLH domain in protein sequences was confirmed by search­
ing Pfam r35.0 (Mistry et al. 2021) using hmmscan from HMMER 
v3.3.2 (http://hmmer.org) with parameter -E 0.00001, followed by 
manual curation using CDvist (Adebali et al. 2015). Unaligned 
homologous sequences were inspected, and nonhomologous ad­
jacent characters were removed using PREQUAL v1.02 (Whelan 
et al. 2018) with default parameters. Multiple sequence align­
ments were generated using MAFFT v7.505 (Katoh and Standley 
2013) with parameters –auto –anysymbol –dash –originalseqonly.
Protein alignments were trimmed using trimAL v1.4.1 
(Capella-Gutiérrez et al. 2009) with parameters -gt 0.9 -cons 60 
-w 3 to remove nonhomologous regions outside the bHLH do­
mains. Maximum-likelihood phylogenetic tree was inferred using 
IQ-TREE v2.2.0.3 (Nguyen et al. 2015) with parameters -B 1000 
-mset JTT -T 32 –seqtype AA. The resulting bHLH phylogeny was 
visualized on iTOL v6 (https://itol.embl.de/), with clades distant 
from the sorghum MS8 clade collapsed for clarity.
Generation of additional ms8 alleles by targeted 
EMS mutagenesis
Sorghum seed for chemical mutagenesis was created by crossing 
the male sterile ms8-1/ms8-1:BTx623 plants with pollen from MS8/ 
ms8-1:BTx623 plants. The F1 seed from this cross was treated with 
30 mM EMS (Sigma-Aldrich catalog# M0880) dissolved in water. 
Briefly, on the day before planting, dry sorghum seeds from this F1 
cross were soaked in 30 mM EMS solution for 12 hours in the dark. 
The EMS solution was decanted into a waste container and seeds 
were rinsed six times with tap water. After the last rinse, these mu­
tagenized (M1 generation) seeds were laid out on absorbent paper in 
a fume hood for three hours at room temperature to dry.
The dried M1 seeds were treated with a slurry of NipsIt INSIDE in­
secticide (Valent U.S.A LLC, San Ramon, CA, USA), Apron XL (fungi­
cide, Syngenta, Basel, Switzerland), Maxim XL (fungicide, Syngenta, 
Basel, Switzerland), and a grass-specific herbicide seed safener 
Concep III (Syngenta, Basel, Switzerland) and then dried for an add­
itional 4 h. After fungicide and safener treatment, the M1 seeds 
were packed into plot packets with ∼37 seeds per packet. The M1 gen­
eration was planted at Purdue University’s Agronomy Center for 
Research and Education farm in the summer of 2023. Each packet 
was planted in the field as a 15-foot plot, with 12.5 feet of planted 
space and 2.5 feet of alley between successive plots. The spacing be­
tween adjacent rows was fixed at 2.5 feet. This spacing achieved a 
planting density of ∼45,000 plants per acre. A final plant count of 
∼2,500 M1 plants was established and subsequently screened at an­
thesis to identify additional alleles of ms8 as chimeric plants with 
white anthers on an otherwise fertile inflorescence with yellow 
anthers.
Bioinformatics analysis of the male sterile 
and male fertile sectors
DNA was isolated from male sterile and male fertile florets col­
lected from a chimeric inflorescence using a modified CTAB 
method (Saghai-Maroof et al. 1984). Whole-genome shotgun se­
quencing was performed using the NovaSeq X Plus platform 
(Illumina Inc., San Diego, CA, USA) by the Novogene Corporation 
(Sacramento, CA, USA). Paired-end reads (2 × 150 bp) were pro­
cessed to remove low-quality base calls and adapter sequences 
using fastp (Chen et al. 2018). The cleaned paired-end reads were 
aligned to the BTx623 v3.0.1 genome (McCormick et al. 2018) 
with the bwa-mem aligner using the default parameters (Li and 
Durbin 2009). Sorted BAM files were used to call SNPs using mpile­
up functions in bcftools (Danecek et al. 2021). As EMS primarily 
causes G > A and C > T transitions, the SNP calls were filtered to 
retain these changes using an awk command. Subsequently, vari­
ant effect prediction using SnpEff (Cingolani et al. 2012) identified 
moderate to high impact changes in the protein-coding regions. 
The sorted BAM files were visualized in IGV (Robinson et al. 2011).
Generation of additional ms8 alleles by gene 
editing
To generate additional ms8 mutant alleles, gene-specific guide 
(g)RNA sequences were designed using CRISPR-P 2.0 (http://crispr. 
hzau.edu.cn/cgi-bin/CRISPR2/CRISPR) and cloned into pMOD_2303 
(Č ermák et al. 2017). Subsequently, the gRNA expression cassettes 
were transferred into a plant binary CRISPR–Cas9 transformation 
vector coexpressing Cas9 and morphogenic regulators (Lowe et al. 
2016). The final vector was transformed into the sorghum Tx430 
genetic background using an Agrobacterium-mediated protocol 
(Wang et al. 2023) in the Eveland lab at the Donald Danforth Plant 
Science Center. Hygromycin selection followed by PCR of the trans­
gene was used to identify positive transgenic T0 events. In total, 15 
independent T0 events were identified. T1 plants were screened for 
absence of the transgene and then Cas9-free lines screened for 
stable edits by DNA sequencing. Primers used for vector construc­
tions are listed in Supplementary Table 1.
Results
BSA maps ms8-1 to chromosome 4
ms8-1 is a recessive male sterile mutant in sorghum with small, 
white, and nondehisced anthers (Fig. 1a and b). We used BSA to 
map the causal lesions responsible for the ms8-1 phenotype 
(Fig. 1c). Two pooled DNA samples, ms8-1 pool1 and ms8-1 pool2 
(Supplementary Table 2), containing 57 and 37 ms8-1 homozygous 
individuals from two independent F2 mapping populations, re­
spectively, were sequenced on an Illumina platform. To eliminate 
background variants from the populations, we sequenced two 
pooled DNA samples, containing 40 and 42 wild-type sibling indivi­
duals from the respective F2 populations. Sequencing yielded a to­
tal of around 350 million paired-end raw reads, with 62.4 to 101.9 
million reads per library. Approximately 96% of reads mapped to 
the BTx623 v3 reference genome. Mapped reads were filtered to re­
move low-quality alignments and PCR duplicates prior to variant 
calling. This resulted in genomic coverages from 8.9- to 14.3-fold 
per pooled DNA sample (Supplementary Table 2).
To identify the chromosomal regions linked to the ms8-1 pheno­
type, we searched for genomic regions enriched for homozygous 
variants in the two ms8-1 mutant pools. We found 5,711 and 4,400 
homozygous variants (allele frequency ≥ 0.99) in the ms8-pool1 
and ms8-pool2 datasets, respectively. We then filtered out putative 
background variants and error-prone positions in these mutant 
pools following procedures outlined in the Methods. After filtering, 
48 and 101 homozygous SNPs remained in the ms8-1 pool1 and 
ms8-1 pool2 data, respectively (Supplementary Table 3). Plotting 
the final filtered homozygous variants across the sorghum genome 
revealed a cluster of homozygous variants on chromosome 4 
Targeted EMS mutagenesis for new alleles | 3
Downloaded from academic.oup.com/genetics/article/230/3/iyaf017/7990424 by guest on 06 September 2026

between 56 and 64 Mbp in both mutant pools (Fig. 1c). This indicated 
that ms8-1 tightly cosegregated with this genomic interval. This ini­
tial ms8-1 mapping interval encodes 968 genes.
We next looked to identify potential causative variants respon­
sible for the ms8-1 phenotype. Given the considerable depth of se­
quencing for the two ms8-1 mutant pools (Supplementary Table 2), 
our datasets were likely to include causative lesions. Among the 48 
and 101 homozygous SNPs detected in ms8-pool1 and ms8-pool2, 
28 were shared in both pools (Supplementary Table 3). These 28 
shared SNPs were located within an overlapping region that nar­
rowed the candidate interval to 58.3–62 Mbp (Supplementary 
Table 4). Using SnpEff (Cingolani et al. 2012), we evaluated the 
potential impact of these 28 variants on gene function. This identi­
fied five variants, four missense variants and one stop-gain 
variant that alter the protein-coding sequence of a gene in the 
mapped window (Table 1). The stop-gain variant, located at 
genomic position 61,494,009, introduced a premature stop 
codon (448C > T, Q150*) within a gene encoding a bHLH tran­
scription factor (Sobic.004G270900). Phylogenetic analysis re­
vealed that Sobic.004G270900 encodes the sorghum ortholog of 
maize bHLH122, rice EAT1/DTD1, and Arabidopsis bHLH010/089/ 
091 (Fig. 2). All three of these transcription factors are established 
regulators of anther development and knockout mutants exhibited 
nondehisced anthers and tapetum development defects (Niu et al. 
2013; Ji et al. 2013; Zhu et al. 2015; Nan et al. 2022) strikingly similar 
to the ms8-1 phenotype (Xin et al. 2017). We hypothesized that 
ms8-1 is a loss-of-function allele of Sobic.004G270900 resulting in 
male sterility.

Isolation of independent alleles of ms8 using a 
targeted EMS mutagenesis approach
The white anther phenotype of ms8-1 homozygotes is easy to dis­
tinguish from the yellow, plump anthers on fertile florets. We rea­

of this seed EMS mutagenesis. Only the MS8/ms8-1 heterozygotes

a sector of florets with sterile anthers on an otherwise fertile in­

supplemental pollination with wild-type pollen. In contrast, ster­

visible on an otherwise male fertile head (yellow and plump an­

During anthesis, the M1 population was scouted daily between 
9 AM and 11 AM for chimeric heads containing a sector of the in­

wise bearing florets with fertile yellow anthers. Sterile florets were 
provided with supplemental pollen to test if they phenocopied the 
ms8-1 mutants. If the sterile florets produced seed, the sector was 
considered a candidate for a new allele of ms8. We identified a sin­
gle fertile sorghum head with a sector displaying white anthers, 
resembling ms8-1/ms8-1 homozygotes, on an otherwise fertile 
head (Fig. 4a). The white anthers in this sector were shriveled 
and did not show any sign of pollen production. The remainder 
of the inflorescence in this sorghum head displayed fertile pollen 
with plump, yellow anthers. To isolate the sterile sector, the 
florets with the white anther phenotype were tagged (Fig. 4b) 
and the surrounding fertile florets were removed (Fig. 4c and d).

BTx623 pollen to assess whether the sterility was limited to the

Identification and engineering of additional ms8 
mutant alleles
We also used CRISPR/Cas9-based gene editing to make additional 
alleles of Sobic.004G270900 in Tx430, a different genetic back­
ground. Tx430 is a sorghum line that is more amenable to trans­
formation (Howe et al. 2006). We used a gene editing toolkit 
(Č ermák et al. 2017) to express four gRNAs designed to target 
SbiRTX430.04G283300, the Tx430 homolog of Sobic.004G270900. We 
obtained two independent gene edited events, designated ms8-3 
and ms8-4, in the T1 generation after removal of Cas9 (Fig. 6). ms8-3 
harbored a 205 bp deletion of coding sequence spanning gRNA2 to 
gRNA4 within exon 2 of SbiRTX430.04G283300. Similarly, ms8-4 had 
a 416 bp deletion spanning from gRNA3 to gRNA4 in the same exon. 
Notably, both ms8-3 and ms8-4 exhibited a clear male sterile pheno­
type, phenocopying the ms8-1 allele in BTx623.
We also searched a sequence-indexed sorghum mutant popu­
lation generated previously (Addo-Quaye et al. 2018; Simons et al. 
2022) for additional alleles at MS8. One accession (PI 678336) car­
ried a nonsense mutation (Q123*) encoded by a C-to-T mutation at 
61493928 bp in MS8 (Fig. 6). We obtained 10 seeds of this accession 
from the USDA National Plant Germplasm System and planted 
them at the Purdue Agronomy Farm in West Lafayette in 
Summer 2024. This material was segregating for male sterility 
two out of eight heads from the progeny exhibited white anthers 
and failed to produce pollen. This allele is designated as ms8-5.
Discussion
Seed EMS mutagenesis has been widely used to generate mutant al­
leles for functional genomics studies. A single mutant allele is often 
sufficient to strongly implicate a candidate gene but isolation and 
molecular identification of independent alleles that fail to comple­
ment is required to unequivocally assign a gene to a phenotype. 
As many genetic resources often return a single allele, publication 
of gene identification and function from mutant studies can be la­
borious and delayed. In this study, we demonstrate the utility of 
pairing sequencing with classic chemical mutagenesis to success­
fully identify and validate novel alleles in sorghum. We identified

a conserved bHLH transcription factor as being necessary for male 
fertility and the locus responsible for the sorghum ms8 phenotype. 
Our results highlight the application of targeted mutagenesis for ac­
celerating gene discovery and validation, particularly when trans­
formation resources are underdeveloped.
Application of targeted seed EMS mutagenesis 
in genetic studies and sorghum breeding
Sorghum is an important agronomic crop that can withstand high 
temperatures and thrive on limited water (Prasad et al. 2021). 
Given the adaptability of sorghum across extreme climates, 
previous work has developed resources to study sorghum’s resili­
ence (Boyles et al. 2019; Xin et al. 2021). Many researchers 
lack access to transformation facilities and technology and regu­
latory hurdles for transgenic plants further limit use of gene 
editing to select countries. Sorghum transformation also requires 
time, specialized resources and expertise and is genotype- 
dependent (Casas et al. 1993; Sharma et al. 2020). As a result, an 
economical and effective method to generate novel alleles and 
validate candidate genes could accelerate the work of geneticists 
and breeders.
In our targeted mutagenesis screen, we used wildtype BTx623 as 
the pollen-parent. Therefore, mutagenesis of the heterozygous 
MS8/ms8-1 material generated a mutant allele that was strictly de­
rived from a wildtype BTx623 MS8 allele. This targeted mutagenesis 
approach could have used any genetic background and allows 
researchers to target the genetic backgrounds of their choice for iso­
lating novel alleles. This makes it possible to generate alleles in trad­
itional varieties or advanced breeding stocks if these are intended 
targets. The ability to generate novel alleles directly in haplotypes 
of choice can streamline the breeding process by eliminating the 
need to transfer mutations from different genetic backgrounds. 
While background mutations introduced during targeted seed mu­
tagenesis require subsequent backcrossing, this approach reduces 
linkage drag and allows breeders to focus on introgression of desired 
alleles into elite lines with fewer generations. Transformation pro­
cedures relying on somatic embryogenesis have eliminated the 
need for amenable genetic backgrounds for transformation, how­
ever, such procedures require specialized laboratory spaces, skills, 
regulatory approvals, and intellectual property licensing that can 
limit their utility in research and breeding. The targeted mutagen­
esis approach is a classical genetic approach that can be readily de­
ployed by researchers across the globe.
In this study, we used this approach to identify a novel allele 
and validate a gene underlying male sterility, but our previous 
work in maize has used a similar experimental design to identify 
intragenic somatic suppressors of dominant alleles of a disease re­
sistance locus (Karre et al. 2021). These experimental designs can 
be used for both recessive and dominant Mendelian traits where a 
phenotype can be readily observed on any visible plant (Candela 
and Hake 2008). Some important agronomic Mendelian traits 
that can be targeted using our approach include leaf color/

chlorophyll content, leaf waxiness, lignin composition (brown

Conservation of male sterility regulatory network 
across species
The ms8-1 allele, caused by nonsense mutation in the sorghum 
ortholog of bhlh122 from maize, exhibits defects in tapetum develop­
ment (Xin et al. 2017). The tapetum, a specialized cell layer that sur­
rounds the developing microspores (pollen mother cells) within the 
anther locules, provides nutrients and structural components ne­
cessary for pollen development and maturation (Wei and Ma 
2023). This helps to regulate the timing and progression of pollen 
development, ensuring the proper formation of functional pollen 
grains. Male sterile mutants caused by tapetum defects have been 
reported in many plant species, including the ms23, ms32, 
bhlh122-1, and bhlh51-1 mutants in maize (Nan et al. 2022). The genes 
ms23, ms32, bhlh122, and bhlh51 encode four bHLH transcription fac­
tors that interact with each other to regulate tapetum and pollen de­
velopment. Orthologs of these genes also regulate tapetum and 
pollen development in multiple angiosperm species including 
monocots and dicots (Niu et al. 2013; Ji et al. 2013; Zhu et al. 2015). 
The conservation of this bHLH-mediated regulatory mechanism 
across angiosperm lineages is remarkable but further research is 
needed to fully understand the extent and nature of this conserva­
tion. The integration of comparative genomics data alongside func­
tional studies across greater diversity of plants is necessary to 
determine if this pathway is flower specific or participates in male 
fertility across the Angiosperms.
Implications of male sterility for sorghum 
breeding and beyond
Male sterility is a trait that is valuable for hybrid seed production, 
as it prevents self-pollination and ensures cross-pollination. In 
sorghum, male sterility is a critical component of hybrid seed pro­
duction and thus a major driver of grain yield. Although cytoplas­
mic male sterility is generally used in sorghum breeding programs, 
the molecular characterization of nuclear male sterility genes like 
MS8 offers opportunities to develop innovative and flexible breed­
ing systems including the engineering of advanced conditional 
male sterility mechanisms (e.g. chemical or environmentally indu­
cible) (Zhou et al. 2014; Wang et al. 2021). Furthermore, the targeted 
seed EMS mutagenesis approach presented here could be used to 
recover novel alleles in any nuclear male sterility genes in sorghum 
within improved genetic backgrounds.
The recovery of novel alleles as mitotically cohesive sectors and 
coupling of screening and sequencing suggest that this approach 
could be valuable beyond species typically used for fundamental 
genetic studies. For example, chemical mutagenesis of clonally pro­
pagated species should similarly result in sector recovery when a no­
vel allele fails to complement a mutant carried by a heterozygous 
individual. This opens the possibility of using EMS mutagenesis 
and DNA sequencing to provide multiple alleles in mutants in long- 
lived species, and species in which crossing is not facile. Working 
with mitotic sectors and recovering multiple independent alleles in 
sectors has the potential to expand the number of plant species 
amenable for gene function discovery. As such, using sectors to mo­
lecularly identify alleles can accelerate functional genetics studies in 
species with long generation times. For example, in poplar trees, cut­
tings from a heterozygous parent plant or heterozygous siblings of a 
recessive mutant can be mutagenized and affected sectors se­
quenced to identify genes with a novel heterozygous mutant, just 
as was done here for ms8-2. This would accelerate and potentiate 
the discovery of gene function by avoiding the necessity of multiple 
generations beyond the generation used to recover the mutant to 
identify multiple alleles. Broadening the tools available to include 
sector approaches is particularly valuable for species with limited re­
sources and therefore single alleles or those systems that are recal­
citrant to genetic transformation.

===== Cridland2025_Genetics_Drosophila-DeNovoGenes =====

GENETICS, 2025, 230(1), iyaf044 
https://doi.org/10.1093/genetics/iyaf044

Investigation
New perspectives on Drosophila melanogaster de novo 
gene origination revealed by investigation of ancient 
African genetic variation
Julie M. Cridland,1,* Elizabeth S. Polston  
,1 David J. Begun1
1Department of Evolution and Ecology, University of California, Davis, Davis, CA 95616, USA
*Corresponding author: Department of Evolution and Ecology, University of California, Davis, Davis, CA 95616, USA. Email: jmcridland@ucdavis.edu
De novo genes can be defined as sequences producing evolutionarily derived transcripts that are not homologous to transcripts pro­
duced in an ancestor. While they appear to be taxonomically widespread, there is little agreement regarding their abundance, their per­
sistence times in genomes, the population genetic processes responsible for their spread or loss, or their possible functions. In 
Drosophila melanogaster, 2 approaches have been used to discover these genes and investigate their properties. One uses traditional 
comparative approaches and existing genomic resources and annotations. A second approach uses raw transcriptome data to discover 
unannotated genes for which there is no evidence of presence in related species. Investigations using the second approach have focused 
on D. melanogaster genotypes from recently established cosmopolitan populations. However, most of the genetic variation in the spe­
cies is found in African populations, suggesting the possibility that fuller understanding of genetic novelties in the species may follow 
from studies of these populations. Here, we investigate de novo gene candidates expressed in testis and accessory glands in a sample 
of flies from Zambia and compare them with candidate de novo genes expressed in North American populations. We report a large num­
ber of previously undiscovered de novo gene candidates, most of which are expressed polymorphically. Many are predicted to code for 
secreted proteins. In spite of much different levels of genomic variation in Zambian and North American populations, they express similar 
numbers of candidate de novo genes. We find evidence from genetic analysis of Raleigh inbred lines that a fraction of rarely expressed 
gene candidates in this population represent deleterious transcription promoted by inbreeding depression. Many de novo gene candi­
dates are expressed in multiple tissues and both sexes, raising questions about how they may interact with natural selection. The relative 
importance of positive and negative selection, however, remains unclear.
Keywords: de novo genes; Zambia; population genomics; Drosophila; gene expression

INTRODUCTION
Investigations bearing on the evolution of genetic novelties and 
their possible functions and contributions to adaptive evolution 
have for many decades, focused primarily on various types of 
gene duplications (Long et al. 2003). However, more recently, an al­
ternative mechanism of novel gene emergence has been pro­
posed. This mechanism, de novo gene evolution, invokes the 
recruitment of ancestral intergenic or intronic sequence into the 
production of derived, mature transcripts that are not homolo­
gous to ancestral transcripts (Begun et al. 2006, Levine et al. 2006; 
Zhao et al. 2014). While candidate de novo genes have been de­
scribed in several taxa (Drosophila, Zhou et al. 2008, mouse; 
Heinen et al. 2009, yeast; Cai et al. 2008; Li et al. 2010; Carvunis 
et al. 2012, humans; Knowles and McLysaght 2009, rice; Zhang 
et al. 2019, and nematodes; Prabh and Rödelsperger 2019) our un­
derstanding of these genes, both evolutionary and functional, is 
still primitive.
While some generalities about de novo genes have begun to 
emerge—for example, they tend to be short, simple, and lowly ex­
pressed (McLysaght and Hurst 2016; Van Oss and Carvunis 2019; 
Weisman 2022; Parikh et al. 2022; Peng and Zhao 2024)—many 
attributes of these genes remain open to question. There is little 
consensus on how to define and detect de novo genes, and thus 
disagreement about their abundance, population frequencies, 
and persistence times in genomes. Whether, or how, these genes 
typically make stable contributions to biological function and the 
proportion of such genes that are protein-coding are also open 
questions. Similarly, their patterns of gene expression across dif­
ferent organs and tissues are poorly described, and the potential 
importance of selection on their spread is not well known. Much 
of the work on these topics in Drosophila melanogaster has focused 
on either analysis of the D. melanogaster reference sequence anno­
tation in a comparative framework (Levine et al. 2006; Zhou et al. 
2008; Heames et al. 2020; Peng and Zhao 2024), or analysis of tran­
scriptome diversity from inbred lines from recently established 
populations from Raleigh, North Carolina, or Europe (Zhao et al. 
2014; Cridland et al. 2020; Grandchamp et al. 2023). This work 
has left unaddressed key questions relating to the origin and 
spread of these genetic novelties in the D. melanogaster model gi­
ven that much of the genetic variation in the species can only be 
found in African populations. Our goal here is to investigate 
some of these open questions by discovering and characterizing 
Downloaded from academic.oup.com/genetics/article/230/1/iyaf044/8086980 by Ulsan Natl Inst of Science & Technology user on 06 September 2026

testis-expressed and accessory gland (AG)-expressed de novo 
genes in a Zambia population of the species.
The African origin of D. melanogaster and the recent coloniza­
tion of non-African regions are clear, and supported by phylogen­
etic, biogeographic, and genetic data (David and Capy 1988; Begun 
and Aquadro 1993; Pool et al. 2012; Coughlan et al. 2022). For ex­
ample, nucleotide heterozygosity is much higher in African popu­
lations, and the non-African variation is primarily a subset of the 
variation present in Africa (Begun and Aquadro 1993; Langley et al. 
2012; Pool et al. 2012; Coughlan et al. 2022). This suggests that a ful­
ler understanding of de novo gene origination and dynamics in the 
species may require a focus on African populations. The Zambia 
population is of particular interest, as population genetic analysis 
has suggested that it has experienced little admixture from re­
cently established non-African populations and is the most genet­
ically variable of the assayed African population samples (Pool 
et al. 2012; Coughlan et al. 2022). Thus, the ancient genetic vari­
ation from Zambia should provide excellent material for further­
ing our understanding of how genetic novelties evolve in the 
species. While our recent work touched on some attributes of de 
novo genes expressed in testis and AG of Zambia vs North 
American populations (Cridland et al. 2023), a weakness was 
that all de novo candidate genes had been identified using tran­
scriptome data from the Raleigh population. Moreover, all popula­
tion level expression estimates were derived from pool data rather 
than line data. Here we use transcriptome data from the import­
ant Zambia population to provide the deepest transcriptome- 
based characterization of young de novo genes in the species. 
Moreover, we use frequency data from individual Zambia and 
Raleigh lines to make inferences about the forces acting on young 
de novo genes and how their attributes differ across populations.
Materials and methods
Flies, tissues, and RNA-Seq data
We used RNA-seq data from a previous study examining expression 
differences in D. melanogaster between North America and Africa 
(Cridland et al. 2023). The Zambian flies were originally collected in 
2010 as described in Pool et al. (2012) and were maintained as isofe­
male lines by the Pool lab (University of Wisconsin-Madison). We 
used 6 lines in these experiments: ZI126, ZI129, ZI131, ZI145, 
ZI156, and ZI181. The focal tissues, the testis and AG + ejaculatory 
duct (AG), were dissected from 3- to 5-day-old virgin males. For 
each of the 6 lines, we generated 3 biological replicates from each 
of the 2 tissues, which were then made into RNA and sequenced 
as previously described (Cridland et al. 2020; 2022, 2023).
In addition to the Zambian isofemale lines, we used our previ­
ously published pooled population data from the same 2 tissue 
dissections from Maine and Panama D. melanogaster populations 
(Cridland et al. 2023). For each of the 2 populations, pooled sam­
ples of each of the 2 tissues from 12 to 13 isofemale lines were gen­
erated for each biological replicate; 2 biological replicates were 
generated for each tissue and population. Finally, we used pub­
lished RNA-seq data from testis and AG from 6 Raleigh inbred 
lines as described in Zhao et al. 2014 and Cridland et al. 2022. 
These existing RNA-seq data were used to identify candidate de 
novo genes expressed in each of the tissues, and to then quantify 
their expression as previously described by Cridland et al. (2022)
(Supplementary Table 1).
Candidate gene identification
For each tissue, we pooled reads from the African lines described 
above, along with the pooled population samples from Maine and 
Panama, and then put the reads through our previously described 
pipeline (Cridland et al. 2022). Trinity (Grabherr et al. 2011) was 
used to generate a collection of de novo transcriptome assemblies 
for each tissue. These transcripts were then passed through a ser­
ies of filters (Cridland et al. 2022) designed to conservatively iden­
tify de novo gene candidates. For intergenic candidates we 
required the candidate to not overlap any known D. melanogaster 
gene features. For intronic candidates we required the candidate 
to match a known D. melanogaster intron, but to not match any 
other D. melanogaster gene features. Additional filters applied to 
all candidates included a minimum length (300 bp), minimum dis­
tance of 500 bp from existing D. melanogaster exon annotations, no 
overlap with existing annotations of Drosophila simulans or 
Drosophila yakuba, and no evidence of homology to de novo as­
sembled transcripts using RNA-seq data from 8 tissues from 
each sex (whole organism, gonad (testis or ovary), reproductive 
tract, terminalia, thorax, viscera, head, abdomen) from each of 8 
Drosophila species (D. yakuba, Drosophila ananassae, Drosophila 
pseudoobscura, Drosophila persimilis, Drosophila willistoni, Drosophila 
mojavensis, Drosophila virilis, Drosophila grimshawi) from Yang 
et al. (2018).
We then integrated these candidates with previously identified 
de novo gene candidates and subjected all candidates to addition­
al filtering based on estimates of transcript abundance. De novo 
gene candidates identified as described above using the Zambia, 
Maine, and Panama transcriptomes for each tissue were com­
pared with each other; those identified in both tissues were 
merged. Next, we combined this set of candidate de novo genes 
with previously identified candidates (Zhao et al. 2014; Cridland 
et al. 2022; Lombardo et al. 2023), merging new candidates with 
previously identified ones where applicable. We then generated 
a custom gtf file including both new and previously identified can­
didates. Reads for each biological replicate and tissue were then 
aligned to the D. melanogaster reference sequence (version 6.41, 
downloaded August 9, 2021, www.flybase.org) (Gramates et al. 
2022) and annotation using Hisat2 (Kim et al. 2015) with default 
parameters. We then used StringTie (Pertea et al. 2015) to calculate 
transcripts per million (TPM) for each candidate de novo gene 
using our custom gtf file. We retained candidates that were ex­
pressed at median across-replicate TPM ≥ 1 in at least one of the 
following: Maine pool, Panama pool, or one or more Zambia isofe­
male lines, and that also had conserved microsynteny with un­
ique, orthologous regions in D. simulans and D. yakuba.
This analysis led to a set of 1,369 candidate unannotated, un­
ique (i.e. not repetitive) D. melanogaster candidate de novo genes 
expressed in either the combined Zambian, Maine and Panama 
(ZMP) AG/testis or the Raleigh AG/testis/female reproductive 
tract. Homologous transcripts observed in multiple data sets 
were retained as potential alternative transcripts. We then per­
formed additional filtering steps.
Intronic candidate screening
Intronic de novo gene candidates could potentially be artifacts re­
sulting from reads derived from partially processed mRNA; we ap­
plied 2 additional filters to these candidates to address this 
possibility. First, for each candidate we calculated the read depth 
for the first and last 150 bp of the intron for every library where the 
candidate was detected. We screened out any candidate where 
any library had a mean read depth of ≥1 for both the first and 
last 150 bp of the intron, the logic being that a retained intron of 
a partially processed transcript should have coverage at the begin­
ning and end of the intron. Second, we pulled all read-pairs that 
aligned either within the range of a given de novo candidate or 
2 | J. M. Cridland et al.
Downloaded from academic.oup.com/genetics/article/230/1/iyaf044/8086980 by Ulsan Natl Inst of Science & Technology user on 06 September 2026

that spanned that region. We categorized them as either belong­
ing exclusively to the de novo candidate, exclusively to the sur­
rounding gene or matching to both the de novo gene and the 
surrounding gene. To identify instances where the intron ends 
were not sampled as described above but the candidate might still 
be physically associated with an ancestral gene, we dropped all 
candidates where ≥5% of read-pairs matched both the candidate 
and the surrounding gene. Overall, these filtering steps should al­
low for the detection of occasional partially processed mRNAs 
present in the data and enrich for true de novo candidates within 
introns.
Splice site and strand identification
A final analysis, which was applied only to the multi-exon candi­
date genes that survived these filters, used Portcullis (https:// 
github.com/EI-CoreBioinformatics/portcullis) to identify the asso­
ciated splice junctions and strandedness. We ran the full 
Portcullis pipeline on all available reads and used the filtered 
junctions file to identify splice sites and strand. We required 
a minimum of 1 read that overlapped the splice site by at 
least 20 bp to identify a junction. Because this analysis leverages 
read information from the entire transcriptome, we also used 
Portcullis to apply an additional filter to, in as much as possible, 
detect candidate de novo genes that are actually unannotated 
exons of known genes. We did this by identifying Portcullis in­
ferred splice junctions where one side of the junction matched a 
de novo candidate and the other matched a known gene. 
Manual inspection indicated that most of these instances (27/37) 
matched a known splice site in an annotated gene. The rest 
were situated within exons. These matches, which are likely un­
annotated exons of ancestral genes, were also removed from the 
set of de novo candidates and are available in Supplementary 
Table 2. We observed a total of 346 unique splice sites. Portcullis 
inferred a strand for 127 (67%) candidates and identified a junc­
tion for 239 (69%) splice sites. Of the splice sites, 212 were canon­
ical GT/AG sites, and another 7 were semi-canonical (AT/AC, GC/ 
AG or reverse complements thereof) sites. Of the identified splice 
sites, 108 were minus strand and 111 were plus strand. Of the 
62 candidates that did not have a splice site identified with 
Portcullis, 57 were expressed in Zambia. Compared with candi­
dates with splice sites identified with Portcullis that are also ex­
pressed in Zambia (123) we find the missing candidates to be 
expressed in significantly fewer Zambian lines (mean 1.44 vs 
1.87, t-test; P = 0.008), suggesting that fewer overall reads likely 
originated from these candidates, thereby reducing the probabil­
ity of sampling reads spanning a splice junction. We find no rela­
tionship between TPM of intronic de novo candidates and that of 
their surrounding genes in either tissue, regardless of the strand of 
the candidate and the surrounding gene or the size of the intron 
the candidate occupies.
Additional outgroup expression screening
To account for incomplete gene annotations and/or absent tran­
script assemblies in outgroup species that may lead to incorrectly 
identifying D. melanogaster candidates as de novo, and to incorpor­
ate a quantitative analysis of outgroup gene expression into our 
filtering, we estimated for each D. melanogaster candidate de 
novo gene, the expression in the orthologous region of D. simulans, 
D. yakuba, and D. ananassae. We were able to identify orthologous 
regions for 98% of candidates in D. simulans, 95% in D. yakuba and 
71% in D. ananassae. Outgroup data were taken from (Lin et al. 
2018; Cridland et al. 2020; Chakraborty et al. 2021; Majane et al. 
2022; Blair et al. 2023; Thompson et al. 2024, and previously 
unpublished data from the lab) (Supplementary Table 1). We in­
vestigated expression from 42 libraries across 5 D. simulans geno­
types, 2 D. yakuba genotypes, and 2 D. ananassae genotypes, as well 
as 4 D. simulans pools.
We first generated gtf records for orthologous regions by blast­
ing the candidate de novo genes to outgroup genomes. We re­
stricted this gtf file to include only the longest transcript for 
each candidate de novo gene candidate. We also required blast 
matches to have at least 80% identity over 100 bp to be included 
and to be at least 25% of the length of the longest transcript. We 
then calculated TPM as described above for regions orthologous 
to the candidate D. melanogaster de novo genes in all 3 outgroup 
species. Orthologous regions with outgroup TPMs of ≥1 were 
screened out; these may correspond to ancestral unannotated 
genes that were not assembled in our outgroup de novo transcrip­
tome assembly pipeline. To investigate the possible influence of 
threshold effects of outgroup TPM estimates on D. melanogaster 
de novo gene classification we investigated those candidates exhi­
biting outgroup expression estimates 0 < TPM < 1. For candidates 
where we identified an orthologous region in D. simulans the me­
dian TPM of the highest TPM observed in all outgroup genotypes 
was 0.144, with only 12 candidates having a highest observed out­
group TPM ≥ 0.75. For D. yakuba these values were a median high­
est TPM of 0.11 and 7 candidates with a highest outgroup TPM ≥  
0.75, and for D. ananassae the values were 0.01 and 5, respectively. 
These results demonstrate that only a small group of de novo gene 
candidates achieved that status based on outgroup TPM estimates 
that fell just below our cutoff of TPM = 1; indeed, most had out­
group TPM estimates very near zero.
We found 143 initial D. melanogaster candidates expressed in 
the ZMP data that were categorized as expressed in orthologous 
regions in one or more outgroup species. Expression in D. simulans 
orthologous regions was observed for 112 candidates; a mean of 
2.9 D. simulans genotypes expressed these candidates. Sixteen of 
these 112 candidates were also expressed in one or more D. yakuba 
genotypes, and a further 44 candidates were expressed in D. yaku­
ba, but not D. simulans. Twenty-five candidates were expressed in 
orthologous regions of D. ananassae, of which, 4 were also ex­
pressed in D. simulans and 1 in D. yakuba. Among our initial candi­
dates, those that were removed due to evidence of outgroup 
transcription exhibited higher median TPMs in Zambia and ex­
pression (TPM ≥ 1) in more Zambia lines, compared with those as­
sociated with no outgroup expression (and were therefore 
retained as candidates), though these differences were usually 
not significant (Supplementary Table 3). Following all filtering 
steps we retained a set of 893 de novo candidates. A fasta file of 
these sequences is available in Supplementary File 1.
Expression variation
We characterized gene expression variation for candidate genes in 
2 ways. First, we identified candidate de novo genes that were ex­
pressed at different frequencies amongst Zambia lines to charac­
terize the genetic component of within-population de novo gene 
expression variation. Second, we carried out an analysis of geo­
graphic expression differentiation by first creating 3 Zambian 
pseudo-pools. We did so by taking the reads from 1 replicate 
from each line and pooling them, thereby creating a data struc­
ture with 3 replicate pools, each of which is comparable with 
the pooled data from Maine and Panama. We then carried out dif­
ferential gene expression analysis for pairwise population compar­
isons as previously described (Cridland et al. 2023). Briefly, we 
generated tables of read counts for each population sample with 
featureCounts in the Rsubread package using -P –countReadPairs

Downloaded from academic.oup.com/genetics/article/230/1/iyaf044/8086980 by Ulsan Natl Inst of Science & Technology user on 06 September 2026

(Liao et al. 2014, 2019). Differentially expressed (DE) genes were then 
identified using limma with lfc = log2(1) and a P < 0.05 (Ritchie et al. 
2015; Phipson et al. 2016). Continent-level DE was identified as 
genes that were DE for both the Zambia vs Maine and Zambia 
vs Panama comparisons, but which showed no DE in the Maine 
vs Panama comparison.
Comparison with previous data sets
We previously investigated de novo gene candidates expressed in 
the testis, AG, and female reproductive tract in the Raleigh, North 
Carolina population (Zhao et al. 2014; Cridland et al. 2022; 
Lombardo et al. 2023). The Zambia population is substantially 
more heterozygous than Raleigh (Pool et al. 2012), likely because 
it retains more ancestral variation, raising questions about 
whether it also expresses more candidate de novo genes, especial­
ly given that most candidate D. melanogaster de novo genes are ex­
pressed polymorphically. Our previous work suggested that de 
novo genes were more abundant and more highly expressed in 
Zambia, however, that inference was indirect, in part due to the 
use of pooled transcriptome data (Cridland et al. 2023) and in 
part because of ascertainment bias in de novo gene discovery 
(Cridland et al. 2022). More direct comparison of de novo gene can­
didate properties in Zambia vs Raleigh requires that the transcrip­
tome sampling is carried out in as similar a fashion as possible. To 
do so, we generated 3 subsets of the Zambian transcriptome data 
for each tissue, each subset containing 1 library from each of the 6 
lines sequenced and then ran our entire pipeline on each subset of 
the data. Thus, we created a Zambia collection of de novo gene 
candidates using a pipeline and data structure identical to that 
previously used for Raleigh AG (Cridland et al. 2022). 
Additionally, since the detection pipeline in Zhao et al. 2014 was 
different from the one used in Cridland et al. 2022 and in this re­
port, we re-ran the Raleigh testis transcriptome data from Zhao 
et al. 2014 through the same pipeline described here.
Identification of potential space for de novo gene 
Candidates
We calculated the set of genomic spaces in which de novo candi­
dates could arise (given our filtering criteria) by identifying intron­
ic and intergenic regions of the genome that met the minimum 
size needed for a candidate. That size is 1,300 bp or greater; 300 
base pairs for the minimum transcript length plus 500 base pairs 
to either side. We then calculated the total amount of space 
for both intergenic and intronic regions for non-overlapping 
100 kb windows across the genome. We performed an ANOVA 
with the following design aov(de novo candidates per 100 kb ∼ 
Chromosome + Region/factor(PercentSpace)) to identify the ef­
fects of chromosome and region on observed de novo gene 
locations.
Signal sequences in de novo gene candidates
We compared the frequency of predicted signal sequences in can­
didate de novo genes to the frequency of predicted signal 
sequence in latent ORFs located in intergenic and intronic se­
quences using approaches similar to (Begun et al. 2006). We ex­
tracted each intergenic and intronic sequence and trimmed 
them such that each met our criteria for potentially harboring a 
de novo candidate. We then passed each sequence through getorf 
(Rice et al. 2011) to identify all ORFs of ≥ 40 amino acids long. 
Getorf was used instead of CPAT (Wang et al. 2013) since CPAT 
assesses ORFs in part by comparing the transcript length to the 
identified ORF length. Repetitive ORFs were screened out by iden­
tifying ORFs with multiple high quality BLAST alignments to the 
reference genome. We also used getorf on the de novo candidate 
transcripts to produce a directly comparable set of ORFs for this 
analysis. We then used SignalP 5.0 (Armenteros et al. 2019) to iden­
tify potential signal sequences in these ORFs. To investigate 
whether other potential candidate subcellular localization signals 
are predicted in ORFs from our candidates, we passed these ORFs 
through DeepLoc2.1 (Thumuluri et al. 2022).
Correlations between de novo genes and selective 
sweeps
We used 2 published analyses of soft sweeps to investigate the 
possibility of selection influencing genomic regions expressing 
de novo gene candidates. First, we compared the de novo candi­
dates identified in the Raleigh data with H12 statistics calculated 
in 400 SNP windows by Garud et al. (2021) in the same population. 
The data and analyses result in regions identified as associated 
with evidence of soft or partial sweeps given the demographic 
model and false discovery rate specified in Garud et al. This al­
lowed us to compare regions displaying signals of soft selective 
sweeps with the regions occupied by our de novo candidates. 
Due to differences in the prevalence of significant H12 windows 
between chromosomes we considered both intergenic and intron­
ic regions on different chromosome arms separately.
Second, we downloaded sweep classification data from 
(Sheehan and Song 2016) Supplementary Table 3, generated using 
the 197 Zambian lines from Pool et al. 2012, the same population 
from which our Zambia lines are derived. Sheehan and Song use 
a trained network to identify windows as hard sweeps, soft 
sweeps, balancing selection, or neutral. We compared de novo 
candidates in Zambia with the windows identified by Sheehan 
and Song to look for enrichment of candidates in hard or soft 
sweep regions vs neutral regions.
RESULTS
Section 1: identification of candidate de novo 
genes in D. melanogaster from Zambia, Maine, and 
Panama
We identified de novo candidate genes in a data set we previously 
used to study expression differentiation in annotated genes be­
tween Africa and North America (Cridland et al. 2023). This data 
set consists of accessory gland + ejaculatory duct (AG) and testis 
data from 6 Zambian lines and 3 replicates each of pooled popula­
tion data from Maine and Panama (Supplementary Table 1). We 
applied the de novo detection pipeline we developed in Cridland 
et al. 2022, plus some additional screening for partially processed 
mRNA and outgroup expression, to this data set. New candidates 
were identified independently for testis and AG. We also gener­
ated new de novo gene calls from testis transcriptomes from 6 
previously described Raleigh inbred lines (Zhao et al. 2014) to cre­
ate a collection of candidate genes identified by the same methods 
for all tissues and samples.
We observed 478 of these candidates expressed in the ZMP data 
(Table 1, Supplementary Table 4). Most were expressed in only 1 of 
the 2 focal tissues, 61 in the AG and 421 in the testis, consistent 
with previous results from the Raleigh population showing 
many more de novo gene candidates expressed in testis than in 
AG (Zhao et al. 2014; Cridland et al. 2022); 4 candidates were ex­
pressed in both tissues. The Zambian population expressed 
more de novo candidates than Maine and Panama in both tissues, 
as well as the largest number of de novo candidates unique to a 
single population. Given that many de novo genes are expressed 
in relatively few genotypes (Supplementary Table 5) and tend to 
4 | J. M. Cridland et al.
Downloaded from academic.oup.com/genetics/article/230/1/iyaf044/8086980 by Ulsan Natl Inst of Science & Technology user on 06 September 2026

be lowly expressed (Zhao et al. 2014; Cridland et al. 2022; 
Grandchamp et al. 2023), we expected to discover many more can­
didates in the Zambian sample than in Maine and Panama given 
that individual isofemale lines were only used for Zambia. We 
will return to this issue later.
While many candidates are expressed at a low level, near the 
threshold used to define a gene as “expressed”, a large number 
are also expressed at substantial levels. The median maximum 
TPM (across lines) for candidates expressed in the Zambian AG 
is 2.09 (Fig. 1a) and is 2.01 in the Zambian testis (Fig. 1b). As ex­
pected, imposing a minimum TPM ≥ 2 to call a gene as expressed 
reduces the number of Zambia candidates, from 446 to 239. There 
are 7 AG-expressed and 32 testis-expressed candidates that have a 
maximum TPM in Zambia ≥ 10. A quantitative analysis of the ef­
fect of the minimum TPM threshold for calling a candidate gene 
as “expressed” can be found in Supplementary Table 6.
Candidate organization
Consistent with previous literature (Zhao et al. 2014; McLysaght 
and Hurst 2016; Cridland et al. 2022; Lombardo et al. 2023; Peng 
and Zhao 2024) de novo gene candidates are simple. Most (59% 
in the testis, 70% in the AG) are single-exon, and the maximum 
number of exons observed in a candidate was five. This pattern 
was the same for intronic and intergenic candidates for both tis­
sues (Supplementary Table 7). By contrast, only 14% of all 
testis-expressed (1,586/11,646) and 12% of all AG-expressed 
(1,086/9,053) annotated D. melanogaster genes are single-exon.
Around half of the candidate de novo genes (49%) were asso­
ciated with only one transcript. A greater proportion of 
AG-expressed candidates (57%, 35/61) than testis-expressed can­
didates (47%, 199/421) exhibit only one transcript, though the dif­
ference is only marginally significant (fisher.test, P = 0.048). We 
observed no difference in the proportion of single- vs multiple- 
transcript candidates between the intronic and intergenic cat­
egories for both tissues (fisher.test AG, P = 0.19; testis, P = 0.08) 
(Supplementary Table 8). The mean length of the longest tran­
script was slightly greater for testis candidates (mean = 828 bp) 
vs AG candidates (mean = 806 bp), but not significantly so (t.test, 
P = 0.83).
Coding potential, signal sequences, and other subcellular 
localization motifs
Six ZMP expressed candidates are potentially protein-coding 
based on a Coding Potential Assessment Tool (CPAT) score ≥ 0.39 
(Wang et al. 2013). Given that CPAT scores tend to be lower for 
short protein-coding genes (Cridland et al. 2022), we further inves­
tigated coding potential by assessing possible presence of signal 
sequences. We used the top 5 open reading frames predicted by 
CPAT for the ZMP expressed candidate genes, regardless of their 
status as predicted coding vs non-coding, and then used SignalP 
5.0 (Armenteros et al. 2019) to identify potential signal sequences 
in these ORFs. We observed 63 (13%) candidates that contain 
strongly predicted signal sequences, 53 testis-expressed and 10 
AG-expressed. Thirty-four are intergenic and 29 are intronic, simi­
lar to the ratio for candidates not harboring predicted signal 
sequences.
The 58 Zambia-expressed candidates carrying predicted signal 
sequences were expressed in a mean of 1.8 lines and with mean 
TPM = 3.2 in expressing lines, similar to the mean number of lines 
and mean expression for all Zambia-expressed candidates. Six 
candidates were predicted to be protein-coding by CPAT and of 
these, 4 had a predicted signal sequence. The abundance of 
ORFs carrying predicted signal sequences in genes not predicted 
by CPAT to be coding supports the idea that CPAT underpredicts 
protein-coding status for short transcripts.
To investigate whether the abundance of potential secreted 
proteins among candidates is more than expected, we estimated 
the proportion of ORFs in intergenic and intronic DNA carrying 
predicted signal sequences. To do so we obtained the annotated 
non-coding DNA and then trimmed each intron/intergenic se­
quence to conform to our criteria for de novo gene candidate loca­
tion. We used getorf to identify in each sequence all ORFs ≥ 40 
amino acids long. These predicted proteins were then passed 
through SignalP 5.0 to identify potential signal sequences. We 
find that 3.7% of intergenic ORFs (3,542/95,821) and 3.9% of intron­
ic ORFs (5,292/135,952) possess a predicted signal sequence, simi­
lar to the results from Begun et al. (2006).
Similar to the CPAT results, using getorf we find that of 444 de 
novo gene candidates that have ORFs ≥ 40 AA in length, 59 (13%) 
have a predicted signal sequence. Thus, there is a dramatic excess 
of signal sequences in de novo gene candidates compared with the 
overall abundance of potential predicted signal sequences in in­
tergenic and intronic DNA, which supports the idea that these 
de novo gene candidates are not a random sample of latent 
ORFs in non-coding DNA.
Passing de novo candidate ORFs through DeepLoc2.1 
(Thumuluri et al. 2022) revealed additional candidates carrying 
subcellular localization signals, including 42 with predicted nu­
clear localization signals and 36 with a predicted mitochondrial 
transit peptide, providing further evidence that a significant frac­
tion of candidates may be protein-coding.
Intergenic vs intronic regions
We observed similar numbers of de novo candidates in intergenic 
and intronic sequence, a pattern that was consistent across tis­
sues and populations (Table 1). We calculated the total space in 
which candidates could have been found given the criteria im­
posed on their locations. More space was available for candidates 
to arise within introns (41,910,767 bp) than in intergenic space 
(36,754,186 bp). However, while only 47% of available space for 
candidates was intergenic, 58% of candidates were in intergenic 
space (277/478) (binomial P-value = 5.56e−7). This suggests a bias 
favoring intergenic regions for de novo gene candidates, which 
is surprising given that intronic sequences are likely much more 
transcriptionally active than intergenic sequences; perhaps new 
intronic de novo genes are more likely than intergenic candidates 
to interfere with surrounding gene function.
Much of the previous literature examining de novo genes fo­
cuses on identifying candidates in intergenic space (Zhao et al. 
2014; Lombardo et al. 2023). However, many annotated 
Drosophila genes are located within introns of other genes 
(Celniker and Rubin 2003). Ancestral intronic and intergenic re­
gions giving rise to de novo gene candidates are likely to have

different selective constraints and the corresponding de novo

lated available intergenic and intronic space in 100 kb windows, 
screening out regions that were too small to accommodate our fil­
tering criteria relating to minimum candidate size and minimum 
distance from ancestral genes/exons. As expected, windows har­
boring de novo gene candidates have, on average, more available 
space for such candidates in both intergenic and intronic regions, 
than windows that do not have candidates (Table 2). Intronic can­
didates are located in windows having more available intron 
space relative to the comparable metric for intergenic candidates, 
though this difference was not significant. A possible interpret­
ation is that intronic candidates may require more space than 
intergenic candidates to avoid interfering with ancestral, sur­
rounding, gene functions.
Section 2: population biology of de novo 
candidates expressed in Zambia
Individual replicated line data for the Zambian population al­
lowed us to investigate several population biology aspects of de 
novo gene candidates. As previously observed in D. melanogaster 
(Zhao et al. 2014; Cridland et al. 2022; Grandchamp et al. 2023), de 
novo genes tend to be expressed in a minority of assayed 
genotypes.
Most Zambian candidates, 59% in the testis (229/387) and 59% 
in the AG (35/59) were observed in only one of the 6 lines. 
There was no difference between tissues in the proportion of 
genes expressed in 1 line (P = 0.09). Six de novo gene candidates

—2 in the AG and 4 in the testis—were expressed in all 6 Zambia 
lines. These genes are also expressed in the majority of Raleigh 
genotypes.
To investigate potential correlates of gene expression fre­
quency in Zambia we compared singleton with non-singleton de 
novo candidates (Supplementary Table 9). Singleton candidates 
were generally similar to non-singleton candidates in transcript 
length and maximum number of exons, though the small number 
of genotypes assayed is likely associated with low power to detect 
potential singleton vs non-singleton effects. However, non- 
singleton genes tended to be more highly expressed in expressing 
lines for intergenic AG candidates and intronic testis candidates, 
consistent with previous results (Zhao et al. 2014; Cridland et al. 
2022). We further compared the distribution of singleton and non- 
singleton candidates per chromosome (Supplementary Table 10). 
We find for testis-expressed de novo candidates an excess of 
X-linked singletons, potentially indicating selection against such 
candidates.
In general, Zambia lines express similar numbers of candidates 
in each tissue; the line expressing the fewest candidates still 
expresses 68% as many candidates as the line expressing the 
most candidates (Supplementary Table 11). Thus, there are no 
major line-effects on the number of de novo genes expressed. 
However, previous work has provided evidence that cis-acting 
genetic variants play a role in driving expression of individual 
polymorphic de novo genes, and that such effects may be greater 
for testis than for AG (Zhao et al. 2014; Cridland et al. 2022). Given 
this, and the large number of new testis candidates discovered 
here, we sought evidence that variation in levels of nucleotide het­
erozygosity across the genome are physically associated with de 
novo gene candidates.
To do so, we estimated nucleotide diversity (π) in 100 kb win­
dows using the SNP data from 197 Zambian genomes described 
in Lack et al. (2015) downloaded from https://www.johnpool.net/ 
genomes.html on 3/4/2022. This data set was converted from 
D.melanogaster v5 to v6 using Flybase’s coordinates converter 
(www.flybase.org). We then compared π for windows that overlap 
a candidate de novo gene with windows that do not and found that 
windows overlapping a candidate exhibit consistently higher nu­
cleotide heterozygosity across all chromosome arms (Fisher’s 
combined probability = 2.5e−3) (Supplementary Table 12). There 
are 2 interpretations of this observation. First, partial sweeps as­
sociated with positive selection on polymorphic de novo gene can­
didates has led to elevation of nucleotide heterozygosity at linked 
regions. Second, greater local nucleotide variation affects the 
probability of de novo gene birth. To distinguish between these ex­
planations we repeated this analysis separately for singleton vs 
non-singleton de novo gene candidates. We observed elevated 
heterozygosity for windows harboring both singleton and non- 
singleton candidates vs windows containing zero candidates. 
We interpret this as supporting the second hypothesis, that local 
heterozygosity influences the probability of de novo gene birth, 
consistent with a role for cis-acting variation on expression of 
polymorphic de novo genes (Zhao et al. 2014; Cridland et al. 
2022). Zambia X chromosome nucleotide variability is similar to 
that of the Zambia autosomes (Pool et al. 2012), consistent with 
roughly equal abundance of X vs autosome de novo gene candi­
dates (after controlling for available space) (Supplementary 
Table 10).
We compared the locations of Zambian de novo candidates to 
regions identified as either hard or soft sweeps, or neutral regions 
by Sheehan and Song 2016. We found no enrichment of candi­
dates in sweep windows, though it should be noted that the 
Sheehan and Song analysis inferred so much of the genome to 
lie in sweep windows (59% of windows were identified as hard 
sweeps and another 4% as soft sweeps) that the lack of enrich­
ment is unsurprising.
Geographic differential expression
Seventy-five candidates were found to be DE between Zambia and 
North America, eleven in the AG (18.6% of candidates) and 64 in 
the testis (16.5% of candidates). While ancestral genes and de 
novo candidates were roughly equally likely to exhibit intercon­
tinental DE in testis, the proportion of AG-expressed de novo can­
didates exhibiting DE was about twice as great as that observed for 
ancestral genes (8.4%) (Fisher’s Exact Test, P = 0.023; Cridland et al. 
2023).
Of the 75 candidates displaying intercontinental DE, 47 were in­
tergenic and 28 were intronic; 73 candidates had higher mean ex­
pression in all Zambian lines, consistent with our previous 
speculation (Cridland et al. 2023) that DE de novo genes tend to 
be more highly expressed in Zambia than in North American po­
pulations. Of the 73 candidates with greater expression in 
Zambia, 56 exhibited median TPM ≤ 0.5 in both the Maine and 
Panamanian populations; DE candidates with higher expression 
in Zambia exhibited mean TPM = 7.0 in Zambian lines. Thus, the 
continental DE genes tend to be expressed robustly in Zambia 
but expressed at very low level or not at all in North America.
To determine whether this pattern is limited to DE candidate de 
novo genes we carried out a similar comparison for non-DE candi­
dates and found a similar bias; of the 279 de novo candidates ex­
pressed in the Zambia testis but not showing DE vs either Maine or 
Panama, 222 have higher expression in Zambia than in Maine and 
Panama, while only 20 have higher expression in both Maine and 
Panama compared with Zambia. This is also seen in the AG where 
30 of 37 de novo candidates are expressed more highly in Zambia 
compared with both Maine and Panama, while only 4 show the 
reverse pattern. Because these inferences use pools of flies, we 
cannot determine the relative contributions of frequency of ex­
pression across genotypes vs level of expression in generating 
DE. Importantly, candidate genes expressed in Zambia are likely 
more easily discovered than candidates expressed in North 
American samples due to the line vs pool nature of the raw 
data. Thus, this widespread pattern of higher expression in 
Zambia could be explained by ascertainment bias in de novo 
gene discovery.
Section 3: comparison of Raleigh, NC vs Zambia
Updating the Raleigh, NC de novo expression calls
With a goal of making more direct comparisons of Zambia and 
North America using line data rather than pools, we updated de 
novo candidate expression calls in Raleigh by estimating the ex­
pression of all 893 high quality candidates using previously col­
lected data from the Raleigh AG, testis, and female reproductive 
tract, requiring TPM≥ 1 to call a gene as expressed and filtering 
out potential partially processed mRNA in intronic candidates ex­
pressed in Raleigh. Most candidates expressed in Raleigh in this 
analysis were previously identified in the Raleigh population 78/ 
89 in the AG (Cridland et al. 2022), 518/558 in the testis (Zhao 
et al. 2014) (Supplementary Table 13). We observed 41 de novo can­
didates that were not previously identified in libraries from 
Raleigh, 35 in the testis and 6 in the AG. These newly identified 
candidates were expressed in an average of 2 libraries 
(Supplementary Table 14).
