dyads. Once established, DNA methylation is subsequently transmit-
ted over DNA replication by the combined functions of UHRF1 and the 
maintenance methyltransferase enzyme DNMT1, which conjugates a 
new methyl group onto the nascent DNA strand2,4. Although the major-
ity of the genome is CpG poor, about 7% of CpGs exist within so-called 
‘CpG Islands’ (CGIs) that are enriched about tenfold for CpG dinucleo-
tides, frequently found at mammalian promoters and constitutively 
unmethylated across most cell types28. In this section, we break down 
the nature of this landscape as it affects distinct genomic features and 
highlight more recently appreciated dynamics.
Gene-dense and gene-poor regions
Mammalian genomes are heterogeneous, with dense pockets of 
transcribed genic regions, comparatively isolated developmental 
genes and expansive gene-poor, repetitive element-rich ‘deserts’29. In 
addition to stereotypic localization to the nuclear lamina, gene-poor 
regions initiate replication later in S phase and from fewer origins than 
gene-dense regions, which limits the time available to copy epige-
netic information before the next cell division30–33. This prioritization, 
together with dedicated de novo methyltransferase recruitment to 
active transcribed regions, gives rise to highly methylated domains 
(HMDs), whereas replication-coupled depletion of methylation leads 
to extended partially methylated domains (PMDs)34–37 (Fig. 1b) that 
heavily overlap large organized chromatin K9 modifications (LOCKs)38, 
lamina-associated domains (LADs)39 and genomic ‘B compartments’40. 
PMDs cover about 50% of the mammalian genome and their regu-
lation is compatible with known biochemical interactions between 
methylated residues and chromatin state, core readers such as the 
methyl binding domain (MBD) proteins, and regulatory complexes 
associated with nuclear lamins and heterochromatin41. PMDs are most 
accurately measured by tracking isolated DNA sequence motifs, such 
as WCGW, that are less impacted by additional layers of regulation and 
better approximate the neutral fidelity rate of DNMT1 (refs. 35,36,42). 
The loss of methylation at PMDs may be linked to the denser nature 
of chromatin within the nuclear lamina, which may impede efficient 
access of maintenance machinery prior to cell division43. Addition-
ally, it is plausible that poor ‘repair’ of lost methylation is caused by a 
difference in the underlying chromatin state that limits active DNMT 
recruitment44,45.
PMDs are apparent within many adult tissues and approach very 
low methylation values after extended in vitro culture or in some 
cancers, but we do not know whether these patterns reflect a change 
in regulation between stem cells and their differentiated progeny or 
adaptations made during disease progression. Human and mouse 
embryonic stem cells (ESCs) can be passaged indefinitely and divide 
rapidly, but do not exhibit the same proliferation-dependent methyl­
ation loss36,46. Why ESCs and, possibly, other cell types are immune 
to these effects is not clear but does suggest that epigenomic fidelity 
can itself be modulated, even for large, predominantly inert genomic 
territories.
Housekeeping and developmental gene promoters
About half of the CGIs annotated in the human genome overlap tran­
scription start sites, with approximately another 25% located within 
coding sequences or gene bodies. As the predominant promoter 
element for constitutively expressed housekeeping genes, CGIs are 
frequently enriched for transcriptional initiation machinery, have 
intrinsically low nucleosome retention and are themselves a major 
hub for CXXC domain-containing proteins that bind to and protect 
Introduction
The covalent linkage of a methyl group to the cytosine base in DNA has 
acquired numerous regulatory functions beyond its originally identi-
fied role in bacterial genomic surveillance1–5. In mammals, DNA methyl­
ation is essential for viability in nearly every fetal and adult cell type 
and serves as the mechanistic standard for epigenetic transmission over 
DNA replication1–4. The relative ease with which this modification can be 
precisely measured at base-pair resolution, coupled with its interesting 
dynamics across many developmental and disease-associated contexts, 
have made it a potent indicator of complex regulatory mechanisms. 
DNA methylation also remains unique amongst covalent chromatin 
modifications because it can be directly measured from sequenced 
molecules to infer its biochemical and cellular dynamics. As such, DNA 
methylation profiling has been widely adopted, including to evaluate 
large cohorts and sensitively recover clinically relevant biomarkers in 
diseases ranging from pre-eclampsia to cancer6–10.
Even though DNA methylation is a classic and well-characterized 
epigenetic modification11, many new discoveries have been made over 
the past decade, including enzymes that deposit, alter or remove 
methylation, additional functional contexts and an expanded number 
of interactions with the histone code. DNA methylation has been pro-
filed for cells and tissues representing the entire human and mouse 
life course2. The number of comprehensive reference atlases has 
grown substantially12, as have opportunities to investigate previously 
hidden parts of the genome13. Together, these advances have led to 
the emergence of numerous, more specialized subfields. Perhaps 
most strikingly, aberrant DNA methylation patterns are a common 
molecular hallmark of human tumours, one that seems to be surpris-
ingly similar in its overall pattern regardless of the cell type of origin or 
mutational profile7,14. DNA methylation dynamics over animal ageing 
have also drawn substantial interest, either as potential targets for 
therapeutic intervention or as indicators of life-altering historical 
exposures15–20.
Several of these topics are well contextualized in recent reviews, 
including the nature and utility of epigenetic clocks15,17,21, cancer-
associated hallmarks22,23, sequencing technologies24,25, molecular 
encoding26 and the comparative biology of plants27. Here, we hope to 
provide a unifying framework by examining the genomic distribution 
of DNA methylation within specific developmental or disease contexts, 
including how these DNA methylation ‘landscapes’ inform our growing 
knowledge about the regulatory function and physiological role of this 
modification. We discuss the canonical and non-canonical patterns 
revealed from extensive mapping efforts as well as current understand-
ing of how they reflect the interplay of DNA methylation with specific 
histone modifications and other aspects of nuclear organization. 
Finally, we summarize current progress in ageing and cancer research as 
they relate to stereotypical and global changes in DNA methylation that 
are just beginning to be mechanistically and functionally understood.
Somatic methylation across genomic features
The majority of cell types over the mammalian life course maintain 
a consistent bimodal methylation pattern that is heavily dictated by 
sequence context. We refer to this state as the ‘somatic landscape’ 
because it emerges during embryo implantation and represents a 
shared signature across downstream cell and tissue types3,7 (Fig. 1a). 
In this context, the DNA methylation status predominantly depends 
on the local density of CpG dinucleotides, the preferred substrate of 
DNA methyltransferases (DNMTs). The de novo enzymes DNMT3A and 
DNMT3B can modify both unmethylated and hemi-methylated CpG

9
Review article
unmethylated CG-rich DNA3,4. These regulatory complexes mechanisti-
cally counteract DNMT3 activity, most prominently through antago-
nistic histone H3 methylated at K4 (H3K4me). Furthermore, nascent 
RNA transcripts can base-pair with genomic DNA to form R-loops, which 
further destabilize DNMT-associated complexes47.
Developmental gene promoters frequently reside within larger 
GC-rich and CGI-rich territories termed DNA methylation valleys 
(DMVs) or canyons48,49 (Fig. 1c). Within native tissues and cell types, 
these multi-kilobase blocks remain largely methylation-free and 
are instead repressed as facultative heterochromatin by high levels 
of H3 lysine 27 trimethylation (H3K27me3), which is deposited by 
Polycomb repressive complex 2 (PRC2)48–50. DMVs overlap a distinct 
fraction of developmental genes, which display broad H3K27me3 
and promoter H3K4me3, so-called ‘bivalent domains’ that enable 
progenitor cells to either activate or inactivate relevant differentiation 
programmes. Although the full regulatory meaning of DMVs remains 
incompletely understood, they are likely to support context-specific 
gene induction. DMV-regulated genes are often genomically isolated 
into discrete topologically associated domains (TADs), either as single 
genes or in co-regulated clusters such as the Hox loci, which contain 
numerous cell-state-specific distal cis-regulatory elements51–53. As 
such, these methylation-free territories may represent an expanded 
interface to facilitate enhancer–promoter interactions during devel-
opmental transitions51. Conversely, PRC proteins and their associated 
chromatin tend to form higher-order condensates, which may benefit 
from the more extensive tracks of GC-rich DNA found in DMVs to 
protect these features from more terminal DNA methylation-based 
silencing54–57.
Although they tend to be maintained in a constitutively unmeth-
ylated state in the absence of transcriptional induction, DMVs seem 
to be highly sensitive to epigenetic perturbation58–61. Members of the 
ten–eleven translocation (TET) methylcytosine dioxygenase family 
co-localize with PRC1 and PRC2, and the genes that encode them are 
frequently mutated in numerous haematopoietic malignancies62. 
TETs enzymatically function to oxidize 5-methylcytosine (5mC) to 
5-hydroxymethylcytosine (5hmC), as well as downstream substrates 
(formylcytosine and carboxycytosine), but the overall fraction of 
methylated cytosines that exist in these alternative forms is generally 
quite low and largely localized to enhancer elements60,62,63. Nonethe-
less, systematic deletion of all three TET enzymes in mouse and human 
ESCs triggers a clear increase in DMV methylation, suggesting they also 
contribute to maintain these regions in an unmethylated state58–60. 
Alongside interaction partners such as QSER1, TETs are likely targeted 
to DMVs through their CXXC domains, providing a CpG sequence-based 
mechanism for recruitment61.
More paradoxically, numerous mutations in the gene encoding 
the de novo methyltransferase enzyme DNMT3A are associated with 
elevated DMV methylation across distinct congenital growth disor-
ders64,65. The phenotypes associated with DNMT3A mutations can be 
diverse, including overgrowth phenotypes in Tatton–Brown–Rahman 
syndrome or dwarfism in Heyn–Sproul–Jackson syndrome. 
The latter syndrome is caused by mutations that functionally alter the 
proline–tryptophan–tryptophan–proline (PWWP) domain of DNMT3A 
and also lead to DMV hypermethylation in mouse models64,65. Notably, 
these molecular alterations resemble a failure to restrict DNMT3A to 
the DMV periphery that effectively blurs the boundary between methyl-
ated and unmethylated regions49,66,67. PRC2 and DNMT3s also seem to 
biochemically interact, suggesting more intricate forms of regulation 
that may change with the developmental or disease context2,68,69.
Actively engaged enhancer elements
In somatic cells, changes in DNA methylation typically reflect active 
transcription factor binding to CpG-poor distal enhancers, which tend 
to equilibrate to intermediate levels and exhibit low, TET-dependent 
enrichment for 5hmC compared with the genomic background58,70–72. 
The presence of both forms of methylation within these regions, as 
well as within DMVs, indicates a substantial degree of DNMT-mediated 
and TET-mediated turnover62,73. For example, conditional knockout of 
TET2 activity within the haematopoietic lineage of mice skews the DNA 
methylation status of distal enhancers towards higher levels of 5mC 
and supports an acute myeloid leukaemia (AML)-like phenotype74. The 
extent of this interplay between DNMT3s and TETs may also be highly 
context-dependent. For instance, both mouse and human ESCs main-
tain high methylation levels at thousands of cis-regulatory elements 
with putative somatic functions via persistent DNMT3A and DNMT3B 
recruitment, and genetically disrupting these enzymes leads to a rapid 
and focused drop in methylation60,63. Despite the clear evidence that 
TETs support enhancer DNA demethylation, investigations into the 
effects of pioneer factor binding have shown that erasure can depend 
on replication-coupled dilution rather than the catalytic removal of 
modified bases75. Taken together, the continuous recruitment of coun-
teracting enzymes at cell state-specific enhancers seems to signify one 
aspect of functional potential: simultaneously reinforcing cellular 
identity while maintaining the opportunity for rapid changes in gene 
regulation.
In sum, the somatic DNA methylation landscape is largely static 
across the majority of mammalian development, but the predomi-
nantly hypermethylated genome is amenable to cell type-specific, 
TET-assisted reprogramming of distal areas downstream of transcrip-
tion factor binding76. Within this global framework, CGIs and DMVs act 
as constitutively protected hubs for essential regulatory machinery, 
including components of active or inducible chromatin states.
Controlling DNMT activity and recruitment
The division of labour within the DNMT family between maintenance 
(DNMT1) and de novo (DNMT3 family) methylation activity was initially 
described in the 1990s, including transgenic studies that established 
each enzyme’s essential role in animal development4. Discoveries of 
new enzymes and developmentally regulated expression and splic-
ing patterns of the genes encoding DNMT family members, alongside 
advanced experimental methods for manipulating DNA methylation 
patterns (Box 1), have collectively deepened our understanding of 
how this epigenetic modification contributes to development and 
disease77,78. Here, we focus on how DNMTs support specific forms of 
molecular regulation.
Interactions with the histone code
Outside of developmental contexts, the prevailing de novo methyl-
transferase in adult cells is DNMT3A1; by contrast, DNMT3B largely 
switches to a catalytically inactive form, DNMT3B31–4. Continued 
expression of de novo methyltransferases into adulthood is a means 
of proofreading errors in DNMT1-based maintenance and supporting 
differentiation from adult stem cells. Despite sharing a highly con-
served carboxy-terminal catalytic domain, DNMT family members have 
undergone substantial evolutionary innovation within their amino-
terminal domains that enable enzyme-specific interactions with addi-
tional features of the histone code4,79–83 (Fig. 2A,B). For example, the 
Atrx–Dnmt3a–Dnmt3l (ADD) domain acts as an allosteric inhibitor: 
it blocks de novo methyltransferase activity when these enzymes

are complexed with H3K4-methylated nucleosomes and supports 
docking to adjacent nucleosomes when they are not79 (Fig. 2C,D). 
The PWWP domain acts as an epigenetic reader that recruits DNMT3 
enzymes to H3K36-methylated chromatin, a modification deposited 
by SETD2 and canonically associated with transcriptional elongation26. 
Reintroduction of DNMT3A and DNMT3B into Dnmt1–Dnmt3a–
Dnmt3b triple genetic knockout mouse ESCs confirmed the strong 
relationship between H3K36me3 in gene bodies and PWWP-based 
DNMT3 recruitment, a mechanism that seems to stabilize transcrip-
tional fidelity and splicing84,85 (Fig. 2C). Beyond this basic mechanism, 
multiple studies have noted that DNMT3A and DNMT3B have subtly 
different affinities for H3 dimethylated at K36 (H3K36me2) versus 
H3K36me3. Emerging evidence indicates that an H3K36me2–DNMT3A 
axis functions to support intergenic methylation and depends primar-
ily on the H3K36 methyltransferase NSD1 (refs. 64,86–89). Notably, 
disrupting aspects of this interaction triggers de novo methylation 
of DMV-embedded developmental gene promoters, suggesting that 
aspects of PWWP binding act to sequester enzymes from essential 
regulatory elements64,86–89. Deeper dissection of these interactions 
identified an N-terminal intrinsically disordered domain within 
DNMT3A1 that interfaces with PRC1-deposited H2AK119 ubiquitina-
tion, another key component of bivalent chromatin within DMVs, to 
act as an additional layer of cross-talk between otherwise distinct 
epigenetic regulators68,89 (Fig. 2D). Precisely how these interactions 
balance hypermethylation of gene bodies with local protection of 
developmental gene promoters remains unresolved, but they highlight 
a critical need to continue investigating how gene regulatory functions 
relate to more global aspects of genome biology.
Increased DNMT3A activity in maturing neurons
DNMT3A-based methylation of intergenic DNA is particularly notable 
during postnatal brain development, during which non-CpG dinucleo-
tide methylation levels continue to rise within postmitotic neurons90–92. 
Although increased non-CpG methylation also occurs in maturing 
oocytes and in ESCs91,93, the striking rise in non-CpG methylation dur-
ing postnatal ‘critical periods’ of enhanced neural plasticity, entrain-
ment and maturation has led to substantial interest in its functional 
role90–92,94,95. Non-CpG methylation signatures are also an effective 
means of stratifying distinct neural cell types from single-cell meth-
ylation data (Box 2), presumably because methylation is deposited 
after initial neuronal differentiation during environmentally induced 
phases of postnatal maturation96–98. Non-CpG methylation tends to 
accrue at H3K36me regions, including at gene bodies and intergenic 
regions, but the individual non-CpG cytosines that are methylated vary 
within populations of cells86,92,95,99,100. As such, this wave of additional 
‘salt and pepper’ methylation may act to reinforce regulatory signals 
over key genomic territories during periods of early neuronal activity.
The increase in non-CpG methylation in maturing neurons is inte-
grated by the MBD-containing protein MeCP2, an essential interface 
to the NCOR1/2 deacetylase complex101. Mutations in the gene encod-
ing MeCP2 have long been associated with the neurodevelopmental 
disorder Rett syndrome, the postnatal progression of which mirrors 
the rising wave of non-CpG methylation, and this neuron-specific 
form of regulation seems to be conserved within vertebrates101–104. 
Unlike other MBD-containing proteins, MeCP2 exhibits an expanded 
affinity for 5mC sequences outside the CpG context, and swapping 
the endogenous MBD of MeCP2 with that of the more CpG-restricted 
MBD2 triggers molecular and phenotypic responses that resemble 
the disease100,102,105. Although a complete understanding of the physi-
ological role for this postnatal wave of de novo methyltransferase 
activity is still lacking, future work that explores the role of MeCP2 
as a stabilizing epigenomic factor will continue to yield molecular, 
developmental and therapeutic insights into how these signatures 
support the vertebrate brain.
Strategies for retrotransposon control
In mammals, DNA methylation has long been associated with control 
of parasitic genomic elements, primarily long interspersed nuclear 
elements (LINEs) and long terminal repeat (LTR)-containing endogenous 
retroviruses (ERVs). In addition to their mutagenic potential, spurious 
transcriptional activation of these elements also has consequences 
for the cell; DNMT inhibitor treatment leads to the production of 
long intergenic RNAs, the formation of double-stranded RNA species 
and the activation of innate immune checkpoints (see ‘Therapeutic

read sequencing (Box 2) has expanded our understanding of the role 
of DNA methylation in host genome surveillance and suppression, and 
has also uncovered novel de novo functions for DNMT1.
KRAB zinc finger proteins. Sequence-based suppression of retrotrans-
posons is predominantly carried out via the Krüppel-associated box 
domain zinc finger proteins (KRAB-ZFPs), a large DNA binding protein 
family that is characterized by a common N-terminal KRAB domain, 
which recruits the key integrator protein TRIM28 (also known as KAP1) 
and the H3K9 methyltransferase SETDB1 to trigger heterochromatin 
formation106,107 (Fig. 2E). Additional factors including histone chaper-
ones such as DAXX that deposit the replication-independent histone 
variant H3.3, chromatin remodelling machinery such as the nucleo-
some remodelling and deacetylase (NuRD) complex, and the DNMT3s 
further consolidate this repression4,106,107. In these contexts, DNA 
methylation seems to be well downstream of the primary, sequence-
based repressor and functions as part of an extended histone code 
that centres on H3K9me3 (refs. 4,106,107). However, many KRAB-ZFPs 
exhibit comparatively restricted expression profiles, including early 
developmental windows when retrotransposons are also expressed; 
DNA methylation may therefore serve to maintain retrotransposon 
suppression throughout the majority of an organism’s lifespan107,108.
The hundreds of KRAB-ZFPs that are encoded within mammalian 
genomes represent a snapshot of continuous evolutionary innova-
tion against a diverse spectrum of mutagenic genomic parasites, 
and are frequently co-opted to support other roles such as the rein-
forcement of methylated imprinting control regions106,107. However, 
a detailed investigation of individual KRAB-ZFP–retrotransposon 
pairs across mammalian phylogenies emphasizes that host adapta-
tion and retroelement counteradaptation occurs across evolutionary, 
and not organismal, timescales109. As such, mammalian cells need to 
deploy multiple additional strategies to recognize and suppress more 
immediate genomic threats.
RNA-based silencing. Alternative mechanisms for retrotransposon 
silencing operate via RNA sensing, particularly through evolutionarily 
ancient germ line-based suppressive machinery that produce distinct 
classes of piwi-interacting RNAs (piRNAs)110,111 (Fig. 2F). Although these 
piRNAs also function in species lacking DNA methylation, such as Dros-
ophila melanogaster and Caenorhabditis elegans, the mammalian Piwi 
orthologue Miwi2/Piwil4 binds nascent retrotransposon transcripts 
and directly recruits de novo DNMTs in complex with the non-catalytic 
co-factor DNMT3L (ref. 2). This initial wave of silencing occurs along-
side global genome re-methylation during late fetal development, and 
mutation of genes encoding Miwi2 or other interaction partners such 
as Spocd1 and Tex15 in mouse prevents de novo methylation at LINE1 
and some ERV regulatory sequences112,113.
Numerous key findings suggest that retrotransposon suppres-
sion within the male germ line depends more directly on de novo DNA 
methylation, particularly the discovery of DNMT3C in muroid rodents. 
Initially annotated as a truncated tandemly duplicated Dnmt3b 
pseudogene — one that preserves the N-terminal ADD domain of 
DNMT3B but lacks its PWWP domain — DNMT3C exhibits male germ 
line-specific expression during late fetal and early postnatal develop-
ment77,78,114. Mutant animals phenocopy many aspects of Miwi2 and 
Dnmt3l disruption, including LINE1 expression, loss of promoter meth-
ylation and early meiotic arrest during sexual maturation, suggesting 
a specific interaction that directly bridges active transcription to the 
targeted assembly of repressive chromatin77,78,114. However, how piRNA-
based suppressive machinery circumvents the intrinsically inhibitory 
nature of active chromatin modifications on DNMT3s remains a major 
unresolved question.
In mammals, RNA-mediated de novo methylation is predomi-
nantly restricted to the male germ line, but other complexes have 
recently been characterized with analogous genomic surveillance 
Box 1 | Manipulating DNA methylation
 
DNA methyltransferases (DNMTs) and the opposing ten–eleven 
translocation (TET) enzymes can be directed to specific parts 
of the genome, including repetitive elements, centromeric regions, 
transcribed gene bodies or distinct types of enhancers. However, 
the catalytic pocket of the enzymes themselves lack detailed 
target specificity beyond subtle variation in sequence preference 
around the CpG dyad4,315. As such, DNMT recruitment is largely 
directed to these genomic features by additional factors4,315. 
To understand context-dependent functions and local genome 
regulation, it is crucial to manipulate DNA methylation and other 
epigenetic modifications in a more controlled fashion beyond 
genetic disruption, ectopic expression or the use of chemical 
inhibitors316–319. DNMT inhibitors are widely used and include 
5-azacytidine (5-aza) and similar analogues that trap catalytically 
engaged DNMTs to DNA, as well as the specific GlaxoSmithKline 
DNMT1 inhibitor (GSK3685032) that reversibly blocks catalytic 
engagement with the target cytosine319. A major step forward 
was achieved when it was recognized that nuclease-deficient 
(dead) dCas9 could be tethered to any enzymatic activity and 
hence serve as a vehicle for targeted recruitment through single 
guide RNAs320. Early attempts using zinc fingers and TAL effectors 
indicated the power of such targeting but were not versatile 
enough to become a routine tool321–323. Not surprisingly, some of 
the first reports on dCas9 fusions were focused on DNMTs and 
TETs324,325. Coupling the catalytic domain of the DNMT3s (‘Cat3’) 
or other repressors to dCas9 leads to efficient de novo methylation 
in various contexts326,327. However, in general it has been difficult to 
efficiently reprogramme chromatin states associated with active 
transcription and, as such, the effects of epigenetic editing have 
often been transient and, typically, not maintained upon withdrawal 
of the dCas9–Cat3 fusion328–331. Ongoing efforts aim to improve the 
catalytic activity or amplify the recruitment signal using epitope 
handles332, for example by fusing additional co-factors, such as 
Krüppel-associated box (KRAB) domains, DNMT3L or MeCP2, or 
via additional combinatorial tools333–340. Many of these approaches 
have been additionally translated to mouse models to enable in vivo 
manipulations341,342. Similarly, the TET enzymes have been used for 
targeted DNA methylation removal, as have many other chromatin 
regulators322. Alternative strategies for dynamic gene control at 
the protein level include the plant hormone-based auxin-inducible 
degron (AID)343 and cell-permeable heterobifunctional degrader 
(dTAG/FKBP) systems344, which induce ubiquitin-directed protein 
degradation. These systems readily phenocopy genetic disruption, 
act within hours and tend to be rapidly and fully reversible. 
As these technologies are further improved and become more 
widely applied, we expect to see a more nuanced picture of various 
regulators and their dynamic context-dependent functions.

De novo functions for DNMT1. In mice, detailed comparison of the 
roles of DNMT1 and DNMT3A/B in global DNA methylation identified 
a non-canonical role for DNMT1 in the de novo methylation of select 
retrotransposons, in particular ERV-K intracisternal A-type particles 
(IAPs)116. Although IAPs are rodent-specific, DNMT1 de novo activity 
appears to involve multiple core components of epigenetic repression 
and maintenance, including components of the KRAB-ZFP pathway and 
UHRF1 (refs. 116,117). How DNMT1 circumvents its need for hemi-
methylated substrates has not been resolved, and neither is it clear 
how findings in mouse might translate to species such as human that 
are less influenced by recent ERV activity. Nonetheless, these new find-
ings highlight the diversity of mechanisms through which DNMTs are 
utilized to alter genomic expression.
Centromeric and pericentromeric chromatin
The chromosomal regions that define the mammalian centromere 
comprise extensive, highly repetitive and rapidly evolving arrays 
that can collectively span megabases and exhibit their own unique 
configuration of epigenetic suppressors118,119. Mutations specifi-
cally affecting DNMT3B are found in patients of the rare, autosomal 
recessive immunodeficiency, centromeric region instability and 
facial anomalies (ICF) syndrome, as are mutations affecting other 
regulators associated with pericentromeric heterochromatin120. 
Fig. 2 | Major hubs of DNMT-supported genome regulation. Mammalian 
DNA methyltransferases (DNMTs) share a deeply conserved carboxy-terminal 
region that contains the cytosine-methylating catalytic domain, but the rest 
of the protein varies among the enzymes and isoforms. Aa, There are at least 
three DNMT1 isoforms, in all of which a flexible linker separates the catalytic 
domain from: two bromo-adjacent homology (BAH) domains; an auto-
inhibitory CXXC domain; a replication foci targeting sequence (RFTS); and 
amino-terminal peptide binding domains (PBDs) that interact with PCNA (a DNA 
polymerase co-factor) and other proteins that recruit DNMT1 to the replication 
fork. Ab, The major function of DNMT1 is to maintain DNA methylation after 
replication by adding a methyl group to the cytosine on the nascent strand. 
DNMT1 activity is therefore localized by interactions with PCNA and allosterically 
activated by interactions with the ubiquitin ligase UHRF1 and its ubiquitinylated 
products. Despite direct recruitment to the replication fork, maintenance 
methylation is not complete until several hours following DNA replication. 
Ac, De novo activity for DNMT1 has also been described for select endogenous 
retroviruses (ERVs), in particular intracisternal A-type particles (IAPs), which 
appears to involve many components used for replication (such as UHRF1) 
as well as factors associated with retrotransposon silencing (such as TRIM28, 
histone deacetylases (HDACs), SETDB1 and, possibly, Krüppel-associated box

novo methylation. All DNMT3s contain an Atrx–Dnmt3a–Dnmt3l (ADD) domain, 
which is involved in their allosteric inhibition in the absence of an unmodified

tryptophan–tryptophan–proline (PWWP) domain, which recognizes H3K36 
dimethylation (H3K36me2) and trimethylation (H3K36me3). Ba, DNMT3A is 
the major de novo DNMT in somatic cells and has two major isoforms, DNMT3A1 
and DNMT3A2, which are distinguished by the presence or absence of an 
intrinsically disordered region (IDR) near the N terminus. Although IDRs have 
been characterized within DNMT1 and DNMT3B as well, the DNMT3A1 IDR 
has been shown to interact with DNA methylation valley (DMV)-associated 
modifications. Bb, DNMT3B is the major de novo DNMT involved in global

reported isoforms. The indented oval indicates an inactive catalytic domain 
generated via alternate splicing that excises two exons and blocks its function

DNMT3C, which is specific to muroid rodents, and the catalytically inactive 
paralogue DNMT3L. Hominid primates may have evolved similar functions 
to DNMT3C within the N-terminal portion of DNMT3A (ref. 80) C, Key factors 
and interactions involved in the epigenetic regulation of promoter-gene DNA 
methylation boundaries. CFP1 binds CpG islands (CGIs) and recruits SET1 to 
methylate H3K4 around the promoter, which blocks DNMT3-based methylation 
via the ADD domain. H3K36me3 is catalysed by SETD2, which is recruited to the 
gene body via interactions with phosphorylated Ser-2 in the C-terminal domain

of DNMT3A1 and Polycomb repressive complex 1 (PRC1)-deposited H2AK119

but mutations within the PWWP domain of DNMT3A1 lead to aberrant de novo 
methylation within the DMV. H3K27me3 is generally mutually exclusive to

DNMT3s to methylate and suppress transposon and/or transgene-associated 
repetitive DNA, including through recruitment of sequence-specific KRAB-
ZFPs (top) and interactions with the human silencing hub (HUSH) repressor

The effects of loss of Y chromosome  
on male health
Bozena Bruhn-Olszewska 
  1, Ellen Markljung 
  1, Edyta Rychlicka-Buniowska 
  2, Daniil Sarkisyan 
  1, 
Natalia Filipowicz 
  2 & Jan P. Dumanski 
  1,2 
Abstract
Loss of Y chromosome (LOY) is the most commonly occurring post-
zygotic (somatic) mutation in male individuals. The past decade of 
research suggests that LOY has important effects in shaping the activity 
of the immune system, and multiple studies have shown the effects of 
LOY on a range of diseases, including cancer, neurodegeneration, 
cardiovascular disease and acute infection. Epidemiological findings 
have been corroborated by functional analyses providing insights 
into the mechanisms by which LOY modulates the immune system; 
in particular, a causal role for LOY in cardiac fibrosis, bladder cancer 
and Alzheimer disease has been indicated. These insights show that 
LOY is a highly dynamic mutation (such that LOY clones expand and 
contract with time) and has pleiotropic, cell-type-specific effects. 
Here, we review the status of the field and highlight the potential of LOY 
as a biomarker and target of new therapeutics that aim to counteract its 
negative effects on the immune system.

Since the first report of the association between LOY and cancer

Here, we review a decade of successful research documenting the 
effects of LOY in somatic cells on the health of male individuals, with 
an emphasis on the genetic and environmental factors that predispose 
to LOY together with the pleiotropic and cell-specific effects of this 
post-zygotic mutation. We highlight findings that indicate causal 
effects of LOY on increased mortality through disturbed homeostasis of 
the immune system in male individuals in the context of cardiac fibrosis 
(as a component of non-ischaemic heart failure), bladder cancer and 
Alzheimer disease. We also summarize our growing understanding 
Introduction
First reports of the loss of Y chromosome (LOY) in normal cells from 
human male individuals were published more than 60 years ago1,2; 
these cells were identified, using cytogenetic analysis, as hypodip-
loid cells with loss of a chromosome from the S1 group. In 1971, LOY in 
normal haematopoietic cells was confirmed using the chromosome 
banding technique3,4. LOY is a commonly occurring post-zygotic 
(somatic) aneuploidy that is often described together with other mosaic 
mutations such as clonal haematopoiesis, clonal haematopoiesis of 
indeterminate potential (CHIP) and autosomal mosaic chromosomal 
alterations. However, LOY is distinguished from other mosaic muta-
tions and germline mutations by its very high frequency and its wide-
spread, well-established effects at the cellular level as well as for the 
whole organism. LOY has only been described as a mosaic event and 
it cannot exist in an inherited form that affects all somatic cells. This 
is well illustrated by findings from Turner syndrome (45,X) — a human 
fetus composed only of 45,X cells is not viable5 such that live-born 45,X 
female individuals always have a rescue line, predominantly with a 
46,XX karyotype but also sometimes with 46,X,del(Xq), 47,XXX, 46,XY 
or 47,XYY5.
LOY received little research attention before 2014, mainly owing to 
the widespread, albeit incorrect, opinion that the Y chromosome makes 
little (if any) contribution to phenotype beyond its roles in sex differ-
entiation and normal sperm production. This notion was reinforced 
by cytogenetic studies of small cohorts that suggested LOY was not an 
important factor for haematological malignancies6–8, although later 
studies showed that LOY is a frequent aberration in bone marrow cells 
and is associated with myelodysplastic syndrome9,10.
Three papers in 2014–2016 suggested that LOY is an impor-
tant factor associated with all-cause mortality, increased risk for 
Box 1 | Terminology for and measurement of LOY
 
The concept of loss of Y chromosome (LOY) was first introduced  
in the 1970s3,4. Since then, numerous terms and abbreviations have 
been used to describe LOY, which calls for a consensus to be reached 
as to the most appropriate nomenclature.
	
• LOY (or LoY) was found to be age related in the haematopoietic cells 
of several population-based Swedish cohorts11–13,15, and this 
nomenclature was subsequently used in various papers28,38,55, 
synonymized as Y chromosome loss and loss-of-Y156.
	
• Mosaic LOY (mLOY) refers to LOY in a subset of cells associated 
with ageing14. It is sometimes used interchangeably with LOY48,82.
	
• Extreme downregulation of Y chromosome (EDY) gene expression 
was described as a male-specific gene expression signature of 
LOY in cancer susceptibility and a possible biomarker in Alzheimer 
disease108,125.
	
• Relative LOY (rLOY) is used to describe when all the segments 
of the Y chromosome are lost but the total copy number is ≥1 
(for example, after genome doubling)102.
	
• Functional LOY (fLOY) was used to describe expression-based loss 
calls in RNA-sequencing data, showing that gene expression can 
reliably detect LOY102.
	
• Retention of Y chromosome (ROY) is a term used to describe 
primary tumours; retention of Y chromosome tumours were 
shown to have fewer genomic alterations than LOY tumours38.
	
• Mosaic X chromosome monosomy (XCM) is usually used to 
describe complete or partial absence of the X chromosome in 
female individuals but can also occur in male individuals as a 
consequence of somatic LOY134.
We believe that there is no need to emphasize in the terminology 
used that LOY is a mosaic alteration. Our opinion is that the shortest 
and originally published LOY terminology is optimal11, and this is the 
terminology used throughout this Review when referring to mosaic 
LOY in somatic cells. Retention of Y chromosome is an appropriate 
counterpart to describe cells unaffected by LOY.
In addition, there are several algorithms to measure LOY, which are 
occasionally used interchangeably:
	
• mLRRY (or mLRR-Y) refers to the median (or mean) log R ratio of 
probes located in the male-specific part of Y chromosome from 
intensity data generated by single nucleotide polymorphism 
arrays11,58,70.
	
• PAR-LOY is a long-range phasing approach for the detection of 
LOY that uses the pseudoautosomal region (PAR), shared by the 
X and Y chromosomes; this approach is useful for larger cohort 
sizes28.
	
• PAR-LOYq combines PAR-LOY and mLRRY with AF-LOY (which 
measures the estimated fraction of cells with LOY)147.

322

of the molecular mechanisms behind LOY. Moreover, the recent 
telomere-to-telomere sequencing of the Y chromosome has revived 
the long-neglected field of Y chromosome genomics and opens the 
door to in-depth studies of individual Y chromosomes and their role in 
biology and disease predisposition in male individuals (Box 2).
Predisposition to and prevalence of LOY
Age is the most significant factor associated with LOY, reflecting 
increased length of time and the greater number of possible cell divi-
sions for this mutation to occur. Although ageing-related chromosome 
loss can affect all chromosomes, including the X chromosome (Box 3), 
the Y chromosome is more prone to be lost than other chromosomes, 
possibly related to specific features of its centromere (discussed later). 
A positive correlation between age and the percentage of LOY in blood 
has been confirmed in all studies addressing this issue11,12,14,28–30. The 
frequency of LOY in male individuals above 40 years increases expo-
nentially with age28. Although data on the occurrence of LOY in male 
individuals under 40 years of age are sparse, recent studies show that 
LOY can be detected in individuals as young as 19–29 years31,32, which 
will provide a basis for future studies of the potential detrimental effects 
of LOY in younger male individuals. LOY associated with age has also 
been reported in other species (Box 4). Thus, age is the major factor 
associated with LOY (Fig. 1).
Environmental factors promoting LOY
The second most important factor associated with LOY is smoking12,14,29,33. 
For example, in our study of 6,014 male individuals, current smokers had 
a greater percentage of haematopoietic LOY than past smokers 
and non-smokers12. Smoking cessation is positively associated with 
improved overall health (for various reasons)34 and, interestingly, is also 
associated with a gradual decline in the occurrence of haematopoietic 
LOY14. The exact molecular mechanisms and order of events by which 
smoking leads to LOY are unknown. However, one can speculate that 
increased mutational burden and smoking-induced DNA methylation 
changes in blood35, subsequent hypomethylation-induced genomic 
instability of repetitive sequences36 and micronuclei formation37 are 
components of a pathway leading to LOY. Furthermore, an analysis of 
13 cancer types from The Cancer Genome Atlas dataset found that the 
smoking mutational signature was detected in LOY-enriched tumours 
of head and neck cancer and lung cancer38. Tumours with this signature 
also had a large number of mutations in TP53, which could link smoking, 
loss of genome stability and the prevalence of LOY in tumours. Given 
the above, it is tempting to suggest that LOY could be considered as one 
of the first indications of a chromosomal genomic instability.
Exposure to toxic compounds, such as arsenic, glyphosate, air pol-
lutants or polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, is positively correlated 
with haematopoietic LOY39–42. Again, the molecular mechanisms are 
unknown but might be associated with increased mutational burden 
caused by these factors. Indeed, glyphosate (a broad-spectrum herbi-
cide) has been reported to have cytotoxic, genotoxic and mutagenic 
effects on human peripheral blood mononuclear cells43, which are 
also often affected by LOY44,45. A positive association has been shown 
between haematopoietic LOY and lifelong exposure to glyphosate40, 
which is considered a potential human carcinogen46. However, these 
results come from a single study involving a relatively small cohort and 
need to be investigated further. An increased percentage of LOY was 
also detected in the peripheral blood of male individuals exposed to 
arsenic, a well-known carcinogen that has deleterious effects on human 
health and can exist in multiple forms, including dust in polluted air39,47.
Genetic factors promoting LOY
Genome-wide association studies have revealed the existence of genetic 
determinants of LOY with an estimated heritability of 31.7%, identify-
ing 156 genomic loci that contribute to LOY28. This underscores that 
non-genetic factors make a major contribution to LOY. The first LOY 
susceptibility locus (rs2887399) to be identified is localized near the 
Box 2 | Complete telomere-to-telomere sequence of Y chromosome
 
Sequencing and other studies of the Y chromosome have lagged 
those of the rest of the genome. This partially reflects the low level 
of research interest in this chromosome but also the methodological 
challenges associated with sequence assembly of the Y chromosome, 
which has large heterochromatic regions and a large number of 
repetitive and palindromic sequences. Two landmark papers57,157, 
published in 2023, finally resolved the complete telomere-to-
telomere assembly for Y chromosome (T2T-Y) with a non-redundant 
call set of 53,744 single nucleotide variants, 23,459 indels and 876 
structural variations, showing tenfold increased recombination rate  
in pseudoautosomal region 1 (PAR1) in male individuals compared 
with female individuals. The Genome Reference Consortium  
Human Build 38, Y chromosome (GRCh38-Y) reference sequence 
(RefSeq v.110) annotates 4 microRNAs, 309 circular RNAs and  
nearly 600 long non-coding RNAs (ncRNAs) on the Y chromosome. 
Disease and regulatory associations are well established for some  
of these ncRNAs158. Compared with the GRCh38-Y reference  
sequence, the T2T-Y sequence has 17.7% more genes157, including  
60% more protein-coding genes. For XY-bearing samples, T2T-Y  
reduces false-positive variant calls, leading to a higher number  
of mapped reads, properly paired reads and a lower proportion of 
mismatched bases. After resolving the challenges in computational 
analysis and interpretation of the T2T-Y assembly159, it is expected 
that it will be of great use for the analysis of ncRNAs in cells with loss 
of Y chromosome or retention of Y chromosome.
T2T-Y annotates 693 genes, of which 110 genes are protein 
coding. In general, these protein-coding genes can be divided into 
four broad functional categories: (1) sex determination, fertility and 
other functions; (2) transcription, translation, and epigenetic and 
post-translational modifications; (3) cell differentiation, migration, 
proliferation and apoptosis; and (4) immune response and immune cell 
signalling44. Although the expression of some Y chromosome-encoded 
genes, particularly those involved in sex determination and fertility 
(for example, ampliconic gene families such as TSPY, DAZ or RBMY), 
is testis specific or testis biased, there are many Y-linked genes that 
are widely expressed in various human tissues. These genes encode 
proteins that carry out global regulatory functions and some of them 
are considered to be crucial for male viability. Examples of such global 
regulators are ZFY (transcription factor), KDM5D and UTY (histone 
lysine demethylases), DDX3Y and EIF1AY (translation initiation factors), 
USP9Y (deubiquitinase), RPS4Y1 (ribosomal protein) and TBL1Y 
(probable component of transcription corepressor complexes)25.

TCL1A gene14. Subsequent analyses replicated this result and identified 
an additional 155 LOY-associated genomic variants28,33. A major fraction 
of the detected loci maps near genes whose products are involved in cell 
cycle regulation, including DNA synthesis and DNA damage processes, 
as well as cancer susceptibility and tumour growth factors.
Of particular interest is the relationship between LOY and the hae-
matopoietic cell lineage as LOY was shown to associate with a range of 
variants overlapping with enhancer marks that are characteristic of hae-
matopoietic stem cells (HSCs)48. The landscape of LOY-predisposing 
genetic loci was expanded by findings from a study of 222,835 UK 
Biobank participants, which identified somatic mutations in TET2, 
TP53 and CBL as being enriched in LOY cases49. All three genes encode 
proteins that, in addition to their canonical functions, are crucial for 
myeloid cell and lymphoid cell development, regulatory T (Treg) cell 
stability, clonal haematopoiesis, modulation of inflammation and 
immune cell activities50–54. Moreover, a study reporting a polygenic 
risk score for LOY prevalence, calculated using 156 genomic vari-
ants, revealed that this approach is a better predictor of LOY than the 
analysis of individual loci55. Furthermore, the prediction of LOY was 
superior when the polygenic risk score was combined with known 
LOY-associated factors such as age and smoking. In summary, LOY is a 
complex phenomenon that, currently, can only partially be explained 
by genetic determinants.
Prevalence of LOY in normal tissues
LOY in leukocytes is the most frequently occurring post-zygotic 
mutation44,56. De novo assemblies of 43 Y chromosomes57 show con-
siderable diversity in size, ranging from 45.2 Mb to 84.9 Mb (Box 2); 
therefore, we can calculate that LOY results in a loss of between 1.5% 
and 2.7% of the total human genome. When analysing bulk DNA, hae-
matopoietic LOY occurs in approximately 20% of male individuals 
(age range 40–70 years) in the UK BioBank study (using the long-range 
phasing approach with a clonal fraction down to 1% of cells with LOY)28. 
Roughly 5% of male individuals under 50 years of age have detectable 
LOY, whereas it affects approximately 40% of male individuals over 
65 years. By the age of 93, 57% of male individuals had LOY at a conserva-
tive threshold of ≥10% of blood cells15. Another study of 29 ageing male 
individuals (median age 80 years, range 64–94 years) showed that LOY 
could be detected in every individual at the single-cell level44.
LOY has also been detected in tissues other than blood, such 
as buccal cells and atherosclerotic plaques, albeit at a much lower 
frequency15,58. A study carried out on a Swedish cohort showed that 
the buccal mucosa (which is essentially free from circulating leuko-
cytes) has a markedly lower percentage of LOY than blood from the 
same individual15. Concordant conclusions were drawn from studies 
in patients after carotid endarterectomy, in which about 3% of patients 
had LOY in atherosclerotic plaques whereas about 16% of patients had 
detectable LOY in blood58. The analysis of forensic material, such as 
blood, saliva and semen, suggests that the level of LOY can be used to 
predict age32 and confirms that LOY is most prevalent in blood. This 
notion is also supported by single-cell and single-nuclei transcrip-
tomic analyses showing that brain-resident haematopoietic cells, 
known as microglia, have a higher percentage of LOY than all other 
brain cells59. LOY levels in microglia increased with age and were also 
higher in patients with Alzheimer disease compared with healthy 
donors, which suggests that there might be a link between LOY and 
brain pathology13,59. Furthermore, by studying LOY in non-cancerous 
tissue (adjacent to bladder cancer), it was shown that LOY occurs less 
frequently in normal urothelium than in blood samples and cancer 
tissue from the same individual60. Collectively, the data suggest that 
LOY is mainly present in actively proliferating cells, of which haema-
topoietic cells (immune cells in the blood and microglia) are prime 
examples. As such, there is a need to address the potential effects of 
LOY on other cell types with high turnover such as skin keratinocytes 
or intestinal epithelium.
Mechanisms of LOY
Cumulative evidence from genetic and cell biology studies sheds light 
on the potential mechanisms by which Y chromosome-deficient cells 
arise28,61 (Fig. 1). The most obvious hypothesis is that LOY originates 
from a mitotic error, ultimately leading to faulty chromosome segrega-
tion and aneuploidy. Mis-segregated chromosomes might be trapped 
in abnormal structures known as micronuclei, which can subsequently 
disintegrate, creating numerous microscopic fragments, or be excreted 
from the cell62. Micronucleus formation probably precedes LOY as the 
analysis of cultured lymphocytes from 53 male individuals showed a 
correlation coefficient of 0.71 (P < 0.005) between the frequency of 
Box 3 | Loss of the X chromosome
 
The mutation rates associated with the loss of sex chromosomes 
in blood exceed by 1,000-fold those of autosomal mosaic 
chromosomal alterations (mCAs). Loss of the Y chromosome 
(LOY) is more prevalent than loss of the X chromosome (LOX) but 
the latter has a higher overall mutation rate owing to different 
effects on cellular fitness, with the loss of active and inactive 
X chromosomes occurring at different rates160. Methylation analyses 
indicate that loss events mainly affect the inactive X chromosome161, 
contributing to its increased mutation rate162. Age-related LOX in 
female individuals is commonly observed in large population-based 
studies and is most common in blood and buccal cells161,163–165. 
The survey of nearly 200,000 male individuals in the UK Biobank 
showed no evidence of LOX, reflecting the deleterious effect of 
such an event on cell survival (clonal fitness) owing to the loss of key 
genes on the hemizygous X chromosome in male individuals166. 
In a cross-sectional study of nearly 500,000 cancer-free female 
individuals from the UK Biobank, those with haematopoietic LOX 
had increased levels of serum biomarkers (such as cholesterol, 
low-density lipoprotein, apolipoprotein B, triglycerides, C reactive 
protein and vitamin D) and decreased levels of insulin-like growth 
factor 1 (IGF1)72. A preprint study suggests that female individuals 
with haematopoietic LOX have an increased risk of myeloid 
and lymphoid leukaemias and pneumonia165. There are several 
studies on the co-occurrence of haematopoietic LOX with clonal 
haematopoiesis of indeterminate potential in female individuals, 
showing that individuals with higher cellular fractions of autosomal 
mCA events were more likely to have LOX, clonal haematopoiesis 
of indeterminate potential and myeloproliferative neoplasms95,96. 
The study of causal associations between smoking and mCAs 
showed that smoking is independently associated with any type 
of mCA: autosomal, LOY and LOX167. LOX has also been found 
outside the haematopoietic system: 14% of female tumours have 
LOX cells, with the highest frequency in chromophobe kidney 
cancer and uveal melanoma102 as well as occurring in renal cell 
carcinoma100, and LOX has been associated with increased rates 
of metastasis in patients with uveal melanoma102.

Y chromosome-positive micronuclei in cells and the frequency of their 
progeny having LOY. Additionally, in this study, the number of micronu-
clei per cell was proportional to the age of the donor63. Of note, specific 
features of the Y chromosome centromere, in particular having the 
shortest alpha-satellite sequence of all chromosomes and the absence 
of centromere protein B (CENP-B) and the CENP-B box, both of which 
have key roles in centromere function64,65, might affect its faulty segre-
gation and loss. Inactivation of the Y chromosome centromere has been 
observed to result in chromosome segregation errors, manifested by 
the formation of micronuclei and subsequent chromosome fragmenta-
tion and aneuploid progeny61,66. Indeed, greater fragmentation of the 
Y chromosome than of other chromosomes was shown to occur in an 
analysis of circulating DNA fragments from healthy male individu-
als, which may be related to the lower density of nucleosomes on the 
Y chromosome than on other chromosomes67. Furthermore, individuals 
with LOY have markedly shorter telomere lengths, which supports a 
micronuclei-based mechanism of LOY as chromosomes with shorter 
telomeres are more susceptible to being trapped in micronuclei62,68.
Consequences of LOY
The most obvious consequence of LOY is the loss of expression 
of Y chromosome-encoded genes (Box 2). However, LOY also has 
marked effects on the expression of autosomal genes in leukocytes 
via an unknown mechanism, which can directly affect their immune 
activities44. Another prominent effect of LOY identified in a recent 
preprint is the global hypomethylation of genes involved in leukocyte 
differentiation69. These consequences can result in dysregulated cell 
functions (see the section ‘LOY manifestations depend on cell type’). 
Interestingly, it has been reported that multipotent progenitor cells 
and HSCs were the main cell populations undergoing clonal expansion 
following LOY48. Moreover, FLI1 transcription factor-binding sites were 
shown to overlap markedly with regions enriched in LOY heritability. 
FLI1 is a key regulator of megakaryocyte differentiation and the overlap 
of its binding sites with LOY heritability loci implies a possible impact of 
LOY on the balance between platelets and red blood cells. Indeed, LOY 
was positively associated with platelet counts and negatively associ-
ated with red blood cell counts48. A similar shift in the balance between 
platelets and red blood cells has been observed in male individuals with 
LOY who are critically ill with COVID-19 (ref. 45). This might be a partial 
explanation for the thromboembolic complications that can occur in 
male individuals with severe COVID-19 (see the section ‘Haematopoietic 
LOY and COVID-19’). LOY in normal haematopoietic cells is a dynamic 
mutation, meaning that a cell clone with LOY will expand and con-
tract in number over time45. Cell clones with LOY most likely follow 
the normal apoptotic programme that regulates the turnover of cells 
and will thus eventually disappear from circulation. Indeed, multiple 
reports have documented increasing and decreasing levels of LOY in 
analyses of blood samples collected from the same male individuals 
at different ages11,45,70.
Also of interest is a potential relationship between sex hormones 
and the occurrence of LOY. In a study of individuals with abdominal 
aortic aneurysm, levels of sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG) 
were increased and free testosterone levels were decreased compared 
with healthy control individuals. Levels of LOY were also higher in the 
patient group, although no direct correlation between LOY and tes-
tosterone markers was carried out71. In two later reports, using the UK 
Biobank cohort, LOY was associated with increased levels of SHBG and 
total testosterone as well as decreased levels of free testosterone49,72. 
Although the association between LOY and SHBG was independent of 
additional covariates, such as age, smoking or other comorbidities49, 
and there was an association between the LOY polygenic score and 
higher SHBG level72, the exact mechanism of how LOY and testosterone 
level are related requires further investigation, including, for example, 
in relation to decreasing testosterone levels in ageing male individuals.
Positive selection of LOY cells?
In contrast to monosomies of most autosomes, mammalian cells with 
LOY are viable and thus the effects of LOY on cellular fitness can be 
studied73. In a study of isolated human HSCs cultured in vitro, larger 
clones were more likely to have LOY74. This suggests that LOY cells might 
undergo positive selection in vitro. However, the situation in vivo seems 
to be more complicated. Given that tumour cells with LOY tend to have 
a higher mutational burden than those without LOY, this shows that LOY 
may promote the clonal expansion of particular cell types by confer-
ring a survival advantage31,38,75. The advantage conferred by LOY might 
also be owing to a LOY-mediated immunosuppressive environment 
that enables tumour cells to evade an immune response, as has been 
shown in the mouse model of LOY75. Here, it has been reported that 
Box 4 | LOY in non-human species
 
Naturally occurring loss of the Y chromosome (LOY) has mainly 
been analysed in humans, with only a few studies in other 
mammals. In rats, LOY increases with age in the cells of brain, 
kidney, liver, blood and testis168. Surprisingly, LOY was not found 
in healthy ageing dogs but it was detected at various levels in 
dogs with haematological malignancies169. LOY affects all-cause 
mortality in humans, with male individuals having a shorter 
life expectancy (by 5.5 years) than female individuals11. Across 
134 mammalian species, females live on average 18.6% longer 
than males170. Away from mammals, in more distant branches of 
the phylogenetic tree, the heterogametic sex does not always 
occur in males — for example, birds with ZW and ZZ chromosomes 
are females and males, respectively. A study in water birds found 
no loss of W chromosome in females, although the sensitivity 
of the detection method was low171. Interestingly, when females 
are the heterogametic sex, the difference in lifespan between 
females and males seems to be less pronounced, being roughly 7% 
compared with 21% for species where males are heterogametic172. 
Moreover, LOY has been shown to affect the immune response, with 
sex differences in immunity having been observed in both humans 
and other species131,173–175.
Mouse models for LOY have been developed by ablating the 
Y chromosome in haematopoietic cells in vitro using CRISPR–Cas9 
and transplanting these cells into irradiated mice82,176. A mouse 
model expressing green fluorescent protein on the X chromosome 
and red fluorescent protein on the Y chromosome has also been 
created for LOY research177. In addition, several cellular models 
facilitate LOY studies. The mouse bladder cancer cell line MB49 
naturally loses the Y chromosome178. Radioresistant non-small-cell 
lung cancer lines have LOY, whereas radiosensitive non-small-
cell lung cancer lines retain the Y chromosome179. Induced 
pluripotent stem cells with LOY from an individual with Alzheimer 
disease have been cultured in vitro124. Moreover, CRISPR–Cas9 has 
been used to produce cell lines lacking the Y chromosome, derived 
from retinal epithelial cells and the MB49 cell line75,79.

Y chromosome-negative tumours grow larger (twofold volume) than 
their Y chromosome-positive counterparts only in immunocompetent 
hosts. It has also been shown that the loss of single genes encoded on the 
Y chromosome accelerates the growth of cancer cells76–78. By contrast, 
LOY in male retinal epithelial cells in vitro did not result in increased 
proliferation but rather increased cell migration, compared with cells 
having retention of Y chromosome (ROY)79. As mentioned above, 
actively proliferating cells might be more susceptible to LOY31,45,59. 
Furthermore, factors causing DNA damage and hypoxia could 
favour LOY in proliferating cells as shown in chronic kidney disease, 
wherein LOY occurs in the proximal tubule cells that undergo extensive 
proliferation to regenerate kidney epithelium31. In summary, the evi-
dence for a proliferative advantage of LOY cells in vivo is still tentative, 
and further studies are needed.
LOY manifestations depend on cell type
The emerging picture is that haematopoietic LOY might have variable, 
pleiotropic80,81 effects on cellular homeostasis, depending on the dif-
ferentiation status of the affected cell. Considering the large number 
of associations between haematopoietic LOY and disease phenotypes 
occurring in other and varied tissues, LOY-pleiotropy might be a plau-
sible concept. Analyses of transcriptome dysregulation in subpopu-
lations of leukocytes with LOY support this concept. The fraction of 
LOY-associated transcriptional effect genes unique to specific cell types 
was substantially larger than the fraction of LOY-associated transcrip-
tional effect genes shared between different subsets of leukocytes44. 
Multiple other analyses also point to different diseases being associated 
with diverse cell types with LOY — for example, natural killer cells in 
the circulation of individuals with AD44; CD4+ T cells and granulocytes 
in individuals with prostate cancer44; microglia cells in brains of indi-
viduals with Alzheimer disease59; monocytes in the circulation and 
macrophages infiltrating heart muscle as a causative factor for cardiac 
fibrosis82; CD8+ cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTLs) in the tumour micro-
environment (TME) of colorectal cancer83; Treg cells in the circulation84 
and in the TME of primary colon cancer and liver metastases83; and 
low-density neutrophils in patients with life-threatening COVID-19 
(ref. 45).
As an example of how the cell-type-specific effects of LOY might 
function together, we hypothesize that LOY in Treg cells and LOY in CTLs 
cooperate to disturb tumour immunosurveillance (Fig. 2). Specifically, 
the CD4+ Treg cell population in peripheral blood has been shown to have 
a higher percentage of LOY than CD8+ CTLs in blood83,84. One poten-
tial hypothesis to explain this observation is that thymus-derived 
‘natural’ Treg cells with LOY could escape negative selection in the thy-
mus, whereas CTLs with LOY could be at least partially eliminated 
during thymic maturation owing to the cell-type-specific effects of 
LOY, although there are other models that could also fit these data. 
Upon infiltration into the TME, both LOY and ROY Treg cells are present. 
However, a higher proportion of CD8+ CTLs with LOY is observed in the 
TME than in peripheral blood or adjacent healthy tissue83. This differ-
ence might be attributed to the increased proliferation of CTLs in the 
TME, resulting in the clonal expansion of LOY cells. CTLs with LOY have 
increased expression of exhaustion markers, such as TIM3 and LAG3 
(ref. 75), potentially either as a direct effect of LOY or an indirect effect 
of Treg cells with LOY, resulting in a decreased antitumour response and 
increased tumour growth.
LOY in leukocytes has been associated with considerable dys-
regulation of the transcriptome, affecting several hundred genes in

many cell types, as has been studied using both bulk and single-cell 
RNA sequencing44,59,69,75,83–85. The main category of dysregulated genes 
includes those important for numerous aspects of immune defence, 
which is not surprising given that the studied cells are crucial compo-
nents of the immune system. Of note, however, is that the differentially 
expressed genes — either increased or decreased expression — include 
many membrane-bound immune-checkpoint receptors and ligands, 
presumably as an effect of LOY (Fig. 3). It is reasonable to assume that 
these changes will affect the normal immunosurveillance functions 
of these cells. For example, in CD8+ T cells, CD4+ T cells and Treg cells, the 
likely and consistent effect is suppression of their immune functions 
as the expression of the co-inhibitory genes LAG375, PDL175, TIM375, 
TIGIT44,83–85 and PD185 is upregulated whereas expression of the 
co-stimulatory gene CD2884 is downregulated (Fig. 3a). By contrast, 
LOY in natural killer cells has the opposite effect, with downregulation 
of LAG344 and TIGIT44, which is consistent with the activation of natural 
killer cells. The picture seems to be more complicated in the case of 
monocytes, with LOY associated with changes in gene expression 
that might be predicted both to amplify and to suppress effector cell 
responses (Fig. 3b). Collectively, results regarding the expression of 
immune-checkpoint receptor–ligand pairs provide perhaps the best 
evidence for the effects of LOY on immune system function in male indi-
viduals, and we believe that this aspect of LOY research warrants more 
attention in the future.

it is unknown whether the exhaustion phenotype of CTLs is directly associated 
with LOY or is a result of the action of Treg cells with LOY. The net result is increased 
tumour growth and decreased survival.

LOY in individuals with neurodegenerative disease and cancer, although 
both conditions are also associated with age and, therefore, it was not 
known whether LOY is merely a passenger mutation related to age or 
is a contributing factor to disease development. However, intensive 
research in the field of sex bias in human disease resulted in the estab-
lishment of multiple links between LOY and disease in male individuals 
(Table 1). In this section, we summarize reports that associate LOY 
with various pathological conditions and with all-cause mortality. We 
focus mainly on cancer, Alzheimer disease, cardiovascular disease and 
infectious disease, for which associations and some mechanistic evi-
dence have been presented in multiple original publications (additional 
conditions associated with LOY are listed in Supplementary Table 2).
Haematopietic LOY and cancer
Biological sex is recognized as an important factor in the pathogen-
esis, diagnosis and prognosis of numerous diseases, with cancer being 
the most notable example. Most types of cancer have a strong male 
bias and worse prognosis in male than in female individuals. Specifi-
cally, male-predominant cancers arise in the lung, colon, bladder, 
kidney, liver, skin and blood86–88. Although LOY is unlikely to be the 
only factor contributing to the sex bias observed in various cancers, 
numerous reports have revealed a strong association between LOY in 
leukocytes and cancer susceptibility11,16,44,89,90. Large population stud-
ies have identified more than 150 autosomal genetic determinants of 
LOY, which include genes involved in cell cycle regulation and cancer 
susceptibility, tumour growth drivers, and targets of cancer therapy28. 
Furthermore, LOY-associated transcriptional effects were observed 
in approximately 500 autosomal genes, resulting in altered immune 
functions in leukocytes, which could also have a role in the link between 
LOY and increased risk for cancer as a result of reduced antitumour 
immunity44. In a case–control study of individuals with colorectal or 
prostate cancer, haematopoietic LOY was found to be a more significant 
predictor of cancer occurrence than age89. Independent measure-
ments of LOY in subpopulations of blood leukocytes in patients with 
prostate cancer showed that CD4+ T cells and granulocytes had the 
highest levels of LOY44.
Of interest in the context of cancer is to better define the link 
between haematopoietic LOY and CHIP, in which mutations in genes 
commonly associated with myeloid neoplasms accumulate in the blood 
of individuals without any signs of haematological malignancy91–93.

Diversity and consequences 
of structural variation in 
the human genome
Ryan L. Collins1,2,3,4 & Michael E. Talkowski 
  1,2,3,5 
Abstract
The biomedical community is increasingly invested in capturing all 
genetic variants across human genomes, interpreting their functional 
consequences and translating these findings to the clinic. A crucial 
component of this endeavour is the discovery and characterization 
of structural variants (SVs), which are ubiquitous in the human 
population, heterogeneous in their mutational processes, key 
substrates for evolution and adaptation, and profound drivers of 
human disease. The recent emergence of new technologies and the 
remarkable scale of sequence-based population studies have begun 
to crystalize our understanding of SVs as a mutational class and their 
widespread influence across phenotypes. In this Review, we summarize 
recent discoveries and new insights into SVs in the human genome in 
terms of their mutational patterns, population genetics, functional 
consequences, and impact on human traits and disease. We conclude 
by outlining three frontiers to be explored by the field over the next 
decade.

Review article
Likewise, the impact of SVs has been underexplored in many human 
diseases and traits as SVs have not been routinely incorporated in most 
large-scale association studies to date. New technologies will capture 
a greater fraction of the SV spectrum34–36,44, but long-read assembly 
studies have been inadequate in terms of the number of individuals 
surveyed that is needed to derive principles of population genetics 
and human disease architecture. In summary, although some general 
patterns of SVs in the human genome have been defined, the specifics 
remain opaque across disparate domains of biology and medicine and 
represent opportunities for dramatic advances in the coming years.
In this Review, we summarize the existing knowledge of germline 
SVs in the human population. First, we discuss the mutational proper-
ties of SVs, including their diversity, complexity and mutation rates. 
Second, we describe the patterns of SVs in the global human popula-
tion, with an emphasis on the role of natural selection. Third, we sum-
marize the modes in which SVs can result in functional alterations to 
protein-coding and non-coding loci throughout the genome. Fourth, 
we review the roles of SVs in rare, common and complex human dis-
eases, and speculate on the role of advancing technologies in this 
area of study. We do not focus on the technical aspects of detecting 
SVs6,7,45–47, the roles of somatic SVs in cancer48 or the impact of SVs on 
three-dimensional genome organization43 as these topics have all been 
comprehensively detailed in other recent reviews. Similarly, we do not 
discuss somatic or mosaic SVs in non-cancerous tissues, which is an 
active area of enquiry with insufficient high-resolution data across the 
complete SV spectrum to definitively contrast such SVs with germline 
variants in the human population49,50. We conclude by enumerating 
three frontiers in SV research that we anticipate will be topics of intense 
interest in the coming years.
Mutational properties of SVs
The term ‘structural variation’ encompasses a remarkably diverse fam-
ily of mutational classes, each of which has distinct properties (Fig. 1). 
In this section, we recap the current taxonomy for germline SVs, sum-
marize their mutational mechanisms, and discuss germline SV mutation 
rates and covariates.
Canonical and complex SV classes
By convention, germline SVs are categorized into several canonical 
mutational classes. Beyond chromosome-scale gains and losses of 
DNA, such as aneuploidies, the most commonly surveyed SV classes 
are deletions and duplications, collectively known as copy number 
variants (CNVs). These CNVs are defined by a loss or tandem gain of 
sequence relative to a reference genome. Canonical CNVs in the human 
germline have just one alternate allele documented in the population 
(that is, a biallelic variant)9,28, whereas multiallelic CNVs (mCNVs) in cer-
tain repetitive loci can reach high copy numbers, sometimes accruing 
dozens of duplicate copies in individual genomes30,51. Although mCNVs 
can be some of the most mutationally diverse SVs in humans, surveys 
to date from existing technologies suggest that they are relatively 
sparse throughout the genome — between 673 and 1,356 mCNV loci 
have been reported31,51, representing <0.05% of all SVs reported to date 
across global population studies. Improved access to complex repeti-
tive sequences from long-read technologies will upwardly revise these 
estimates as they are applied across large population data sets44,52. Inser-
tions are the second-most common class of SVs in humans and comprise 
numerous subclasses such as mobile element insertions (for example, 
LINE1 and Alu)53–55, novel non-reference insertions (for example, viral 
DNA insertions)56–58, nuclear insertions of mitochondrial DNA59, and 
Introduction
Human genetic variation is often categorized into three major 
classes based on the number of DNA nucleotides altered per variant: 
single-nucleotide variants (SNVs), short insertion or deletion vari-
ants (indels; 1–50 bp), and structural variants (SVs; ≥50 bp)1. Among 
these, SNVs and indels, collectively referred to here as short variants 
(<50 bp), have been extensively studied due to their high mutational 
densities in humans and the relative ease of their detection using a 
multitude of technologies1–4. By contrast, SVs have proven more dif-
ficult to interrogate due to several factors, foremost among which are 
the technical challenges of SV ascertainment5–7. Beyond these techni-
cal challenges, the density of SVs throughout each human genome is 
two orders of magnitude lower (tens of thousands) than that of SNVs 
and indels (millions)1 while encompassing a much broader spectrum 
of mutational classes8–10. Consequently, our nascent capabilities to 
capture and interpret SVs in genetic research and clinical diagnostics 
remains substantially less precise than for short variants11.
Despite these limitations, the last 60 years in human genetic 
research have witnessed remarkable progress in defining the muta-
tional spectrum of SVs. Since the initial discovery of the human chromo-
some number in 1956 and the discovery of trisomy 21 in Down syndrome 
in 1959 (refs. 12,13), progressive generations of technological break-
throughs have reliably yielded transformative new insights into SVs. 
The use of microscopic techniques, such as karyotyping or fluorescence 
in situ hybridization, revealed that chromosome-scale rearrange-
ments were rare in the general population but enriched in individuals 
with developmental disorders and in cancer genomes14–18. In the early 
2000s, the application of microarray technologies led to the discovery 
of the widespread existence of large DNA copy number variants (CNVs) 
throughout the human genome19–24. These observations were extended 
by shallow (~4–12×) whole-genome sequencing (WGS), which revealed 
that every human genome harbours thousands of CNVs and other types 
of SVs9,10,25,26 and that these SVs generally adhered to the same principles 
of population genetics established for short variants26,27. More recently, 
deep (≥30-fold coverage) WGS of large populations has demonstrated 
that there are likely tens of millions of unique SVs segregating in the 
human population, most of which appear in just one or a handful of 
individuals worldwide28–31. Furthermore, the maturation of long-read 
sequencing and other technologies continues to reveal thousands of 
cryptic SVs embedded in the most complex and repetitive sequence 
contexts32–37.
Advancing our nascent understanding of the forces and factors 
influencing where new SVs arise in the human germline and how they 
are subject to natural selection requires large, population-scale char-
acterization studies. Major initiatives have been launched to catalogue 
SVs in the human genome, such as the Genome Aggregation Database 
(gnomAD)28, 1000 Genomes Project and Human Genome Structural 
Variation Consortium (HGSVC)9,25,31, UK Biobank38, and the All of Us 
Research Program39, yet there remains a limited representation of 
SVs that exist across global populations, especially in non-European 
populations. Even within European populations, the most repetitive 
~10% of the genome remains intractable to most technologies. Recent 
breakthroughs using the combination of multiple new technologies 
and sophisticated analytic approaches that have achieved near com-
plete telomere-to-telomere (T2T) assemblies are beginning to dissolve 
these technical barriers and are poised to enable the study of these 
genomic loci that were inaccessible to prior technologies40,41. Another 
major challenge in human genetics is the prediction of the functional 
consequences of SVs on gene function and cis-regulatory networks42,43.
