~30% of synonymous mutations were estimated to be under weak-to-
strong negative selection, with s<−1/Ne. Additionally, compared with 
intronic single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs), human synony-
mous SNPs predicted to increase and decrease the relevant mRNA’s 
half-life show site frequency spectrum-based signatures of positive 
and negative selection, respectively100. Nevertheless, the estimations 
discussed here typically relied on simplifying assumptions, including 
those about the demography and/or neutrality of control sites that are 
often violated or difficult to verify. Furthermore, population genetic 
estimates may not be directly compared with experimental estimates of 
fitness effects, described below, because population genetic estimates 
represent an average effect of many synonymous mutations over a long 
evolutionary time in a changing natural environment, whereas experi-
mental estimates are typically obtained for individual synonymous 
mutations in a specific, laboratory environment. Although a population 
genetic estimate of s can in principle be obtained from any species, 
experimental measurement of s has thus far been obtained almost 
exclusively in microorganisms, because creating many mutants and 
assaying their fitness remains daunting for multicellular organisms.
Experimental estimates from case studies
Natural selection can sense a fitness effect with a magnitude exceeding 
1/Ne. However, even the most powerful experiment today cannot reli-
ably detect |s|<0.001, and many studies have sensitivities on the order of 
0.01. Because Ne is typically >107 for the microbes used in experimental 
fitness quantification, experiments are orders of magnitude less sensi-
tive than nature in detecting fitness differentials. In other words, labora-
tory measures are expected to underestimate the fraction of mutations 
that are non-neutral to varying degrees, depending on the experiment. 
For this reason, fractions of non-neutral mutations reported by differ-
ent studies are usually not directly comparable. For the same reason, it 
is often useful to compare the DFEs of synonymous and nonsynonymous 
mutations in the same study, because the experimental sensitivity is the 
same for the two types of mutations and because most nonsynonymous 
mutations are known to be strongly deleterious101,102.
A number of case studies, each focusing on a set of non-randomly-
chosen mutations, reported substantial fitness effects of synonymous 
mutations103–108. For example, Agashe et al. made dozens of synony-
mous mutations in the fae gene, which encodes the highly expressed 
formaldehyde-activating enzyme FAE, of the bacterium Methylobacte-
rium extorquens103. Interestingly, using only unpreferred synonymous 
codons in the gene lowered the fitness by 40%, whereas using only 
preferred codons reduced the fitness by 90%. Both the mRNA level 
and protein level per mRNA molecule were lower in these mutants 
than in the wild type, and increasing fae expression partially recov-
ered the fitness loss of the mutants. Note that this study estimated 
the combined effects of multiple synonymous mutations rather than 
their individual effects.
Experimental estimates from systematic studies
Systematic studies, often comparing the DFEs of synonymous and 
nonsynonymous mutations18,109–114, have addressed the generalizability 
of observations made in case studies103–108 that some synonymous muta-
tions are strongly non-neutral. Many systematic studies focused on viral 
genomes, and we estimated from five such studies that, on average, 
43% of synonymous mutations are significantly non-neutral115–119. One 
of the first systematic studies in cellular organisms constructed 38 syn-
onymous and 88 nonsynonymous mutants of Salmonella typhimurium 
by engineering individual random point mutations in two ribosomal 
protein genes109. By having each mutant compete with the wild type in 
a poor medium, the authors measured s with a high precision of 0.003. 
They reported that s ranged from 0 to −0.0279 for synonymous muta-
tions and from 0 to −0.0763 for nonsynonymous mutations (Fig. 3a). 
About 95% of synonymous and 94% of nonsynonymous mutations were 
significantly non-neutral. The DFEs of synonymous and nonsynony-
mous mutations differ significantly, with a longer left tail for nonsyn-
onymous than synonymous mutations (Fig. 3a). The authors did not 
find that mutating preferred codons synonymously to be significantly 
more deleterious than mutating unpreferred codons synonymously, 
but they observed a significant negative correlation between s and 
the absolute value of the synonymous mutational effect on mRNA 
folding strength, suggesting that altering mRNA folding strength is 
deleterious109. However, a subsequent study detected no significant 
fitness effects of synonymous mutations but substantial effects of 
nonsynonymous mutations in three genes of S. typhimurium required 
for rapid growth on l-arabinose113.
Sane et al. measured the fitness effects of 17 synonymous and 
39 nonsynonymous random mutations in E. coli in 16 different 
environments114. They observed that the fraction of mutations with 
|s|>0.1 in an environment was on average 36% for synonymous and 
45% for nonsynonymous mutations, although the mean s of a muta-
tion across environments was not significantly different between 
synonymous and nonsynonymous mutations. Similar patterns were 
observed when the analysis was expanded to 138 synonymous and 
382 nonsynonymous random mutations120.
Using CRISPR editing, Shen et al. created 8,341 synonymous, 
nonsynonymous or nonsense mutants of 21 yeast genes with diverse 
functions and expression levels18. Because their experimental proce-
dure prohibited the study of essential genes, the authors focused on 
nonessential genes with relatively large fitness defects upon deletion. 
They reported a mean s of −0.012 for synonymous mutations and of 
−0.015 for nonsynonymous mutations. About 77.2% of synonymous 
mutations and 77.4% of nonsynonymous mutations were significantly 
non-neutral. Although the DFEs look overall similar between synony-
mous and nonsynonymous mutations (Fig. 3b), they are statistically 
significantly different; mutations with s<−0.05 are overwhelmingly 
nonsynonymous. In both Fig. 3a and Fig. 3b only one mode is apparent 
in each DFE, and the nonsynonymous DFEs exhibit a longer left tail rela-
tive to the synonymous DFEs. In the yeast study, Shen et al. discovered 
that the mRNA level of the gene mutated in a mutant frequently deviates 
from the wild-type level, with 25% of mutants deviating by at least 20%. 
When the mutant mRNA level is below the wild-type level, a positive 
correlation was observed between the mutant mRNA level and mutant 
fitness, suggesting that the fitness effects of both synonymous and 
nonsynonymous mutations in this study were attributable at least in 
part to a reduction in the mRNA level. Furthermore, the mutant mRNA 
level correlated positively with the abundance of preferred codons of 
the mutated gene, suggesting a role for translation-dependent mRNA 
degradation in determining the fitness effects of the coding mutations 
studied. In estimating mutant fitness, Shen et al. used a wild-type con-
trol that was constructed separately from the mutants, which raised 
doubts about their results121. However, new experiments in which the 
control and mutants were constructed simultaneously in the same test 
tube confirmed the original finding122.
Widespread non-neutrality is also evident for ‘immunizing’ syn-
onymous mutations placed in or near the protospacer adjacent motif 
to avoid re-cleavage of the genome after CRISPR editing. Specifically, 
Yang et al. monitored the growth of about 50,000 CRISPR-edited

They reported that 9% of mutants, each with more than one synony-

have significant growth effects. These findings require consideration 
of the potential effects of immunizing synonymous mutations when

Large fitness effects of synonymous mutations are also evident 
in synthetic biology. Nyerges et al. attempted to synthesize an E. coli 
genome that uses only 57 of the 64 codons124. They encountered numer-
ous instances of strongly deleterious synonymous codon swaps and 
discovered that replacements of (multiple) synonymous codons 
cause frequent changes in gene expression and the generation of new 
promoters and antisense RNAs.
The above studies measured the fitness effects of de novo 
mutations, which likely differ in DFE from polymorphisms, because 
polymorphisms are affected by selection in addition to mutation. For 
example, compared with neutral mutations, deleterious mutations are 
selectively purged so have reduced probabilities to appear as polymor-
phisms. To our knowledge, two studies have systematically analysed 
the fitness effects of natural polymorphisms in yeast. Sharon et al. con-
structed Saccharomyces cerevisiae mutants by individually replacing 
the allele in a laboratory strain (BY) with that in a vineyard strain (RM) 
at 16,006 sites125. They reported that 572 of these polymorphisms had 
significant positive fitness effects in a glucose medium and that the 
probability to show up in this subset is similar between synonymous 
and nonsynonymous polymorphisms (Fig. 3c). Synonymous polymor-

with strong CUB. Because the ancestral relationship between BY and RM 
alleles is unknown, whether the polymorphism-generating mutation is 
beneficial or deleterious is undetermined here. Complementary to the

for a synonymous SNP to affect growth was 76% of that for a nonsynony-

Systematic studies are not necessarily unbiased, because they 
might have focused on certain genes that are particularly important 
or highly expressed, such as ribosomal protein genes, but some sys-
tematic studies114,120,124–126 are agnostic to such biases because they 
examine a random subset of mutations or polymorphisms in the 
genome. Note that many deep mutational scanning studies, even 
when they serve their original purposes well, do not aim for nor allow 
reliable estimation of the DFE of synonymous mutations, because 
they express focal genes in non-native systems (for example, using 
non-native promoters)127–129, measure protein expression or activity 
but not fitness128, lack appropriate controls (for example, assuming 
a zero median fitness effect of synonymous mutations)129, or have 
relatively large measurement errors129. Therefore, comparing syn-
onymous and nonsynonymous mutations from such studies130 can 
be misleading131.
Beneficial synonymous mutations
The estimated DFEs have shown that, although the vast majority of 
non-neutral synonymous mutations are deleterious, a small fraction 
are advantageous18,110,114,120,123. Furthermore, synonymous beneficial 
mutations have been observed in experimental evolution106,108,110,132 
and other studies133,134. For instance, when subjecting M. extorquens 
strains containing synonymous mutations in fae to experimental 
evolution, Agashe et al. observed several highly beneficial synony-
mous changes in the evolved populations that each increased fitness 
by >10%, probably by raising mRNA and protein levels108. In another 
example, Bailey et al. evolved a Pseudomonas fluorescens population 
in a glucose minimal medium and observed the accumulation of two 
synonymous mutations in the gtsB gene that increased fitness by 7% 
and 9%, respectively, likely by boosting the gtsB mRNA level135. A subse-
quent study found that many random synonymous mutations in gtsB 
have detectable benefits, likely by promoting the transcription of gtsB 
and downstream genes in the same operon111. Nevertheless, beneficial 
synonymous substitutions are much rarer than beneficial nonsyn-
onymous substitutions in experimental evolution110,136. Apart from a 
potential reporting bias due to the common belief that synonymous 
mutations are neutral, clonal interference in asexual experimental 
evolution is likely a major reason. Specifically, due to clonal interfer-
ence, only the fittest mutant among simultaneously present advan-
tageous mutants can reach fixation. Because more nonsynonymous 
than synonymous mutations are expected by chance and because the 
fitness effects may be greater for beneficial nonsynonymous than 
beneficial synonymous mutations, clonal interference exacerbates 
the difference in fixation probability between synonymous and non-
synonymous mutations110. Given the suspected difference in effect 
size between beneficial synonymous and beneficial nonsynonymous 
mutations, we predict that the contribution of beneficial synonymous 
mutations to adaptation is larger as the population approaches the 
fitness optimum.
Evolutionary consequences
Because many evolutionary analyses and conclusions depend on 
the assumption that synonymous mutations are neutral, findings of 
non-neutral synonymous mutations demand a re-examination of these 
analyses and conclusions. Below we discuss analyses and conclusions 
that are potentially affected if synonymous mutations are broadly 
non-neutral and those that are unlikely to be affected.
Impact on the neutral theory of molecular evolution
The neutral theory holds that most interspecific nucleotide differences 
and intraspecific nucleotide polymorphisms are selectively neutral 
rather than adaptive2. Note that the theory does not require most 
mutations to be neutral. In fact, the neutral theory acknowledges the 
prevalence of deleterious mutations, which are selectively purged so 
contribute little to nucleotide divergence and polymorphism. Hence, 
the discovery of many detrimental synonymous mutations, analogous 
to the discovery of many detrimental nonsynonymous mutations, does 
not by itself shake the standing of the neutral theory.
Although King and Jukes used the presumable neutrality of syn-
onymous mutations to support the neutral theory in their foundational 
paper137, this is not a necessary condition for the neutral theory, as long 
as some synonymous mutations are neutral. That the nonsynonymous 
substitution rate (dN) of a gene is typically much lower than the corre-
sponding synonymous substitution rate (dS) is commonly interpreted as 
evidence for the neutral theory, because, under the neutral assumption 
of synonymous mutations, dN<dS can be explained without invoking 
positive selection2. If synonymous mutations are mostly deleterious, 
dN<dS can be explained by stronger purifying selection against non-
synonymous than synonymous mutations; again, there is no need to 
invoke positive selection. That is, the common interpretation of the 
observation of dN<dS remains valid.
Impact on parameter estimation in population genetics 
and molecular evolution
The estimation of many parameters in population genetics and 
molecular evolution relies on nucleotide changes that are selectively 
neutral. For example, the rate and molecular spectrum of mutation 
are often estimated from synonymous polymorphisms or substi-
tutions. This strategy inevitably leads to an underestimation of the 
mutation rate if many synonymous mutations are detrimental. In 
fact, it was noticed more than 40 years ago that the mutation rate 
estimated from synonymous substitutions in a mammalian α-globin 
gene is approximately one-half that estimated from substitutions 
in an α-globin pseudogene138. Similarly, the molecular spectrum of 
mutation inferred from synonymous substitutions may be biased. 
Fortunately, with the reduced cost of DNA sequencing, mutation 
rate and spectrum can now be estimated by genome sequencing 
of parents and offspring, or by mutation accumulation followed by 
genome sequencing, in which repeated bottlenecks render the impact 
of natural selection minimal139.
Ne is a fundamental population genetic parameter pertinent to 
many evolutionary processes and theories. It is also key to conser-
vation biology because it summarizes the demographic history of 
a wild population, predicts the risk of inbreeding and assesses the 
effectiveness of human-aided genetic management in the future. The 
Ne of a diploid population is typically estimated by dividing its neutral 
genetic diversity (π) by 4μ, in which μ is the neutral mutation rate per 
site per generation. If μ is reliably estimated, for example from muta-
tion accumulation or genome sequencing of parents and offspring, 
whereas π is estimated from synonymous polymorphisms, as is often 
the case, Ne will be underestimated when many synonymous mutations 
are detrimental. Ne estimated using the coalescent theory may share 
the same problem if the estimation relies on the neutral assumption of 
synonymous mutations. The extent of Ne underestimation depends on 
the DFE of synonymous mutations and is expected to be larger when the 
actual Ne is larger, because the selection on non-neutral synonymous 
mutations intensifies with Ne.

Nature Reviews Genetics | Volume 26 | November 2025 | 789–804
798

Evolutionary events such as speciation and gene or genome dupli-
cation are sometimes dated by dividing the number of synonymous 
substitutions per site accumulated in evolution by the synonymous 
mutation rate, under the assumption that synonymous mutations 
are neutral. When the mutation rate is reliably estimated, evolution-
ary time would be underestimated if synonymous mutations are on 
average deleterious.
Impact on selection tests
A variety of statistical tests are commonly used to detect positive or 
negative selection from DNA sequences. There are generally three 
classes of such tests, depending on whether the data used are intraspe-
cific polymorphisms, interspecific divergences or both. Tests using 
intraspecific polymorphisms include those based on the site frequency 
spectrum, haplotype structure or population differentiation. Because 
these tests do not typically distinguish between synonymous and non-
synonymous changes, they are not affected by the non-neutrality of 
synonymous mutations. This said, significant results from these tests 
do not always implicate selection because they could also be caused 
by demographic changes. Tests based on interspecific divergences 
typically compare dS and dN, so they can be influenced if synonymous 
mutations are non-neutral (Box 2).
Two commonly used selection tests are based on both intraspecific 
polymorphisms and interspecific divergences: the Hudson–Kreitman–
Aguadé (HKA) test140 and the McDonald–Kreitman test141. The HKA test 
does not generally assume the neutrality of synonymous mutations, 
so its results are not affected if the said mutations are non-neutral. 
The McDonald–Kreitman test compares the number of polymor-
phisms with that of divergences at two types of sites — synonymous 
and nonsynonymous — and detects deviation from independence in 
a 2×2

Structural variants in the  
3D genome as drivers of disease
Varun K. A. Sreenivasan1, Verónica Yumiceba1 & Malte Spielmann 
  1,2 
Abstract
The spatial organization of the genome within the nucleus — also 
known as genome architecture or 3D genome — is important to the 
regulation of gene expression. Disruption of the 3D genome, for 
example, by structural variation, can contribute to disease, including 
developmental disorders and cancer. Structural variants can rearrange 
higher-order chromatin structures, such as topologically associating 
domains, and disrupt interactions between cis-regulatory elements, 
which can lead to altered gene expression, a phenomenon known as 
position effects. New experimental and computational approaches are 
revealing the effect of structural variants on the 3D genome and gene 
expression and can help interpret their pathogenic potential, which 
has important implications for patients. Here, we review mechanisms 
of disease caused by position effects owing to disruptions of genome 
architecture, and more specifically topologically associating domains, 
as well as their consequences and clinical impact.

dynamic bidirectional relationship with gene expression. This relation-
ship is crucial for all aspects of physiology, including development26,27, 
ageing28 and disease29. In particular, the discovery that SVs can disrupt 
enhancer–promoter interactions and the boundaries of topologically 
associating domains (TADs) (Fig. 1) has provided a mechanistic basis 
for many position effects and been instrumental in understanding 
how non-coding changes in 3D genome architecture contribute to 
disease25,30. The recent application of long-read sequencing technolo-
gies and the development of new computational tools to improve SV 
genotyping from short-read sequencing data have led to the discovery 
of many new SVs31, highlighting the growing need to interpret their 
effect on 3D genome architecture also in a clinical context.
In this Review, we describe TAD formation and the positional 
effects caused by SVs that affect this process. We limit the Review 
to position effects explained by changes to cis-regulation that are 
mediated by the 3D genome architecture, excluding effects mediated 
via epigenetic modifications, such as position variegation32. Empha-
sis is on SVs whose mechanistic and phenotypic consequences arise 
from altered 3D genome architecture owing to the removal, copying, 
interruption or displacement of coding, regulatory or structural ele-
ments. We provide a roadmap to assess the disease-causing potential 
of candidate SVs based on possible mechanisms leading to dysregu-
lated gene expression and disease. We do not review the molecular 
mechanisms of chromatin organization in depth33–35, or methods to 
detect SVs by genome sequencing or chromosome conformation 
capture technologies36–38, although we briefly highlight emerging 
technological and computational approaches to resolve candidate 
SV effects. Given our expertise, we focus on rare genetic diseases but 
provide supporting evidence from cancer examples and refer readers 
specifically interested in cancer to a recent in-depth review39.
3D genome organization
Understanding 3D genome organization is key to interpreting 
non-coding position effects. In the interphase nucleus, the mammalian 
genome appears hierarchically organized40. This organization serves 
a multitude of roles, including in gene regulation, genome compac-
tion and partitioning41 as well as DNA replication timing42, repair43 and 
recombination44, among others41,45. At the macro level, each chromo-
some occupies a distinct territory within the nucleus (Fig. 1a). Within 
these territories, chromatin is partitioned into two main types: open 
chromatin (A compartments, euchromatin) and closed chromatin 
(B compartments, heterochromatin), mirroring high versus low gene 
expression, respectively. These compartments could be further divided 
into sub-compartments, each characterized by a distinctive epigenetic 
profile23,37,46. The transcriptionally active A sub-compartments (A1 and A2) 
are typically located in the nuclear interior and are enriched in long-range 
chromosomal contacts47. By contrast, B sub-compartments (B1, B2 and B3) 
exhibit lower transcriptional activity and are often associated with 
repressive chromatin marks23,46. The next major level of genome organi-
zation, TADs (Fig. 1b,c), typically spans several hundred kilobases48–50. 
TADs have been described as self-contained genomic units51, with high 
internal physical contacts within and reduced contacts across their 
boundaries52,53. TADs harbour genes and their regulatory elements, 
providing a structural framework that facilitates proper cis-regulatory 
interactions while limiting interactions between neighbouring TADs. Of 
note, the organization of the 3D genome into three hierarchical layers as 
described here is a simplification that serves the purpose of explaining 
most rare genetic disease mechanisms. We include a more nuanced look 
into this hierarchy in the section ‘Gene regulation across boundaries’.
Introduction
Whole-genome sequencing (WGS) is increasingly becoming the first-tier 
test for diagnosing rare genetic disorders, surpassing standard diagnostic 
tests such as cytogenetics, comparative genomic hybridization and 
whole-exome sequencing1,2. WGS has demonstrated clinical relevance 
also in cancer by confirming or redefining diagnoses and suggesting 
potential targeted therapies3, becoming a central component of preci-
sion oncology4. Nevertheless, our ability to understand the molecular 
and phenotypic consequences of non-coding variants has lagged behind 
the characterization of protein-coding variation, and most identified 
non-coding variants are therefore ignored for diagnostic purposes5. 
Hence, nearly 50% of patients with a rare disease remain without a molec-
ular diagnosis even after WGS6. Interpreting non-coding mutations in 
cancer presents an even greater challenge as it requires distinguish-
ing between driver and passenger mutations as well as decoding the 
tumour-specific genetic landscape7. A key limitation of WGS for diagnos-
tics, which relies predominantly on short-read sequencing, has been its 
inability to accurately resolve structural variation. The recent applica-
tion of population-level long-read sequencing efforts has highlighted 
structural variants (SVs) as a major contributor to disease8.
SVs, defined as variants affecting ≥50 contiguous bases, are 
a major source of sequence variation in the non-coding genome9. 
SVs include five major types: deletions, tandem duplications and 
insertional duplications, which are classified as unbalanced SVs or 
copy number variants (CNVs), as well as translocations and inver-
sions, which can also be balanced SVs with no loss or gain of genetic 
information10. It is estimated that the average human genome har-
bours around 20–25k SVs affecting 11 Mb, far exceeding the changes 
introduced by single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNPs)11. Popula-
tion studies show that breakpoints of common SVs are depleted in 
protein-coding sequences owing to strong loss-of-function effects 
of sequence truncation12,13. However, non-coding SVs (in which the 
breakpoints do not disrupt genes) can also cause substantial changes 
to gene expression due to ‘position effects’14,15. Position effects were 
originally defined as deleterious changes to gene expression follow-
ing a change in the genomic position of a gene relative to its normal 
chromosome environment16. Despite attempts to assign the deleteri-
ousness to unidentified genes at the breakpoints proximal to known 
disease genes, it is now conclusive that position effects are mediated 
via disruptions to the cis-regulatory landscape of genes17–20. These 
include the separation of distal cis-regulatory elements from a gene, 
juxtaposition of a gene with an enhancer from another gene, removal 
of insulators or boundary elements, competition for enhancers by new 
genes introduced by genomic rearrangement, position variegation — 
relocation of a transcriptionally active gene in a heterochromatin 
region leading to silencing16, originally described in Drosophila — and 
transcriptional silencing with CpG ­methylation mediated by antisense 
RNA transcription21.
The rarity of causative SVs with breakpoints 400–800 kb from 
disease-associated genes, observed at the turn of the twenty-first 
century, already suggested that the chromatin architecture at the 
sub-megabase scale is a likely mediator of position effects22. Over 
the past decade, the mechanisms underlying non-coding position 
effects have become clearer, as techniques such as chromosome con-
formation capture23 and assay for transposase-accessible chromatin 
using sequencing (ATAC-seq)24 have provided detailed insights into 
chromatin architecture, revealing how changes in chromatin folding 
exert long-range effects on gene regulation. Seminal experiments first 
uncovered that SVs can modify 3D genome architecture25, which is in a

The origin of TADs
TAD formation is best described by the loop extrusion model48,54. 
Loop extrusion is a dynamic process involving two key players: 
loop-extruding cohesins and the boundary insulator protein CTCF54,55. 
Once the ring-shaped cohesin complex is positioned on chromatin, 
it binds to two contiguous regions56 (Fig. 1d). Cohesin then pulls in 
chromatin from both sides through its motor activity, progressively 
enlarging the loop as more distal genomic regions pass through the 
ring. This extrusion process can be halted by physical barriers, such as 
other architectural proteins (CTCF and other cohesins), transcription 
machinery (RNA polymerases), DNA double-stranded breaks or DNA 
replication machinery55,57–59. If the interruption happens on one side, 
the other side of the chromatin keeps rolling inside the cohesin ring 
until reaching a barrier. CTCFs in particular are found to be enriched 
at loop boundaries albeit in a symmetrical manner, with the 3′ ends of 
CTCF-binding motifs oriented towards the inside of the loop, indicating 
their pivotal role in regulating the loop extrusion process54,60 (Fig. 1). 
Recent models based on single-molecule studies indicate that loop 
extrusion involves a series of complex topological manoeuvres, in 
which cohesin reels hundreds of bases of DNA per step and can even 
accommodate DNA-bound proteins (even larger than the diameter of 
the cohesin ring) to be passed through the loop35,61.
The chromatin contacts introduced by this dynamic loop extru-
sion process, when averaged over thousands of cells, result in TADs, 
which are visible as triangles in Hi-C maps, with more saturated colours 
indicating increased pairwise interactions between genomic regions. 
The two ends of the triangle that lie along the genome axis demarcate 
the TAD boundaries and represent the CTCF-bound motifs, where loop 
extrusion is halted within many cells of a population. Although Hi-C 
maps are only a snapshot of the average cell nucleus, the biological 
mechanism that built these structures should be thought of as an inces-
sant process62. Of note, the loop extrusion model is a ‘working model’ 
of a more complex system of genome organization that sufficiently 
explains molecular phenotypes or diseases arising from perturbations 
to the various components of this model. It is also possible to describe 
the molecular mechanisms that determine the emergence of distinct 
TAD patterns on a Hi-C map63.
Functionally, TADs seem to facilitate the establishment of 
interactions between enhancers and promoters that are separated 
along the linear genome, by increasing their physical proximity48,64. 
However, multiple mechanistic and knockdown experiments have 
shown that the gene regulation afforded by TADs is nuanced. For 
example, the acute loss of several molecular factors necessary for 
loop extrusion such as CTCF, components of the cohesin complex 
or the cohesin-releasing factor WAPL only modestly affects the 
tissue-averaged (as opposed to single-cell) measurements of gene 
expression, despite the perturbation resulting in the widespread 
disruption of TADs and abolishment of boundaries throughout the 
genome65. Follow-up experiments interrogating the apparent dis-
crepancy between TAD disruption and mostly unperturbed gene 
expression arrive at multiple explanatory models. One such model is 
the time-buffering model, whereby cohesins facilitate the establish-
ment of enhancer–promoter contacts by accelerating the target search 
of transcription factors, but are not required for their maintenance, 
at least in the short (<3 h) timescale used by many of these studies to 
assess changes in gene expression66. Experiments querying the length 
scales at which cohesins regulate gene expression additionally reveal 
that distal enhancers (>100 kb from gene) are more reliant on cohesin 
than proximal ones67–69. Finally, some of the discrepancy between TAD 
disruption and modest expressional changes could be resolved by 
single-cell transcriptional measurements, in which cohesin removal 
does cause an increase in the co-expression of genes located several 
millions of bases apart in separate regulatory domains70. This finding 
indicates that the loss of cohesin increases the crosstalk between genes 
owing to the ectopic colocalization of such genes within transcrip-
tional hubs, as was observed by single-molecule imaging70. Thus, the 
exact role of the 3D genome architecture in gene regulation seems to 
be sophisticated, with multiple working models explaining various, 
sometimes contrasting observations. Irrespective of whether the 
proposed models remain valid or further observations refine our 
understanding of the role of TADs, there is substantial evidence that 
disruptions in the loop extrusion process by SVs can lead to devel-
opmental disorders and cancer18,25,71–74. Identifying and cataloguing 
pathogenic SVs can help pinpoint sensitive TADs that are intolerant to 
rearrangements and can uncover new mechanisms of disease.
SVs can change 3D genome architecture
SVs have a key role in maintaining human genetic diversity75,76 while 
contributing to somatic77 and congenital diseases78. SVs disrupt, dys-
regulate or create gene products through various mechanisms, includ-
ing altering the sequence, dosage or context of genomic elements. 
Sequence disruption owing to SV breakpoints can result in loss-of-
function or gain-of-function and is usually interpreted through the 
concept of ‘gene dosage’. In the case of unbalanced SVs, dosage-based 
effects can also occur because of copy number changes (of genes or 
regulatory elements)79,80. That is, disease-causal SVs can encompass 
copy number-sensitive genes themselves, as in the case of gonadal 
dysgenesis81,82 or limb malformations83, or SVs can harbour their cog-
nate regulatory elements, as in the case of isolated microtia — a congeni-
tal anomaly of the ear84. Here, a duplication includes an evolutionary 
conserved ear-specific enhancer region of HMX1, which encodes a 
transcription factor crucial for the development of craniofacial struc-
tures, driving its overexpression. Another duplication example occurs 
at the Xq26.1 locus, which contains enhancer elements that drive the 
overexpression of ARHGAP36 in hair follicles, basal cell carcinoma 
and trichoepitheliomas of patients with the cancer predisposition

function or gain-of-function owing to breakpoints within the coding 
region of genes80,87, with novel adjacencies created by SVs generat-
ing fusion gene products or regulatory elements. Fusion genes occur 
frequently in human cancers, for example, PAX3–FOXO1 in the case 
of rhabdomyosarcoma, and some fusions have been implicated as 
driver oncogenes74,88,89. Fusion regulatory elements can drive ectopic 
gene expression that causes disease, a mechanism that can occur in 
balanced as well as unbalanced SVs90.
In all the aforementioned scenarios, the disease mechanism can 
be understood from a linear genome perspective, with only the coding 
or non-coding sequence requiring consideration. However, when 
the identified variant does not cause obvious disruptions to known 
disease-associated functional elements, 3D genome architecture must 
be taken into account30,91–94. In these cases, the misplaced genomic ele-
ments may drive disease through position effects, with the 3D genome 
architecture having a key role in regulating these effects. A notable 
example is adult-onset demyelinating leukodystrophy (ADLD), which is 
primarily associated with duplications encompassing the LMNB1 gene. 
Until recently, the disease mechanism of typical ADLD was attributed 
to gene dosage resulting from gene duplications. However, a recent 
report described atypical ADLD caused by deletions upstream of LMNB1

or larger duplications that did not present with dysautonomia or cer-

be considered, as discussed in the following sections.
Gene misexpression by SVs
Changes to gene expression can be caused by TAD reorganization 
resulting from the five types of SV: fused TADs (deletions), neo-TADs 
(tandem duplications and non-tandem duplications) and shuffled TADs 
(translocations and inversions). These reorganizations alter the regula-
tory landscape and context of a gene, leading to enhancer ‘hijacking’ 
and gene misexpression (Fig. 2). For each type of SV, our discussion is 
centred around a recently reported molecular diagnosis.
Unbalanced SVs involving TAD boundaries
Unbalanced SVs, such as deletions, duplications or insertions, can 
cause gene misexpression through several mechanisms, including 
copy number changes and sequence disruptions. Here, we limit the 
discussion to mechanisms related to 3D genome architecture.
Deletions. Deletions that encompass TAD boundaries can lead to TAD 
fusions, as loop extrusion progresses onto the neighbouring TAD, 
bringing into contact genomic elements from two, otherwise separate, 
adjacent TADs. This rearrangement can result in ectopic enhancer–gene 
interactions, termed ‘enhancer hijacking’96 or ‘enhancer adoption’92, 
which can lead to gene misexpression and disease (Fig. 2). Experimen-
tally, this disease mechanism was first described at the EPHA4 locus25. 
Remarkably, only structural changes to either of the two boundaries 
of the EPHA4-TAD, but not the inactivation of Epha4 (which was found 
to be deleted in three affected families) in mice, resulted in abnormal 
limb skeletal development. The disease mechanism was identified to 
be the ectopic expression of genes, WNT6 and IHH (in the TAD centro-
meric to EPHA4-TAD) and PAX3 (in the TAD telomeric to EPHA4-TAD), 
driven by the aberrant interaction with the EPHA4 enhancer. A more 
recent example involves deletions found in seven unrelated fami-
lies with complex cardiac electrical and structural phenotypes97. All 
deletions, ranging from 15 kb to 330 kb in size, overlapped a minimal 
critical region encompassing two CTCF-binding sites located 1 Mb from 
the PITX2 gene and fused two neighbouring TADs, as verified using 
human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived cardiomyocytes 
(Fig. 3a). Molecular phenotyping in mouse models revealed that TAD 
fusion resulted in ectopic expression of Pitx2 in the sinoatrial node 
of the mouse heart. Tissue specificity of misexpression was driven by 
the adoption of pacemaker-cardiomyocyte-specific enhancers, lead-
ing to a partial phenotypic transformation towards an atrial working 
myocardial phenotype. This tissue transformation likely contributed 
to the observed cardiac phenotype, including arrhythmias. This study 
highlights the tissue-specific effects of TAD fusion, as loss of con-
tact probability within the original PITX2 TAD led to reduced PITX2 
­expression in the ventricles97.
Boundary deletions can also result in gene downregulation, as 
observed in the EPB41L4A locus98. The TAD boundary located at the end 
of EPB41L4A is one of the strongest (in terms of insulation scores) TAD 
boundaries across human embryonic stem cells. Deletions and dupli-
cations encompassing this boundary have been found in patients with 
neurodevelopmental phenotypes. Deletion of this boundary in mice 
causes repression of Nrep98, although whether repression results from 
silencer adoption or enhancer competition remains unclear. The det-
rimental effects of deletion can also result from a combination of TAD 
restructuring and dosage effects, as in the case of deletions in HDAC9 
in individuals with craniofacial and limb malformations, resembling 
Saethre–Chotzen syndrome99. The disease mechanism was traced back 
to deletion of CTCF-binding sites and craniofacial and limb enhancers 
of TWIST1, located within the HDAC9 protein-coding region, which 
caused distorted cis-regulatory interactions and misexpression lead-
ing to skeletal malformations. Enhancer hijacking is also a recurring 
phenomenon in cancer100. In a study across 50 samples representing 
17 cancer types, a machine-learning-based prediction tool, NeoLoop-
Finder, estimated that 1,510 SVs in the cohort would result in a total of 
4,672 novel contacts affecting nearly 3,100 genes not directly disrupted 
by the breakpoints101. Although there are no accurate estimates on the 
frequency of enhancer hijacking in the context of congenital diseases, 
an analysis of CNVs in a cohort of individuals with limb malformations 
revealed that nearly half of these causal variants caused position effects 
that could be linked to disease mechanisms102.
Tandem duplications. Tandem duplications are one of the major 
classes of duplications, with direct-orientation tandem duplication 
accounting for 80% of all duplications103. Tandem duplications encom-
passing a TAD boundary can cause ectopic enhancer activation and 
Fig. 2 | Enhancer hijacking and topologically associating domain 
reorganization. a, Topologically associating domains (TADs) function 
as self-contained regulatory units51, within which cis-regulatory elements 
(such as enhancers and silencers) control gene expression. These domains are 
separated by CTCF-bound boundary elements (left). Within a TAD, an enhancer 
A specifically regulates the expression of its target gene A in a spatiotemporal 
manner — for example, in the limb bud during embryonic development. However, 
SVs that span TAD boundaries (inter-TAD SVs) can lead to TAD reorganization. 
This can reposition foreign cis-regulatory elements in close proximity — both 
spatially and linearly — to genes they would not normally regulate, allowing 
aberrant enhancer–promoter interactions. This process, known as enhancer 
hijacking or enhancer adoption, can drive gene misexpression and cause disease 
(right). As a result, enhancer A, which originally controlled gene A in the limb bud, 
now ectopically activates gene B in the same region. Previously, the expression 
of gene B was restricted to the spinal column owing to the tissue and temporal 
specificity of enhancer B. Three types of TAD reorganization have been 
described, each distinguished by the nature of the SV. b, TAD fusion25: deletion of 
a TAD boundary disrupts the original TADs flanking the SV breakpoints, leading 
to their fusion into a single, larger domain. c, Neo-TAD formation104: a tandem 
duplication that includes a TAD boundary, along with a regulatory element and 
a gene from adjacent TADs, can create a neo-TAD. This newly formed domain 
increases interactions between the duplicated regulatory element and gene, 
which were previously separated by a boundary, potentially resulting in enhancer 
hijacking. d, TAD shuffling18: translocations and inversions spanning TAD 
boundaries bring distant genomic regions into proximity, effectively reshuffling 
TADs. Inversions and balanced translocations typically create two shuffled 
TADs, both of which can serve as sites for enhancer hijacking. Non-tandem or 
insertional duplications can also contribute to neo-TAD formation. Additionally, 
deletions, translocations and inversions can lead to the loss of a cis-regulatory 
element for a gene, a phenomenon known as disconnection, which can impair 
gene expression.

gene misexpression, owing to the formation of neo-TADs104 (Fig. 2). 
Neo-TADs arise from the formation of new chromatin loops that enable 
ectopic contacts between genes and regulatory element regions pre-
viously well isolated from each other, while retaining the previous 
TADs (Fig. 3b). A recent clinical example of neo-TAD formation and 
ectopic enhancer activation as a disease mechanism was found in 
individuals from two unrelated families affected by isolated bilateral 
hypoplasia of the femoral and pelvic bones17. These individuals had 
~0.5-Mb tandem duplications on chromosome 10q24.32. Although the 
duplication directly affected six genes, duplications affecting all but 
FGF8 had been reported to cause split/hand malformation. Moreover, 
individuals with smaller duplications of FGF8 do not exhibit a skeletal 
phenotype, indicating that the disease mechanism likely does not 
result from altered FGF8 dosage. Chromatin capture experiments in 
patient fibroblasts and in the hindlimbs of a mouse model revealed 
that duplications resulted in increased chromatin contacts between 
FGF8 and an enhancer region in the neighbouring TAD (Fig. 3b). The 
mouse model exhibited skeletal abnormalities of the limbs and severe 
shortening of the humeral and femoral bones, mirroring the human 
phenotype. Increased FGF8 expression in patient fibroblasts, along with 
altered expression in developing limb buds, suggested that ectopic 
expression was driven by enhancer adoption. The study ruled out 
gene dosage effects by simultaneously introducing a duplication in 
one allele and a deletion in the second allele, which still resulted in the 
skeletal phenotype17.
Neo-TAD formation and enhancer adoption were recently shown 
to occur owing to duplications at the Xq26.3 locus, causing aggres-
sive growth hormone-secreting pituitary tumours during early 
childhood in individuals with X-linked acrogigantism105. Here, the 
duplications involving a tissue-invariant and evolutionarily conserved 
TAD boundary introduced ectopic contacts between GPR101 and mul-
tiple pituitary-specific enhancers, predicted by GeneHancer106, from 
the neighbouring TAD. Validations by the luciferase reporter assay 
confirmed that several of these GPR101–enhancer interactions were 
driving gene expression in pituitary tumour cells but not in embryonic 
kidney cells. Another recent example includes multiple tandem dupli-
cations linked to retinitis pigmentosa, in which neo-TAD formation 
resulted in the misexpression of GDPD1. The gene GDPD1 is normally 
lowly expressed everywhere except in testis and brain but showed 
tissue-specific ectopic activation by retinal YPEL enhancers107. Similar 
neo-TAD formation can occur in the case of higher CNVs, such as in the 
case of triplications at the Xp21.2 locus, causing 46,XY mild-to-total 
gonadal dysgenesis108,109.
Non-tandem duplications. In non-tandem or insertional duplica-
tions, the duplicated region is relocated outside its original genomic 
context, facilitating ectopic interactions between newly juxtaposed 
genes and regulatory elements110. A notable example of gene misexpres-
sion resulting from a non-tandem duplication is an isolated case of an 
ultra-rare, rapidly progressive form of heterotopic ossification, with 
disease onset at 5 months of age and death at 8 years from respiratory 
complications111. An 820-kb duplicated region from chromosome 2 
containing eight genes was found to be inserted into Xq26.1. Hi-C indi-
cated ectopic inter-chromosomal contacts between chromosome 2 
and the X chromosome around the breakpoints. Gene-dosage-based 
disease mechanisms were ruled out for all eight duplicated genes, 
because two of them lacked functional transcripts and the other six 
were functionally irrelevant and/or were not overexpressed based on 
RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) in fibroblasts. However, Hi-C data showed 
the formation of two neo-TADs on either ends of the insertion (Fig. 4). 
The neo-TAD centromeric to the insertion contains the gene ARHGAP36, 
which was found to have the greatest upregulation of any gene in the 
proband. The enhancer prediction tool CRUP112 indicated adoption of 
the predicted enhancers, which are active in fibroblasts, chondrocytes 
and bone marrow cells. Follow-up experiments further demonstrated 
that overexpression of ARHGAP36 in mesenchymal stromal cells results 
in upregulation of pathways related to skeletal development, providing 
a likely disease mechanism111.
Another example of non-tandem duplication involves duplica-
tions at the HOXD genes causing Fryns type mesomelic dysplasia in two 
patients113. Here, the duplicated regions were inserted in an inverted 
orientation between the HOXD cluster and its telomeric enhancers. 
Although the exact pathomechanism remains unknown, the authors 
proposed that the phenotype could result from a combination of the 
disconnection of forearm-specific telomeric enhancers from the 
HOXD9–HOXD11 genes, because of the increased linear distance, and/or 
hijacking of these enhancers by the duplicated digit-specific HOXD13 
gene, which is now expressed early during forearm development114. 
Identifying which of these two mechanisms has the more dominant 
causal effect will require profiling local chromatin architecture and 
interactions in the duplicated allele.
Balanced SVs affecting TAD boundaries
Given that balanced SVs do not lead to a change in the copy number 
of genomic elements, their effects are exclusively a result of sequence 
disruptions, fusions and position effects, with TAD organization having 
a determining role (Fig. 2).
Translocations. Translocations relocate large chromosomal regions 
(thousands to millions base pairs), either separating or juxtaposing 
genomic elements, leading to enhancer disconnection or hijacking. 
A recent example of gene misexpression by enhancer adoption was 
reported in a large family, in which six individuals exhibited central 
iris hypoplasia, which is characterized by enlarged pupils owing

demarcate active enhancers116, across various tissues from the EpiMap 
database117, the authors identified a tissue-specific enhancer cluster 
active in the eye and embryonic stem cells near the chromosome 6 
breakpoint, which was repositioned to the derived chromosome 18 
in patients. RNA-seq data revealed that APCDD1, now positioned adja-
cent to the enhancer cluster in patients, was the only gene among 12 
genes neighbouring the breakpoints to be upregulated by more than 
twofold. Simultaneous loss of GJA1 expression owing to enhancer 
disconnection was observed but could not be linked to the phenotype. 
Enhancer knockout experiments confirmed that APCDD1 overexpres-
sion was driven by ectopic contacts in the shuffled TAD, and a zebrafish 
model with overexpressed APCDD1 paralogues validated the disease 
mechanism.
Enhancer disconnection due to translocations can also have an 
impact on dosage-sensitive genes. A notable example is PAX6 haploin-
sufficiency causing aniridia, a partial or complete absence of the iris. 
In 2 individuals from a cohort of 110, a t(6;11) translocation — initially 
dismissed as non-causal owing to non-coding breakpoints — was found 
to downregulate PAX6 expression by disrupting one enhancer and 
removing another more distal enhancer118. Thus, the disease mecha-
nism arising from translocations can be manifold, including new regula-
tory contacts established via shuffled TADs, loss-of-function because of 
removal of chromatin contacts with enhancers across the breakpoint, 
or disruption and fusion of functional genomic elements.
TAD shuffling, enhancer hijacking and subsequent ectopic expres-
sion of oncogenes are frequent in cancer in the form of recurrent chro-
mosomal translocations73,96. A recent study identified 46 translocation 
events in 14 out of 18 patients newly diagnosed as having T-lineage acute 
lymphoblastic leukaemia with half of the identified breakpoints located 
in non-coding regions119. A total of six neo-TAD formations resulted in 
ectopic contacts of three genes, TLX3, TAL2 and HOXA, with multiple 
putative enhancers. These enhancers were shown to be active in Jurkat 
and Loucy T-lineage acute lymphoblastic leukaemia cells, suggesting 
that translocations can lead to misexpression of otherwise silenced 
genes to modulate the cancer phenotype.
Inversions. Inversions that cross TAD boundaries can create shuffled 
TADs, causing gene misexpression. A recently described isolated case 
of an 89-Mb inversion was confirmed to be causative of branchio-oculo-
facial syndrome120. Whole-genome short-read sequencing uncovered 
that one of the heterozygous inversion breakpoints was located ~40 kb 
downstream of the TFAP2A gene, which was previously associated with 
branchio-oculo-facial syndrome in humans121 and mice122,123. On the 
basis of histone chromatin immunoprecipitation followed by sequenc-
ing (ChIP–seq), ATAC-seq and circular chromosome conformation 
capture (4C) data, activated and functional enhancers were identified in 
human iPSC-derived neural crest cells (NCCs) within, but across one of 
the breakpoints, the TFAP2A-TAD120 (Fig. 5b). CRISPR–Cas9 deletion of 
the identified regulatory region from control cells resulted not only in 
a reduction of TFAP2A expression but also delayed NCC differentiation. 
Allele-specific RNA-seq analysis in patient-iPSC-derived NCCs indicated 
that TFAP2A expression stemmed exclusively from the wild-type allele. 
Expectedly, allele-specific 4C experiments further confirmed loss 
of interaction of TFAP2A with its cognate enhancers in the inverted 
allele. Interestingly, none of the genes brought close to the cognate 
TFAP2A enhancers by the inversion appeared dysregulated, hinting 
that enhancer hijacking is contingent on other factors. As a result, the 
disease mechanism in this patient seemed to be haploinsufficiency 
owing to enhancer disconnection.
In another example, a combination of enhancer disconnection and 
gene disruption was found to be causal of the complete phenotype in 
the case of two maternal half-brothers with muscular dystrophy, autism 
spectrum disorder, developmental delay and sensorineural hearing 
loss124. Both had inherited a pericentric inversion from the carrier 
mother, with one breakpoint within the intron of the DMD gene and 
a second one upstream of the POU3F4 gene. Although the disruption 
of the DMD gene explained the muscular dystrophy, enhancer discon-
nection from POU3F4 correlated with the hearing loss experienced by 
these individuals.
Context dependency of  
TAD-mediated dysregulation
Enhancer hijacking or disconnection is increasingly accepted as a dis-
ease mechanism of SVs in close proximity to known disease genes, 
at least in the research context. Indeed, deletion of boundaries next 
to developmentally relevant and disease genes results in discern-
ible phenotypes45 and is increasingly being considered as sufficient 
evidence of pathomechanism8. However, not all TAD boundary dele-
tions result in enhancer hijacking and ectopic gene expression. In fact, 
individuals carrying complex genomic rearrangements (Box 1) in the 
germline with no or mild symptoms have been reported125. A study by 
the Pan-Cancer Analysis of Whole Genomes Consortium on somatic 
and germline SVs in 2,658 cancers found that only 14% of the 2,655 
boundary-affecting deletions resulted in greater than twofold change 
in expression of genes in the affected TADs, even after accounting for 
the inherent transcriptional activities of the TADs being fused71. Similar 
percentages have been reported from gene expression assays on the 
highly rearranged balancer chromosome in Drosophila melanogaster126. 
TAD boundary deletion experiments at multiple developmentally 
critical genomic loci have further confirmed the robustness of TAD 
boundaries and corroborated the, increasingly accepted, non-essential 
role of TADs in the regulation of gene expression127,128. Together, these 
lines of evidence suggest that TADs are instructive in gene regulation, 
but their disruption does not always perturb gene expression. Other 
mechanisms must be at play, and the interpretation of variant-induced 
changes to TADs must take these factors into account.
Compensatory mechanisms and tissue specificity
CTCF-binding sites at TAD boundaries are often clustered129–132, which 
offers buffering against deletion of these sites. This compensatory 
mechanism was found to provide robustness to the boundary between 
TADs at the MEF2C locus130 and at the Kit locus133, which harbours the 
developmental regulator genes Pdgfra, Kit and Kdr, each located in 
a separate TAD demarcated by strong boundaries, and where the 
boundary shifted towards the next intra-TAD CTCF-binding site upon 
CTCF-motif deletion. Sequences upstream and downstream of TAD 
CTCF-binding motifs also seem to contribute to the boundary insula-
tion, at least in the Sox2 domain, via binding of CTCF zinc fingers to 
DNA134. Thus, removal of an individual CTCF-binding site rarely results 
in enhancer hijacking owing to compensatory mechanisms that provide 
robustness to the 3D genome.
Even when SVs create new TADs, enhancer hijacking depends on 
the local regulatory landscape135. CpG-methylated genes can resist 
enhancer adoption136, whereas competition between transcription fac-
tors, CTCF and cohesin influences chromatin contacts60. For instance, 
at the mouse Kit locus, boundary deletion triggered tissue-specific Kdr 
activation in melanocytes but not in mast cells, in which Kdr remained 
repressed133. Tissue-specific enhancers and active transcription can

stabilize gene regulation, preventing enhancer adoption even in dis-
rupted TADs137–139. Transcripts of a gene can also show differential 
enhancer adoption in a tissue-specific way, as was found recently in 
a case of retinal dystrophy110. Together, whether enhancer hijacking 
takes place is dependent on the regulatory and the transcriptional 
landscapes within the TADs being reorganized.
Although TADs are broadly conserved, their internal contacts and 
even their existence can be tissue-specific26,140,141. SV effects vary across 
tissues, influenced by cohesin loading at enhancers or active promoters 
and phase separation driven by master transcription factors67,142–144. 
A recent study suggested that phase separation caused by high con-
centrations of master transcription factors is critical in manipulating 
TADs in preparation for reprogramming and achieving cell-type-
specific chromatin conformation144. These phase-separation-based 
chromatin ‘nanodomains’ in turn might also be a mechanism that 
provides robustness to TAD boundaries upon boundary deletions144,145. 
Understanding such mechanisms is relevant to diagnostics, espe-
cially in the light of a recent finding that frameshift mutations in the 
DNA-binding protein HMGB1 cause aberrant, altered phase separation, 
leading to brachyphalangy, polydactyly and tibial aplasia/hypoplasia 
syndrome146. Deletions at the PITX1 locus that cause Liebenberg 
syndrome also lead to tissue-specific misexpression. The deletion 
removes a hindlimb-specific insulator between PITX1 and its native 
enhancer Pen, which normally drives PITX1 expression only in the 
forelimb. This phenomenon, in which ectopic expression is driven 
by the native enhancer of a gene, is termed ‘regulatory endoactiva-
tion’147. Intriguingly, the insulating element deleted here seems to be 
non-canonical and appears to depend on the active transcription of a 
house-keeping gene. Finally, CTCF-binding motifs contain CpG and 
can undergo tissue-specific and allele-specific methylation, as in the 
case of the H19–IGF2 locus148,149. CTCF has a lower binding affinity for 
methylated sites150, which provides another layer of tissue specificity 
to TAD boundaries.
Gene regulation across boundaries
TAD boundaries have been demonstrated to bring together 
cis-regulatory elements from two separate TADs, rather than insulating 
them, by a process referred to as boundary stacking151. TAD formation 
in such cases has the effect of reducing the spatial distance between 
promoters and distal enhancers from neighbouring TADs152. The block-
ing effect of CTCF is subject to DNA tension153, providing yet another 
mechanism to allow cross-boundary interactions. As mentioned ear-
lier, strong enhancer–promoter interactions, such as developmental 
enhancers, can span TAD boundaries66,154 — a mechanism that seems 
to be at play at the DBX2 locus, in which the mammalian-specific distal 
limb enhancers regulate three genes separated by TAD boundaries155.
Protein complexes other than cohesin and CTCFs can also medi-
ate long-range interactions independent of TAD boundaries, such as 
the Polycomb-repressive complexes that mediate interactions across 
genomic distances up to 100 times farther than CTCF-mediated 
contacts156–159. In fact, high-resolution chromatin maps obtained 
with Micro-C indicate that more than 20% of enhancer–promoter 
contacts span TAD boundaries66. Nonrandom chromatin interac-
tions at much larger scales have also been shown to be physiologi-
cally relevant. For example, a recent study identified that increased 
chromatin contacts across the 33 Mb-long p-arm of chromosome 16 
mediate the convergence of functional consequences of common 
autism spectrum disorder-associated variants in 16p and rare autism 
spectrum disorder-associated CNVs located in 16p11.2 (ref. 160). 
The exact mechanisms that facilitate chromatin interactions across 
such long genomic distances, and even across chromosomes, and 
how exactly these long-range contacts are perturbed by SVs requires 
further investigation161,162.
In summary, the currently available evidence indicates that multi-
ple levels of 3D genome architecture, including the chromosomal terri-
tories, chromosomal A/B compartments and their sub-compartments, 
as well as genomic looping mediated by cohesin and other

have provided great insight into the dynamics and predictability of 
evolution. The rise of high-throughput sequencing technologies over 
the past two decades has driven a massive expansion in the scale and 
power of these experiments. However, until recently our abilities to 
connect genetic with phenotypic changes and analyse the molecular 
basis of adaptation have remained limited. Rapid technical advances 
to measure and manipulate both genotypes and phenotypes are now 
providing opportunities to investigate the genetic basis of phenotypic 
evolution and the forces that drive evolutionary dynamics. Here 
we review how these methodological advances are being used to 
predict and manipulate the course of laboratory evolution, analyse 
eco-evolutionary interactions, and how they are beginning to bridge 
the gap between laboratory and natural evolution.

at the genetic level.
In this Review, we examine the technological advances that are 
reshaping the field of experimental evolution. We begin by overviewing 
these technologies that enable manipulating and measuring geno-
types and phenotypes at scale, specifically barcoding, lineage track-
ing, high-throughput phenotyping and gene-editing approaches. We 
then focus on three areas of research for which new tools are having 
a substantial impact: predicting and potentially controlling evolu-
tionary outcomes, understanding of eco-evolutionary interactions, 
and bridging the gap between laboratory and natural evolution. As 
we explore these developments, we discuss how the integration of 
high-throughput technologies with classical experimental evolution 
approaches is reshaping our understanding of evolutionary processes 
and enabling for a more predictive science of evolution.
Manipulating and measuring genotypes and 
phenotypes at scale
Recent technological advances in high-throughput sequencing, 
genome editing and phenotyping methods have dramatically expanded 
our ability to manipulate and measure genetic and phenotypic changes 
at unprecedented scales, transforming how evolution is studied in the 
laboratory. These methodological breakthroughs enable researchers 
to systematically explore genotype–phenotype relationships across 
thousands of variants simultaneously.
Barcoding, lineage tracking and  
high-throughput phenotyping
Since its introduction into experimental evolution about a decade 
ago, DNA barcoding has revolutionized our ability to analyse evolv-
ing populations27. This technique involves stably integrating diverse, 
short (typically 8–30 bp) and random DNA sequences into the genome, 
permanently marking each lineage with a unique ‘barcode’ identifier 
(Fig. 1). By amplicon sequencing these barcode regions, researchers 
can measure the relative frequencies of different lineages. As potential 
barcode diversity is generally high compared with actual diversity, 
true barcodes differ by multiple mutations and thus barcodes can be 
correctly identified even in the face of sequencing errors. Therefore, 
the resolution of this approach is limited only by sequencing depth and 
barcode diversity33,34; it is typically possible to detect lineages present 
at frequencies as low as 10−6.
DNA barcoding has been used to analyse how the dynamics of 
competing lineages within a population shape long-term evolutionary 
outcomes. Researchers introduce diverse barcodes at a neutral locus to 
label lineages within an initially clonal microbial population, and track 
their frequencies through time as lineages acquire mutations and their 
frequencies change owing to genetic drift and natural selection27,29,35. 
Provided barcode diversity is sufficiently high, each lineage initially 
consists of only a few cells, making it possible to infer the distribution of 
fitness effects of the mutations that drive short-term evolution36. This 
approach makes it possible to directly observe evolutionary dynam-
ics in real time and better understand how evolutionary forces shape 
statistical patterns of genetic diversity and evolutionary trajectories. 
For example, such work has helped to reveal that beneficial mutations 
occur at surprisingly high rates in microbial populations, with multiple 
advantageous variants arising and competing simultaneously27,29. This 
pervasive clonal interference, rather than sequential selective sweeps, 
maintains substantial genetic variation within asexual populations even 
during strong directional selection, blurring the distinction between 
Introduction
All the diversity of the biological world — the disparate forms and func-
tions we find across organisms — has been generated by evolution. As 
evolutionary processes typically occur over long timescales, evolution 
has historically been studied almost exclusively retrospectively, infer-
ring past evolutionary dynamics through palaeontology or population 
genetics. These approaches have provided fundamental insights into 
many aspects of evolution, including the importance of stochastic 
forces such as genetic drift and the role of historical contingency1,2. 
However, evolutionary processes can also be studied through experi-
mental evolution, in which populations of organisms are cultivated in 
laboratory conditions, to observe evolution in real time while control-
ling and manipulating key parameters such as population sizes, genetic 
backgrounds, spatial structure, mutation rates and environmental 
conditions. This approach is particularly powerful for understanding 
the relative contributions of deterministic and stochastic forces, as 
replicate populations provide insights into the repeatability of evo-
lutionary outcomes by controlling for initial conditions. Thus, experi-
mental evolution offers opportunities to test hypotheses generated 
from natural systems in controlled settings and to explore alternative 
evolutionary trajectories that may not be accessible through the study 
of historical patterns alone.
Early laboratory evolution experiments pioneered the use of 
simplified microbial systems to study fundamental questions in 
evolution3–8. Among the most famous is the Escherichia coli long-term 
evolution experiment (LTEE), initiated by Richard Lenski in 1988, which 
has tracked the evolution of 12 replicate E. coli populations in a simple, 
constant environment for more than 35 years so far. The LTEE and 
other evolution experiments have provided important insights into 
the tempo of genetic evolution9, the role of fitness landscapes and 
epistasis10–12, niche partitioning and eco-evolutionary dynamics5,13–15. 
These experiments generally rely on relatively small numbers of repli-
cate populations, and have used low-throughput and indirect methods 
(for example, clonal sequencing16,17 and colorimetric6,18 or fluorescent 
markers19) to measure any evolved genetic and phenotypic changes. 
Partly because of the limitations of such methods, researchers faced 
substantial challenges in characterizing the properties of inherently 
stochastic evolutionary processes, connecting observed genotypic 
changes to phenotypic outcomes, and establishing clear links between 
laboratory evolution and natural evolutionary dynamics. These limita-
tions have underscored the critical need for more modern techniques 
and approaches in experimental evolution.
Over the past two decades, the field of experimental evolution has 
responded to the need for more modern techniques by undergoing 
a dramatic transformation driven by advances in high-throughput 
sequencing and liquid handling20,21. The use of high-throughput 
sequencing to track genome evolution has now become almost rou-
tine in experimental evolution, enabling researchers to track genetic 
changes over extended time periods and across hundreds or even 
thousands of replicate populations. Advances in high-throughput 
library preparation have made it possible to sequence hundreds to 
thousands of individual clones9,22–24 or metagenomic samples25,26, also 
enabling researchers to quantify the evolution of genetic diversity 
through time. Furthermore, techniques such as DNA barcoding har-
ness the power of high-throughput sequencing to connect these geno-
types to phenotypic outcomes in highly parallelized assays27–29, and 
new genome-editing methods enable researchers to create millions 
of genetic variants in parallel30–32. Together, these methods have 
opened many new avenues of enquiry, such as investigations of the 

Nature Reviews Genetics | Volume 27 | January 2026 | 81–95
83
Review article
adaptation from new mutations and adaptation from standing genetic 
variation.
Barcode tracking experiments face two main limitations. First, 
selection reduces and eventually eliminates barcode diversity, obscur-
ing future dynamics. Recent work has addressed this challenge by devel-
oping methods to efficiently re-barcode populations and periodically 
restore diversity29. Second, identifying the mutations responsible for 
fitness changes in specific lineages typically requires labour-intensive 
single-cell or single-clone sequencing22. Although this limitation can 
be partially addressed by coupling barcoding with high-throughput 
genome manipulation methods, such deliberately introduced 
­mutations may not reflect naturally occurring evolutionary changes.
Beyond lineage tracking, DNA barcoding can be used to efficiently 
measure any phenotype that can be quantified based on relative bar-
code enrichments. This approach has been valuable in microbial func-
tional genomics for identifying gene function through genome-wide 
barcoded knockout studies28,30,37,38. For example, researchers have 
used barcoded knockout approaches to identify genes involved in 
stress response, such as heavy metal tolerance and motility30. Bar-
coded knockout experiments inspired by such functional genomic 
screens have recently been used to probe how the distribution of fitness 
effects changes across evolutionary time39,40, and represent prom-
ising approaches in general to measure statistical distributions of 
evolutionary trajectories and phenotypic effects of mutations. More 
sophisticated experimental designs enable measurement of other, 
more complex phenotypes of interest (Box 1). For example, a recent 
study used barcoded H1N1 influenza virus variants to simultaneously 
measure neutralization by human sera across numerous related viral 
strains41, providing insights into the evolutionary dynamics governing 
viral escape from antibody-mediated immunity.
Constructing and manipulating genomes
A key challenge in barcoded evolution experiments is connecting 
observed changes in competitive fitness to their underlying genetic 
causes and broader phenotypic effects. Even when sequencing iden-
tifies mutations in evolved lineages, determining which mutations

drive phenotypic changes remains difficult owing to the abundance 
of passenger mutations25. To address this limitation, researchers have 
developed various high-throughput genome manipulation methods 
that enable systematic measurement of both competitive fitness effects 
and, in some cases, specific phenotypes across many engineered gen-
otypes (Fig. 2). Many of these methods were developed to address 
challenges in functional genomics and have been widely applied to 
that field28,30,38,42; however, we focus here on how such methods can 
be applied to questions that arise in experimental evolution. These 
methods vary in both methodology and scope, ranging from satu-
rating mutagenesis approaches that systematically explore local fit-
ness landscapes to combinatorial methods that examine all possible 
­combinations of selected mutations.
At the genome level, saturating mutagenesis has been imple-
mented through techniques such as barcoded transposon muta­
genesis28,30. This approach uses transposons that randomly insert 
themselves into microbial genomes, disrupting gene expression and 
creating knockout mutations. With sufficient coverage, every gene in 
the genome can be disrupted multiple times. A single high-throughput 
sequencing step links each barcoded transposon to its genomic loca-
tion, which enables subsequent barcode sequencing to measure the 
fitness effects of thousands of knockouts in parallel. This technique can 
provide a crucial bridge between adaptive mutations identified in evolu-
tion experiments and their phenotypic consequences by systematically 
perturbing the same genes that acquire mutations during adaptation. 
For example, recent work has revealed how knockout effects change 
during long-term evolution in the LTEE39,40, demonstrating that genes 
acquiring adaptive mutations often show substantial fitness effects 
when disrupted, and that these effects change predictably as popula-
tions adapt to their environment. Similar studies in Saccharomyces 
cerevisiae43 have shown that the distribution of beneficial and deleteri-
ous knockout mutations changes predictably with background fitness, 
helping explain the diminishing returns patterns observed across mul-
tiple experimental evolution systems. Related approaches include 
genome-wide barcoded CRISPR interference, which has been used 
to generate knockdown libraries and titrate gene expression44,45, ena-
bling researchers to correlate the degree of expression change with 
fitness outcomes and better understand the mechanistic basis of 
adaptive expression changes. Conversely, genome-wide overexpres-
sion libraries can be used to probe the effects of increased expres-
sion of any given gene in the genome42, often mimicking the effects 
of promoter mutations observed in evolution experiments. Other 
methods such as CRISPEY-BAR (Cas9 retron precise parallel editing 
via homology with barcoding)46,47 have been used to introduce spe-
cific, natural variants into multiple different S. cerevisiae genetic back-
grounds. In doing so, this method has revealed widespread background 
dependence of mutations31 and provided direct evidence for how the 
same adaptive mutations identified in laboratory evolution can have 
context-dependent phenotypic effects.
Saturating mutagenesis approaches can also be applied at the 
level of the evolution of individual proteins, through techniques such 
as deep mutational scanning (DMS)32,48,49. DMS approaches generally 
aim to quantify not only the competitive fitness effects but also spe-
cific molecular phenotypes, such as binding affinity, protein stability 
or enzymatic activity, for all possible single amino acid changes to 
a protein using error-prone PCR (or related methods) coupled with 
pooled assays. DMS approaches have been applied to a wide variety of 
different proteins, enabling researchers to quantify which sites tolerate 
mutations and those that might enable fitness gains. These approaches 
have been used to forecast protein evolution; for example, by using 
DMS on influenza and SARS-CoV-2 proteins, researchers have been 
able to predict which evolutionary paths are probably available to the 
pathogens by uncovering mutations that enhance host cell receptor 
binding and immune escape32,48,49.
Box 1 | Phenotypes important for evolutionary dynamics
 
We define a phenotype as any measurable property of an organism 
affected by some combination of genetic, environmental or 
stochastic causes. Under this definition, the relative reproductive 
success of a given genotype (that is, its fitness) is considered a 
phenotype, albeit a special one that directly affects short-term 
evolutionary dynamics. The high-throughput methods described 
throughout this Review have dramatically improved our ability to 
measure fitness — along with other phenotypes — across large 
numbers of genotypes, enabling us to investigate the statistical 
patterns that shape evolutionary trajectories.
The distribution of fitness effects of new mutations represents one 
of the most fundamental statistical properties governing evolution. 
Experimental measurements across diverse systems have revealed 
general patterns that shape distributions of fitness effects — such 
as widespread diminishing returns and increasing costs epistasis — 
providing evidence for general statistical principles in adaptation 
despite the idiosyncratic molecular details of specific mutations.
Beyond fitness measurements, it is often unclear which other 
phenotypes should be measured in an evolving population to gain 
insight into the underlying evolutionary process. When we have an 
a priori reason to be interested in specific phenotypes (for example, 
disease phenotypes, transcriptomes or antibody-binding affinities), 
tracking how these phenotypes change across replicate populations 
and evolutionary time can reveal the forces driving phenotypic 
evolution. Such information may enable researchers to predict and 
potentially manipulate phenotypic evolution during future adaptation. 
For example, by systematically measuring how environmental 
conditions alter the relationship between specific phenotypes and 
fitness, experimenters could develop predictive models for how these 
phenotypes will evolve under new or changing conditions.
Alternatively, we may measure phenotypes because we believe 
they are important determinants of selection. Quantifying how multiple 
phenotypes collectively contribute to fitness through statistical 
modelling approaches might enable us to forecast evolutionary 
trajectories under novel conditions. When it is unclear which 
phenotypes contribute to fitness, one study169 proposed measuring 
fitness in various environments and using linear decomposition to 
infer abstracted ‘fitnotypes’ that could predict fitness effects in other 
environments. However, such predictions face an inherent difficulty: 
fitness typically emerges from complex, often nonlinear interactions 
among multiple traits and genetic variants in specific environments. 
This complexity means that even large phenotypic datasets and 
sophisticated models may struggle to accurately generalize beyond 
the immediate neighbourhood of the dataset.

tools can generate an order of magnitude more combinations. For 
example, a recent study used a recombining CRISPR-gene drive system 
in S. cerevisiae to construct most of the possible 210 = 1,024 combina-
