Partly owing to the ease of working with smaller sequences, com-
binatorial gene-editing methods have been applied more widely at the 
level of nucleotide sequences and proteins to investigate intra-protein 
epistatic interactions between residues51–56. As before, a priori infor-
mation is often needed to choose which genetic variants to include. 
For example, one study chose to mutate just three residues known 
to be important in conferring trimethoprim resistance in a key E. coli 
metabolic gene, folA, which encodes dihydrofolate reductase57. Each of 
the three residues were mutated such that each site could be any of the 
20 amino acids, resulting in nearly 49 = 262,144 variants. This study 
found a fitness landscape with many separated peaks (indicating a 
rough landscape), but the highest peaks were all nevertheless found 
to be accessible through paths that monotonically increase fitness. 
Another option is to construct all possible evolutionary intermediates 
between a known wild-type sequence and an evolved sequence58–60. 
Exploring all intermediates has enabled the elucidation of the evo-
lutionary and epistatic forces that shaped protein evolution and 
the constraints on evolutionary trajectories. This approach has also 
proved valuable for understanding how epistatic interactions constrain 
directed evolution efforts, as demonstrated in studies of industrially 
relevant proteins such as tryptophan synthase61.
Predicting and manipulating evolution
A fundamental question in evolutionary biology is the extent to which 
evolution is repeatable and predictable62–64. The degree and manner of 
predictability is thought to depend on both the genotype–phenotype–
fitness map and the relative strength of various population genetic 
forces — such as natural selection, genetic drift and mutation — acting 
on the population36,65,66. Recent studies leveraging high-throughput 
methods have revealed that evolution typically shows high levels of 
phenotypic repeatability but relatively lower levels of genetic repeat-
ability. For instance, when replicate populations are evolved under iden-
tical conditions, they often achieve similar fitness improvements and 
converge on similar phenotypic solutions, but the underlying genetic 
changes can vary substantially across replicates12,26,67 (Fig. 3 and Sup-
plementary Information). Such phenotypic repeatability implies a 
many-to-one relationship between genotypes and phenotypes, and 
has also been referred to as ‘genetic redundancy’ 68.
The application of high-throughput molecular phenotyping 
approaches has begun to reveal the mechanistic basis for pheno-
typic repeatability. These methods have shown how different genetic 
changes can produce similar effects on phenotypes through vari-
ous mechanisms. For example, studies combining evolution experi-
ments with transcriptomic profiling have revealed how distinct 
mutations and evolutionary paths can lead to similar gene expression 
changes69 and similar changes in traits such as cell size70. The hierar-
chy of phenotypic organization has a crucial role in determining the 
level at which evolutionary outcomes become predictable. Recent 
work using high-throughput phenotyping has shown that although 
genetic changes may be highly variable, they often affect a common set 
of cellular processes or regulatory pathways71. Similarly, metabolomics 
approaches have revealed how different genetic changes can lead to 
similar alterations in metabolic fluxes in experimental systems72.
Global patterns of epistasis have emerged as crucial factors driving 
evolutionary repeatability. Epistasis has long been recognized to have 
an important role in evolutionary dynamics, but traditional experi-
mental approaches were limited to studying interactions between 
small numbers of mutations. Experimental evolution helped to shift 
our understanding of the patterns and role of epistasis by revealing 
genetic interactions between large numbers of genetic variants across 
the genome. Specifically, studies tracking adaptation in replicate popu-
lations first identified the striking pattern that beneficial mutations 
yield diminishing returns in more fit backgrounds, whereas deleterious 
mutations become increasingly costly43,67,73. In contrast to traditional 
genetic approaches that could generally identify epistasis between spe-
cific mutations, experimental evolution with whole-genome sequenc-
ing showed how fitness effects depend on the background fitness of the 
organism, regardless of the specific mutations involved. Such patterns 
of global epistasis have revealed that whereas epistatic interactions 
could, in principle, be incredibly high dimensional, they seem gener-
ally more low dimensional with the phenotypic effects of mutations 
being largely explained by background fitness alone (Box 2). This pat-
tern can explain how genetically distinct mutations can nevertheless 
produce similar phenotypic outcomes, leading to genetic variability 
despite phenotypic convergence12. Recent work using high-throughput 
methods to construct and measure the effects of large numbers of 
mutations has revealed that these patterns of global epistasis can arise 
from idiosyncratic epistatic interactions50, ­confirming theoretical 
predictions74.
Eco-evolutionary interactions
Experimental evolution has repeatedly shown that even in simple, 
constant environments, microbial populations often develop complex 
ecological interactions, including the stable coexistence of distinct 
lineages. High-throughput methods are providing deeper insights into 
the mechanisms underlying these emergent ecological dynamics and 
how they shape ongoing evolutionary trajectories.
Characterizing emergent ecological forces
One of the most striking findings in experimental evolution is the spon-
taneous emergence of negative frequency-dependent selection and 
stable coexistence of lineages5,13,15,26,75–81. Such ecological diversifica-
tion has been found to occur with surprising frequency, even in envi-
ronments specifically designed to minimize ecological complexity82 
(Fig. 4). These simple ecological communities have been detected 
across unrelated systems (although they do not arise in all experi-
mental systems83). These lineages maintain their coexistence through 
various mechanisms, including resource partitioning15,84, spatial niche 
construction76 or cross-feeding5,77,85. Importantly, adaptive evolution 
continues beyond initial diversification — coexisting lineages coevolve, 
diverging at genetic, transcriptomic and metabolomic levels26,86–88. This 
ongoing coevolution can alter the relative frequencies of lineages and, 
in some cases, lead to the extinction of one lineage, thereby collapsing 
the ecological system26,76,89. Similar dynamics have been observed in 
natural populations, including in the microbial communities of the 
human90 and mouse gut91. Together, these observations have led to 
the crucial realization that ecological and evolutionary dynamics often 
occur on similar timescales in microbial communities. This insight has 
sparked a surge of interest in using experimental evolution to better 
understand eco-evolutionary dynamics.
High-throughput methods have improved our ability to charac-
terize the nature and evolution of emergent ecological interactions,

generations13,86. These lineages were named S and L for their small and 
large colony sizes, respectively, on certain agar plates; the obvious 
phenotypic differences were key to uncovering the ecological structure 
of the population. It was later found that the mechanism of coexistence 
primarily relied on metabolic niche specialization and glucose-acetate 
cross-feeding14,85,88. For a time, this ecological diversification was 
thought to be a fluke — a population that stumbled upon a rare evolu-

metagenomic sequencing to characterize the genetic changes that have 
occurred over 60,000 generations of evolutionary time in the E. coli 
LTEE26. Contrary to prior expectations, this study found that ecologi-
cal diversification into two coexisting lineages occurred in 9 out of the 
12 populations and was followed by subsequent coevolution of both 
lineages. The unbiased and high-throughput nature of the metagen-

ecological interactions, without depending on observing phenotypic

Artificial and assembled communities
A complementary approach to understanding ecological interactions 
during evolution comes from the emerging field of experimental ecol-
ogy. This approach, often led by the same groups that study experi-
mental evolution and employing similar high-throughput methods, 
provides crucial insights into the principles governing community 
assembly and stability, which are essential for understanding evolution 
in complex natural systems. By constructing artificial microbial com-
munities with defined compositions, researchers can systematically 
test hypotheses about ecological interactions that would be difficult 
to isolate in natural settings92,93.
Ecosystems are sometimes thought to be intractably complex, 
depending on a multitude of idiosyncratic interactions that challenge 
our ability to predict and understand these systems. However, some 
recent findings have suggested that community structure is governed 
by a type of emergent simplicity. For example, high-throughput 
metagenomic approaches have revealed that the natural microbi-
omes of bromeliads vary substantially between plants on the taxo-
nomic level, but are surprisingly consistent on a functional level94,95. 
This observation suggests that community assembly may be pre-
dictable, provided that we look at the right level of organization. 
Box 2 | Epistasis and contingency in the predictability and repeatability of evolution
 
The predictability and repeatability of evolution ultimately depend 
on the structure of genotype–phenotype–fitness landscapes. Fitness 
landscapes are inherently complex due to their high dimensionality. 
In a typical microbial genome, millions of possible single mutations 
exist around a wild-type (WT) genotype. When considering 
combinations of mutations, the number of possibilities grows 
exponentially (Box 2 figure, left panel). Whereas earlier work focused 
primarily on mapping fitness landscapes for individual proteins 
or small genetic systems10,11,56, new high-throughput approaches 
enable the exploration of genome-wide landscapes. These studies 
have revealed several key patterns in the architecture of fitness 
landscapes, suggesting that low-dimensional representations of 
fitness landscapes are often possible owing to global patterns of 
epistasis and many-to-one genotype–phenotype relationships. 
For instance, many studies have documented widespread ‘global’ 
epistasis, where the effect of a mutation depends on a higher-level 
property of genetic background in which it occurs11,12,43. This global 
epistasis often takes a specific form, where the effect of a mutation 
is negatively correlated with the fitness of the genetic background 
(Box 2 figure, right panel)74. Such diminishing returns and increasing 
costs epistasis helps explain how different genetic changes can 
lead to similar phenotypic outcomes, contributing to the observed 
patterns of high phenotypic but low genetic repeatability in evolution 
experiments9,26,67. These simple patterns may emerge from the 
combined effects of many higher-order, idiosyncratic epistastic 
interactions50,74.
Another crucial feature that emerges from widespread epistasis  
is the prevalence of contingency, such that the availability of 
beneficial mutations depends strongly on previous evolutionary 
history. For example, studies combining systematic genetic 
perturbations with molecular phenotyping have shown how proteins 
and organisms can evolve new functions through specific sequences 
of mutations, with each step requiring previous changes to be 
accessible75. Understanding these landscape features is essential 
for predicting evolutionary outcomes and potentially for steering 
evolution in desired directions. For instance, knowledge of 
landscape architecture can help identify genetic changes that 
might facilitate or constrain future adaptation, as well as suggest 
intervention strategies to prevent the evolution of antibiotic 
resistance or slow cancer progression. As our ability to map  
and analyse these landscapes continues to improve, we may  
develop increasingly sophisticated approaches for predicting  
and manipulating evolutionary trajectories in both laboratory and 
natural settings.

With the help of high-throughput metagenomics, such predictability 
on the functional (but not taxonomic) level has been recapitulated 
in experimental microbial communities, which can be explained 
with consumer–resource models93,96. Simple, quantitative rules have 
been found to be surprisingly powerful in predicting the outcomes 
of microbial community assembly experiments97–100. For example, 
the outcomes of community assembly experiments have also been 
found to be largely predictable by applying quantitative rules to small 
numbers of initial measurements92. Such ‘assembly rules’ may again be 
explained by consumer–resource dynamics101. If these patterns prove 
broadly applicable across different ecosystems, they may provide 
the insights needed to predict and control ecological dynamics with 
relatively limited data.
The integration of these ecological insights with evolution-
ary approaches represents a promising frontier for understanding 
eco-evolutionary dynamics. Although we have begun to uncover the 
rules governing community assembly and function, how these prin-
ciples shape and are shaped by evolutionary processes remains an 
open question. Recent pioneering work has begun evolving simple 
artificial communities to investigate these dynamics, which has led 
to preliminary evidence for quantitative eco-evolutionary rules that 
parallel those seen in community assembly102,103. These studies suggest 
that the predictable patterns emerging from ecological interactions 
may extend to evolutionary trajectories as well.
As high-throughput molecular methods continue to advance, the 
integration of experimental ecology and evolution offers a powerful

Developing a quantitatively predictive understanding of evolution 
in multispecies communities represents a substantial challenge that 
will shape the field in coming years, potentially helping to bridge the 
gap between simplified laboratory evolution and the complexity of 
natural systems.
Laboratory versus natural evolution
Laboratory evolution experiments serve as powerful model systems for 
understanding natural evolution, but it often remains unclear which 
aspects of experimental evolution can be generalized to natural systems. 
In this section, we explore how high-throughput sequencing and pheno-
typing methods offer new insights into the similarities and differences 
between evolutionary processes in controlled laboratory settings and in 
nature. We then examine two complementary trends that are bridging 
the gap between laboratory and natural evolutionary studies: the devel-
opment of laboratory environments that more closely mimic complex 
natural systems, and the application of experimental evolution tech-
niques to track and analyse evolution in natural settings. These emerg-
ing approaches demonstrate how the integration of laboratory and 
natural studies is enhancing our ability to understand and ­potentially 
predict evolutionary outcomes in complex biological systems.
Key differences between laboratory and natural evolution
Laboratory evolution experiments are intentionally designed as sim-
plified models of natural populations. These experimental systems 
often feature low interspecies diversity, minimal spatial structure, 
absence of recombination and simplified environments83,104. Despite 
these stark differences, experimental evolution has uncovered evo-
lutionary phenomena that prove to be important in natural settings. 
One such example is clonal interference105, in which multiple benefi-
cial mutations arise simultaneously in large asexual populations and 
compete for fixation25,106–109. This phenomenon can substantially alter 
evolutionary trajectories by, for instance, hindering the fixation of 
moderately beneficial alleles36. Initially described in detail in laboratory 
populations, clonal interference has since been recognized as crucial 
in the evolution of natural asexual populations, including within-host 
tuberculosis populations110,111 and global influenza populations112. Simi-
larly, ecological diversification through cross-feeding or resource 
partitioning — extensively studied in experimental settings15,78,85 — has 
been observed in some natural populations91.
As the evolution of natural populations in real time has become 
more deeply studied, other studies have revealed key differences 
between laboratory and natural evolution. For example, although 
some natural microbial populations evolve asexually (often over short 
timescales), it has become increasingly clear that horizontal gene 
transfer has a substantial role in natural microbial evolution113–116, which 
is scarcely studied in laboratory evolution. Horizontal gene transfer 
enables the recombination of genetic variants across backgrounds 
(within and between species), limiting the effects of clonal interference 
and enabling deleterious mutations to be purged more efficiently117,118. 
The rates and lengths of transferred genetic fragments can vary widely 
across strains119. Overall, horizontal gene transfer may be a more impor-
tant force generating diversity than spontaneous mutations in many 
natural systems116. Additionally, although epistasis has often been 
shown to be widespread in experimental populations, the importance 
of epistasis in natural populations with pervasive recombination is 
still largely unclear.
The mode of evolution in natural systems also seems to deviate 
at times from the expectations of experimental evolution. More spe-
cifically, purifying selection and neutral forces seem to be stronger in 
natural versus experimental systems, as indicated by comparing dN/dS 
ratios120 and effective population sizes121. Although it is often unclear 
why neutral forces are generally stronger in natural (versus experimen-
tal) systems, possible reasons include occasional severe bottlenecks 
caused by strongly fluctuating environments or predation, or large 
variability in offspring numbers. The nature of ecological interac-
tions may also systematically differ in natural microbial populations, 
especially as the important role of phage-mediated interactions has 
become apparent in recent years90.
Towards more complex laboratory systems
Recent efforts have focused on studying evolutionary dynamics in more 
complex laboratory systems, which retain a degree of experimental 
control while also introducing selected complexities of natural sys-
tems. Two notable examples of this approach are genetically tractable 
mouse models for cancer evolution and in vivo studies of gut microbial 
communities.
Genetically tractable mouse models have emerged as a powerful 
system to study cancer evolution in vivo122. Such systems have enabled 
researchers to probe previously inaccessible fundamental evolutionary 
questions concerning the functional importance of mutation order 
and how epistatic interactions between mutations shape evolution-
ary trajectories in cancer. Although the sequence of genetic changes 
in cancer evolution has been documented in many cases123–125, the 
evolutionary significance and fitness consequences of such mutations 
remained speculative. Technologies such as Cre-loxP126, transposon 
mutagenesis127 and CRISPR systems128,129 enable researchers to induce 
targeted genetic changes in mice, connecting genetic alterations with 
phenotypic and evolutionary outcomes. Low-throughput approaches 
have been used to quantify the fitness effects of cancer-driver 
mutations130 and uncover epistatic effects131. The development of DNA 
barcoding in cancer models has substantially increased the power and 
throughput of experiments characterizing evolutionary dynamics and 
genotype–phenotype maps in various cancer models132–134. For instance, 
Tuba-seq (tumour barcoding with ultradeep barcode sequencing) lev-
erages CRISPR–Cas9 to mediate the inactivation of different tumour 
suppressors in parallel in genetically engineered mouse models of lung 
adenocarcinoma134,135. Many replicate tumours are formed across sev-
eral mice by each oncogenic genetic change and, by deep sequencing 
the barcodes across all tumours, researchers can determine the relative 
size of the tumours and associate each with genotype. This technology 
has been used to determine the effects of different nucleotide changes 
within the KRAS gene135, the effects of diverse oncogenic mutations 
across the genome136,137, and has revealed widespread epistasis and 
context-dependence among cancer-driver mutations138,139.
The resident microbial communities of animal guts have also 
emerged as a promising in vivo system to study evolution in real time. 
A number of model host animals have been used for this purpose, 
including Drosophila melanogaster140, zebrafish (Danio rerio)141,142 
and Caenorhabditis elegans143. Mice have been an especially common 
system to study intra-host evolution, especially owing to the large 
population of microbes supported in the gut144 and the similarity to 
other mammalian guts, including those of humans. Germ-free mice

typically involve colonizing the gut with a single species (for example,

experiments have been crucial in better understanding how the tempo 
and mode of evolution varies by host environment.

of in vivo CRISPR screening
Antonio J. Santinha 
  1,5, Alessio Strano 
  1,5 & Randall J. Platt 
  1,2,3,4 
Abstract
A fundamental goal in genetics is to understand the connection 
between genotype and phenotype in health and disease. Genetic 
screens in which dozens to thousands of genetic elements are 
perturbed in a pooled fashion offer the opportunity to generate 
large-scale, information-rich and unbiased genotype–phenotype 
maps. Although typically applied in reductionist in vitro settings, 
methods enabling pooled CRISPR–Cas perturbation screening  
in vivo are gaining attention as they have the potential to accelerate 
the discovery and annotation of gene function across cells, tissues, 
developmental stages, disease states and species. In this Review, 
we discuss essential criteria for understanding, designing and 
implementing in vivo screening experiments, with a focus on pooled 
CRISPR-based screens in mice. We also highlight how the resulting 
datasets, combined with advances in multi-omics and artificial 
intelligence, will accelerate progress and enable fundamental 
discoveries across basic and translational sciences.

types and model organisms, we focus primarily on pooled direct in vivo 
screens carried out in mice and do not discuss screening approaches 
based on non-mouse model organisms29,30, pathogen infection31,32, 
organoids14,33,34 or synthetic genomics35 or non-screening in vivo 
applications of CRISPR–Cas tools such as lineage tracing36,37. How-
ever, many of the concepts we describe are directly relatable to these 
alternative approaches. We conclude by discussing our vision for the 
future and how solving some of the current limitations will further 
expand the in vivo CRISPR screening toolbox, ultimately creating entry 
points for exploring and answering many long-standing biological and 
biomedical problems.
Types of in vivo CRISPR screen
In vivo CRISPR screens can generally be classified into a few distinct 
types based on the mode of delivery of guide RNAs (gRNAs) and on 
phenotypic read-outs (Fig. 1b,c). Differences between these types of 
screen have important implications for experimental implementation 
and suitability for a specific biological question. Independent of the 
mode of gRNA delivery and the phenotypic read-out, Cas effector pro-
teins are either delivered concomitantly with the gRNA or pre-installed 
in the cell or animal model through genetic engineering (see ‘Direct 
expression of Cas proteins in target cells’).
Types of screen
A critical feature of in vivo CRISPR screens is when and how 
gRNAs are introduced into the target cells (Fig. 1b). Specifically, in 
transplantation-based in vivo screens the gRNAs are delivered to cells 
in vitro (or ex vivo) and these are then transferred to a host mouse. By 
contrast, in direct in vivo screens the gRNAs are delivered directly to 
the target cells within their endogenous niche in situ. A third possibil-
ity is the generation of transgenic mice carrying an array of gRNAs38, 
but because this approach has not yet found widespread uptake we 
do not discuss it further.
Transplantation-based in vivo screens. In transplantation-based 
in vivo screens, gRNA libraries are delivered to cells in culture using 
well-established methods developed for in vitro CRISPR screening. Cas 
effector proteins are either already encoded in the cellular genome or 
introduced at the same time as the gRNA library. Unlike in vitro screens, 
after selection for expression of the CRISPR machinery the cells are 
transferred into a host mouse, typically by intravenous injection or 
by subcutaneous or orthotopic transplantation39. Depending on the 
transplantation route and the biology of the targeted population, 
the cells that survive the procedure may expand in situ, repopulate 
their original niche and/or migrate to new locations.
Seminal studies demonstrated the power of transplantation- 
based in vivo CRISPR screens to understand tumour growth and 
metastasis40,41, and this approach has now been widely adopted for 
a wide range of questions in cancer biology, including resistance to 
therapeutics42 and interactions between tumours and the immune 
system41,43. Transplantation-based screens in non-cancer cell lines 
have been more constrained and largely focused on cells of the hae-
matopoietic lineage, in particular haematopoietic stem cells44–46, 
CD8+ T cells20,47–53 and other immune cell types54–60. Beyond the hae-
matopoietic lineage, transplantation-based screens have also been 
employed to identify genetic perturbations that reduce rejection 
and improve survival of insulin-producing cells in mouse models of 
type 1 diabetes61,62.
Introduction
Understanding the roles of protein-coding and non-coding DNA 
sequences and their variants in molecular, cellular and organis-
mal phenotypes has been a long-standing goal in the biological 
sciences1. Reverse genetics approaches, which investigate individual 
genetic elements based on prior knowledge, have been instrumental 
in understanding causal genotype–phenotype linkages2. However, 
with the surge in deep sequencing initiatives spanning the biological 
and clinical sciences, reverse genetics approaches are becoming insuf-
ficient to understand and causally validate the deluge of new biological 
insights and gene–variant associations being generated across diverse 
organisms and phenotypes.
In forward genetics screens, by contrast, hundreds to thousands 
of genetic elements are perturbed (for example, by altering DNA 
sequences or their expression) in parallel, offering the opportunity for 
fast, high-throughput and unbiased mapping between genotype and 
phenotype. Early screening approaches used random genetic mutagen-
esis techniques (such as chemical mutagenesis or gene traps) or tar-
geted RNA knockdown (such as RNA interference), but more recent 
approaches are based on RNA-guided CRISPR–Cas enzymes3–6 (Box 1). 
In particular, the explosion in CRISPR–Cas-based technologies has ena-
bled the execution of a large variety of programmable and precise per-
turbations, which can be targeted to virtually any part of the genome7, 
epigenome8 or transcriptome9. Forward genetic screens implemented 
with CRISPR–Cas technologies have been extensively deployed in 
mammalian cells grown in vitro to map connections between genetic 
elements and phenotypes, encompassing broad biomedical research 
questions such as identifying essential genes10, tumour suppressors11, 
cancer-specific dependencies12, immune regulatory checkpoints13, 
causal factors among disease-associated risk alleles14, regulators of 
stem and progenitor cell differentiation15, and many more16.
Notwithstanding the advantages of in vitro cellular models and 
the insights gained from them, there are intrinsic limitations in using 
reductionist cell culture systems to model complex biological pro-
cesses occurring within an organism17,18. Studies conducted in vivo in 
animal models provide the opportunity to interrogate complex biology 
that is currently difficult or impossible to model in vitro, such as com-
plex 3D tissue organization, cell type diversity and maturity, cell–cell 
interactions among tissue-resident cells and the immune system, 
vascularization and organismal physiology (Fig. 1a). Indeed, multiple 
studies carried out in animal models have successfully demonstrated 
that in vivo CRISPR screens are feasible and can reveal novel insights not 
found in equivalent in vitro screens19–22. As a result, CRISPR screening 
tools are increasingly being applied to investigate biological questions 
in vivo, building on the lessons learned from pioneering studies that 
performed in vivo screens with RNA interference technology23–27.
In this Review, we discuss recent advances in in vivo CRISPR 
screening and how they are being used in combination with con-
temporary methods in molecular and cell biology to construct 
high-resolution  genotype–phenotype maps. We first provide 
an overview of different types of in vivo CRISPR screen, including 
transplantation-based (that is, perturbations in xenograft models) and 
direct in vivo (that is, direct perturbation in situ within a living animal) 
approaches, and their application across models of health and disease. 
We then discuss experimental designs for direct in vivo CRISPR screens 
with count-based or information-rich read-outs and how these devi-
ate from conventional in vitro screens. We do not discuss in detail the 
diversity of perturbation methods and computational approaches to 
analyse screening data as these topics have been extensively reviewed

The main benefit of transplantation-based screens is that they rely on 
relatively straightforward approaches for gRNA library delivery and can 
be performed using human cells, potentially boosting the therapeutic 
relevance of the screen results. However, transplantation-based screens 
are only suitable for studying cell types amenable to both in vitro cell 
culture and transplantation, and the transplantation itself represents a 
bottleneck that can severely reduce the starting pool of transduced cells. 
Moreover, heterogeneity in clonal expansion leads to increased noise 
and makes depletion screens particularly difficult40,63–67. This limitation 
is being addressed by the development of screening technologies that 
take clonality into account using unique molecular identifiers65,67–70 or 
internal controls generated by stochastic recombination71.
Direct in vivo screens. Direct in vivo screens perturb target genes 
in cells within their natural milieu, thereby enabling functional inves-
tigations in arguably the most physiologically relevant context. They 
also offer the opportunity to explore gene function in cell types not 
amenable to in vitro culture and/or not easily transplanted. However, 
delivery of gRNAs can prove more challenging in this type of screen 
as numerous factors must be taken into account, including the acces-
sibility and abundance of target cells; specificity (that is, tropism) of 
the gRNA delivery vector for the target cells; and the potential for 
unwanted immune responses triggered by the delivery vehicle72. 
The complexities of in vivo delivery can also make it challenging to 
control how many gRNAs are present in each cell (see ‘Multiplicity of 
infection’). Nevertheless, several studies have overcome these delivery 
challenges through the use of different delivery routes and vectors, and 
have demonstrated the power of direct in vivo CRISPR screens for stud-
ying a range of phenotypes in endogenous and non-transplantable cell 
types, including cell populations in the liver73–82, brain83–88, lung68,89,90, 
pancreas91,92, heart93, testes94, embryonic ectoderm95,96 and mammary 
gland97,98 (Table 1 and Supplementary Table 1).
Types of screen read-out
In organismal screens in which a single perturbation is introduced 
per animal, the identity of that perturbation is either known or easily 
recovered by genotyping. By contrast, in pooled in vivo screens many 
different perturbations coexist in the same genetically mosaic animal. 
Which questions can be studied using in vivo CRISPR screens therefore 
chiefly depends on the choice of screen read-out and how this is coupled 
to the phenotype of interest. There are two broadly defined types of 
screen read-out: count-based and information-rich (Fig. 1c).
Count-based screens. As long as perturbation information can be 
recovered from defined cellular populations, screens with count-based 
read-outs offer a low-cost and highly scalable way to link genotype 
Box 1 | The CRISPR toolbox
 
CRISPR–Cas systems are a diverse family of prokaryotic adaptive 
immune systems that enable archaea and bacteria to defend against 
foreign invaders such as phages219,220. Many CRISPR–Cas systems 
have been adapted for the manipulation of DNA, RNA and numerous 
other features of eukaryotic cells7,221. These tools are typically 
composed of two elements: a Cas effector protein and a short RNA, 
termed a guide RNA (gRNA), that site-specifically binds to target 
sequences via Watson–Crick base pairing of the ~20 nucleotide 
‘spacer’ segment of the gRNA. In cells, the Cas protein and gRNA 
form a ribonucleoprotein complex capable of targeting, seemingly, 
any genetic sequence of interest, where the function of the Cas 
effector protein is unleashed. CRISPR–Cas-based tools are highly 
customizable and well suited to high-throughput applications, such 
as pooled genetic screens.
The prototypical Cas protein for genome editing applications is 
the nuclease Cas9, which can create double-stranded breaks in DNA; 
repair of these breaks generates frameshifting insertion–deletions, 
leading to functional knockout of targeted genes222,223. Knockouts 
can also be generated using the nuclease Cas12a, which additionally 
possesses RNase activity that can process a single transcript 
encoding multiple gRNAs into its constituent elements, thereby 
enabling simultaneous targeting of multiple loci in the same cell 
(multiplexing)224–226. Multiplexed targeting and degradation of RNA  
can similarly be achieved using Cas13 proteins227,228. Cas9, Cas12a  
and Cas13 currently represent the most established and widely  
used Cas proteins, but others have been described and are being  
used in emerging technologies for manipulating eukaryotic cells, 
including the CRISPR transposases Cas12k229 and CAST (type I-F 
CRISPR-associated transposase)230, the RNA-targeting ribonuclease 
Cas7-11231 and others232.
Beyond the naturally occurring activities of Cas proteins, 
engineered versions have been developed to leverage the 
unprecedented targetability of CRISPR systems for different types 
of manipulation7,221,232. Nuclease-dead (that is, inactive) Cas9 or 
Cas12a fused to transcriptional repressor or activator domains 
can be used to modulate the expression level of target genes. 
These technologies are respectively called CRISPR inhibition 
(CRISPRi) and CRISPR activation (CRISPRa)233,234. Chromatin 
modifiers can similarly be fused to Cas proteins to create tools 
for manipulating the epigenome. To perform more specific 
sequence modifications, base editors were developed by fusing 
a nickase (that is, single-stranded nuclease) version of Cas9 to 
deaminases that catalyse specific nucleotide conversions in the 
target locus235–237. Prime editors, consisting of a Cas9 nickase fused 
to a reverse transcriptase, are able to use a long gRNA containing 
both the spacer sequence and a reverse transcription template to 
mediate precise replacement of the sequence at the target locus 
with the desired sequence238,239. Catalytically dead Cas13 variants 
can similarly be modified to localize effectors to RNA for RNA base 
editing240 or modifying RNA splicing241, translational inhibition242 or 
activation243. The CRISPR toolbox mentioned here represents just 
the tip of the iceberg and we direct readers to recent reviews for 
further exploration7,221,232.
Although these tools have already revolutionized how we 
manipulate eukaryotic cells, they were derived from only a small 
number of the staggeringly diverse CRISPR systems found in 
nature244. Through future efforts focused on characterizing and 
engineering these diverse systems, new technologies will surely be 
discovered and further expand the CRISPR toolbox.

to specific phenotypes, resulting in high-throughput identification 
of genetic elements affecting the process of interest. Most pooled 
CRISPR screens, both in vitro and in vivo, identify relevant pertur-
bations by deep sequencing-based counting of perturbations (for 
example, insertion–deletions in the target gene) or, more commonly, 
of perturbation identifiers (for example, gRNA sequences or barcodes) 
and comparing their frequency in a population of interest against a ref-
erence population (for example, treated versus untreated, early versus 
late time points, enriched versus non-enriched). Count-based screens 
are therefore suitable to study perturbations that alter cell numbers, 
such as through cell death, proliferation or migration, or which alter 
the frequency of cell types and states identifiable by expression of par-
ticular markers. They are commonly used to study gene essentiality78,85 
and identify regulators of cancer proliferation and metastasis40,83 
and response to immunotherapy99–103. Combined with cell sorting for 
expression of specific markers, count-based screens can be used to 
study protein uptake, cellular fate choice and differentiation, and a 
myriad of other processes45,49,56,82. Count-based screens have limited 
use for studies exploring multiple phenotypes simultaneously, such 
as the unbiased discovery of cellular states and types, which require 
in-depth exploration of biological processes that do not necessary 
involve changes in cell numbers or easily identifiable populations.
Information-rich screens. To expand the phenotypes that can be 
investigated using in vivo CRISPR screens, researchers are developing 
ways to couple perturbation information with high-content read-outs 
such as omics technologies and imaging. This marriage facilitates 
forward genetic screens that investigate complex phenotypes in 
high-dimensional parameter spaces (for example, transcriptomes 
or cellular morphology) without requiring changes in cell numbers or 
marker expression. Information-rich screens are bridging the divide 
between forward and reverse genetics, enabling scalable experiments 
that are of both high throughput and high content, thereby moving 
beyond merely identifying a set of hits to generating comprehen-
sive genotype–phenotype maps. Owing to the higher read-out costs 
involved, information-rich screens typically use smaller, more tailored 
libraries than count-based screens. Although this does not limit their 
use across different areas of study, these screens may be less unbiased 
as they require preliminary work to define restricted lists of target 
genes with potential biological relevance. Depending on the read-out 
technology used, information-rich screens can be further categorized 
into single-cell CRISPR (scCRISPR) or spatial CRISPR screens.
scCRISPR screens involve the quantification of one or more 
omics phenotypes (for example, transcriptome or epigenome) upon 
genetic perturbation at the single-cell level, enabling the elucidation 
of how these perturbations affect cell types and states. The retrieval of 
perturbation-specific omics vastly enlarges the catalogue of biological 
questions amenable for screening. The development of in vivo scCRISPR 
screens is being powered by a recent wave of technical advances, 
including the generation of CRISPR transgenic mice104–106 (Supple-
mentary Table 2), improved delivery reagents107,108 and protocols

In information-rich screens, multidimensional phenotypes are recorded for each 
perturbation either with single-cell omics or with imaging technologies. Different 
sample preparation methods are required for each type of read-out.

for cell or nuclei isolation from complex tissues109,110. The majority of 
scCRISPR technologies have been developed to combine single-cell 
RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) with CRISPR perturbations111–115. Other 
protocols have been established to combine perturbations with tar-
geted transcriptomics116, epigenomic read-outs117–119 and cell surface 
proteomics120–122. Screens with single-cell read-outs are particularly 
useful for investigating biological systems involving cellular hetero-
geneity and cell state changes where transcriptional phenotypes are 
informative, such as stem cell123,124 and organoid differentiation14,15,125, 
cancer heterogeneity118,126 and drug resistance127. In vivo scCRISPR 
screens have been used to study genetic contributions to autism spec-
trum disorder84, gene function in 22q11.2 deletion syndrome86, tumour 
necrosis factor signalling in squamous carcinoma evolution96 and gene 
regulatory networks involved in antitumoural immunity53.
Beyond scCRISPR, an exciting new avenue of research is focus-
ing on coupling genetic perturbations with spatial read-outs. Spatial 
information is especially appropriate for studies in which cell location 
and tissue organization are of interest (such as in developmental con-
texts, tumour evolution or tissue regeneration), as well as for directly 
measuring physical cellular phenotypes (such as cellular volume or 
intracellular protein location)128,129. Current and emerging implemen-
tations combining genetic perturbations with multiplexed protein 
imaging, in situ sequencing and spatial transcriptomics have focused 
on studies of tissue organization130, tumour composition131,132 and 
immune microenvironment133,134.
Designing direct in vivo CRISPR screens
Every application of direct in vivo CRISPR screening requires strategies 
to deliver all components of the chosen CRISPR system to the cells of 
interest within a living animal, and to recover perturbation and phe-
notypic information from targeted cells. Unlike transplantation-based 
screens, which have similar considerations to in vitro screens in terms 
of gRNA delivery, direct in vivo screens are bound by the characteristics 
of the cell type of interest within its physiological niche (for example, 
location, abundance and transducibility). These properties then deter-
mine the delivery modality and screenable library size. In the following 
sections we discuss experimental implementation and design strategies 
to ensure successful direct in vivo screens.
Direct expression of Cas proteins in target cells
Expression constructs for CRISPR–Cas-based nucleases and effec-
tors constitute large cargos whose direct delivery to cells in vivo is 
particularly challenging135. For example, Cas9 from Streptococcus 
pyogenes (SpCas9) is 4.1 kb and the prime editor PEmax is 6.4 kb, 
whereas the packaging limit of commonly used viral-based delivery 
methods is 4.7 kb (adeno-associated virus (AAV)) and 10 kb (lentivi-
rus). Vector-based delivery of all-in-one constructs containing both 
gRNA and Cas protein expression cassettes is possible, but only for 
some cell types73,74,91. Consequently, the creation of Cas9 knock-in 
mice136,137, which obviate the need for exogenous nuclease delivery, 
represented a major breakthrough in achieving the full potential of 
in vivo screens. Many more transgenic mouse lines, genetically engi-
neered to express various Cas nucleases and effectors, have since 
been generated, substantially expanding the in vivo CRISPR toolbox 
(­Supplementary Table 2). Unmodified SpCas9 remains the go-to nucle-
ase of choice in most in vivo screens, but there is increasing interest in 
exploiting variants for precise gene editing (for example, base105 and 
prime editors106) or gene expression modulation138–140 (for example, 
inhibition with dCas9-KRAB or activation with dCas9-p300), and the 
properties of other Cas nucleases, such as Cas13 for targeting RNA141,142 
or Cas12a (refs. 104,143) for easier perturbation multiplexing (Box 1).
Effector proteins can be expressed in a constitutive, conditional 
or inducible manner. Constitutive effectors are expressed in all cells 
at all times. Although constitutive expression enables screening by 
delivery of the gRNA cassette alone, it also makes the specificity of 
the screen for a target cell type wholly dependent on the specificity 
of the gRNA library delivery method, which is often only partially spe-
cific. This limitation, as well as concerns about the potential collateral 
effects of long-term constitutive expression of effector proteins in an 
entire organism, led to the creation of more regulated expression sys-
tems. Conditional and inducible expression systems, of which Cre/loxP 
and TetOn are the most commonly used, carry an inactive effector 
transgene that is activated only in selected cells and/or at selected 
times. In conditional systems, effector expression is switched on 
based on genetically regulated expression of an activator, such as Cre 
recombinase, and is then typically maintained. In inducible systems, 
expression is regulated through additional exogenous stimuli, such as 
the administration of doxycycline in the TetOn system. Both control 
strategies can be made cell type-specific by combining them with 
the use of cell type-specific promoters. Constitutive animal models are 
suitable for screens in which multiple cell types are to be targeted or the 
gRNA delivery modality cannot carry Cas nucleases or Cre recombinase 
(for example, space limitation in the AAV genome). Conditional and 
inducible systems are ideal when perturbations are to be targeted to 
specific tissues or cell types, or when gRNA delivery and perturbations 
should happen at different time points76–78,81–83,86,92.
Direct viral-mediated delivery of CRISPR reagents
Delivery of genetic material, including reagents for direct in vivo CRISPR 
screens, remains one of the fundamental limitations of inducing per-
turbations in vivo. Although there is no one-size-fits-all tool, reagents 
have been delivered mainly using viral vectors, namely lentivirus or 
AAV, and in certain cases with non-viral alternatives, such as virus-like 
particles107, hydrodynamic tail vein injection (HTVI) of plasmid DNA82 
or plasmid electroporation144. We refer the reader to recent reviews on 
CRISPR reagent delivery145,146, and only focus here on features of viral 
vectors relevant to screening.
Among viral delivery methods, lentivirus has two advantages: it 
can package a relatively large payload (~10 kb) and it integrates into 
the cellular genome, which is particularly beneficial for screens in 
proliferating cells as it ensures that the link between the perturba-
tion reagent and the perturbed cell is not lost. Although its large pay-
load is sufficient to accommodate most Cas nucleases and all-in-one 
approaches, lentivirus is still preferable to use in conjunction with a Cas 
nuclease knock-in model, as the semi-random integration of lentiviral 
genomes leads to non-uniform levels of lentivirus-based Cas nuclease 
expression across cells, ultimately affecting perturbation efficiency 
and data quality142. Owing to its restricted biodistribution, in vivo appli-
cations of lentivirus typically involve accessible cell types68,78,81,89,90, 
local injection85,88,94 or delivery in utero84,95,96, although efforts are 
being made to broaden its tropism through pseudotyping147,148. Local 
injections have additional disadvantages in screening contexts — for 
example, they cause physical damage which induces confounding alter-
ations to cell states; and they have a restricted area of viral spreading, 
which results in few usable cells per animal and many cells harbouring 
­multiple perturbations84.
AAV is a more versatile viral vector. There is a vast catalogue of nat-
ural and engineered AAV variants available for tissue-specific and cell

type-specific delivery of genetic material, many compatible with sys-
temic delivery149–151. The two main disadvantages of AAVs are their rela-
tively small packaging capability (~4.7 kb) and the fact that they remain 
episomal, therefore perturbation identity (that is, the gRNA sequence) 
is lost upon cell division. However, the payload can be increased by 
using dual-AAV systems, which deliver large transgenes as two parts 
within separated AAV genomes, which are later joined together in 
target cells via mRNA trans-splicing152 or split intein-mediated pro-
tein trans-splicing153. To circumvent maintenance as episomes, AAV 
genomes can be engineered to deliver transposons flanked by inverted 
terminal repeats recognized by a transposase enzyme, which then 
integrates them into the cellular genome57,80,87,154 (Fig. 2).
Recent efforts have generated mouse transgenic lines in which the 
expression of both SpCas9 and the adeno-associated virus receptor 
(AAVR) is dependent on Cre recombinase; these lines hardwire targeted 
AAV-mediated delivery into the mouse genome and capitalize on the 
ability of established Cre recombinase lines to activate delivery and 
construct expression in many cell types that have no known effective 
or specific vector-based delivery method155.
Design of expression vectors
Universal design features. Expression vectors for the delivery of 
CRISPR components generally contain two expression cassettes 
(Fig. 2a). The first is composed of an RNA polymerase (Pol) III pro-
moter, predominantly the human or mouse U6 promoter, to drive the 
expression of a gRNA156. More elaborate versions may also contain 
loxP sites within or adjacent to this cassette to exploit Cre-mediated 
recombination to modulate gRNA activity71,157 or, as reported in a pre-
print article, to make gRNA read-out cell type-specific158. The sec-
ond expression cassette contains a Pol II promoter, which is used to 
control the expression of infection markers, typically fluorescent 
proteins, and additional genes specific to the research question or 
experimental model. The Pol II promoter can be either constitutive93,95 
or cell type-specific159 and consequently can drive expression in all 
infected cells or only in certain cell types of interest, respectively. For 
experiments using nuclei isolation rather than whole cells, the fluores-
cent protein should be associated with a nuclear localization signal or 
nuclear membrane-insertion element (such as KASH) to ensure it can 
be detected by flow cytometry. Other expressed genes include Cre 
recombinase to conditionally induce Cas effector protein expression136 
or transposases to mediate integration of non-integrating (for example, 
AAV or plasmid) payloads57.
Additional considerations for single-cell screens. A critical aspect 
of expression vectors for information-rich screens is that the omics 
read-out should be compatible with the detection of perturbation 
identities, typically in the form of gRNA capture (Fig. 2b). In scCRISPR 
screens with transcriptomic read-outs, there are indirect and direct 
gRNA capture strategies. For indirect capture, a gRNA-matching bar-
code, or the gRNA expression cassette itself, is located within the Pol II 
transcript, which is poly-adenylated and thus amenable to capture 
and sequencing with most 3′-based single-cell kits112,114. Direct cap-
ture has been engineered with 3′ and 5′-library preparation kits from 
10x Genomics120,160 (note that 3′-based kits are no longer commercially 
available). Although 3′-based approaches are dependent on modify-
ing the gRNA scaffold to include capture sequences compatible with 
beads carrying poly-d(T) and targeted-capture reverse transcription 
primers, 5′-based approaches require no modification of the expression 
vector. Instead, the single-cell library protocol is modified to include a 
gRNA-specific reverse transcriptione primer that can be used to cap-
ture gRNA sequences alongside cellular mRNAs. 5′-Based direct capture 
protocols are particularly attractive for in vivo applications. First, 
they are compatible with standard gRNA expression vectors. Second, 
direct gRNA capture is more effective than indirect 3′-based methods 
when nuclei isolation and sequencing is preferred over whole cell 
sequencing, principally for highly structured tissues (such as the adult 
brain) where it is challenging to create single-cell suspensions86. More 
generally, 5′-based direct capture methods tend to be more efficient 
at gRNA capture within single cells160, which is critical for accurately 
assigning gRNAs and perturbations (see ‘Read-out of information-rich 
screens’). Further scCRISPR-compatible single-cell library prepara-
tion strategies are emerging to overcome current bottlenecks associ-
ated with cost, scale, sensitivity, and/or compatibility with fixed cells 
and tissue using technologies based on combinatorially indexing161, 
multiplexed targeted amplification162, and multiplexed probe-based 
detection on fixed samples130.
Additional considerations for spatial screens. Constructs used 
in spatial screens should be compatible with gRNA detection using 
spatial biology methods, such as multiplexed protein imaging133, 
in situ RNA sequencing 130, and as shown in a preprint article, spatial 
transcriptomics131 (Fig. 2c). For multiplexed protein imaging, expres-
sion constructs carry gRNAs uniquely associated with a triplet combi-
nation of epitopes (ProCodes) fused to a scaffold protein122. Antibody 
staining allows for proteome-based read-outs by simultaneous imaging

of endogenous proteins and gRNA-associated ProCodes133,134. One 
drawback of the current implementation of this system is that the total 
number of unique epitope combinations available limits the number of 
targets. Adaptations to expression constructs used in spatial transcrip-

in a position that facilitates indirect detection163, and inclusion of a T7 
promoter for in situ amplification of gRNA sequences to increase the

an in situ polyadenylation step131. Imaging-based spatial approaches 
directly measure phenotypes using a few dozen to hundreds of proteins 
or RNAs. By contrast, spatial transcriptomics offers the opportunity to 
retrieve transcriptome-scale gene expression data and is not limited 
to a predefined panel of genes of interest.
Multiplicity of infection
Regardless of the delivery method employed, the number of distinct 
gRNAs entering each cell is an essential parameter that should be con-
sidered. In in vitro CRISPR screens, the target cells are typically equally 
transducible and the number of gRNAs delivered to each cell follows a 
Poisson distribution whose average is represented by the multiplicity 
of infection (MOI). Because of the known relationship between the MOI 
and the proportion of transduced cells, most in vitro screens aim for 
a transduction rate of ~30%, corresponding to an MOI of ~0.3, which 
ensures that most transduced cells contain only one gRNA. However, 
this relationship is not as straightforward for in vivo screens, in which 
the spatial complexity of tissues and non-uniformity of delivery results 
in heterogeneous distributions of MOIs rather than a single fixed MOI. 
For example, an increased number of transductions per cell might be 
observed in certain cell types within proximity to the site of injection85, 
lumen97 or capillaries164. Furthermore, for in vitro screens the MOI 
refers to an average that includes uninfected cells, but the choice of 
reference population for which to calculate a transduction rate in an 
in vivo screen is not obvious. Various approaches have been used to 
understand the distribution of the number of gRNAs per cell in in vivo 
screens, including co-delivery of multiple viral vectors encoding dif-
ferent fluorescent proteins to assess the rate of multiple transductions 
per cell78,86,97 or counting gRNAs in scCRISPR datasets15,84.
Although the most common approach is to limit multiple 
transductions per cell, it may not be a strict requirement in all 
contexts. In addition to cases in which multiple transductions are 
desired to study perturbation interactions, ‘high MOI’ screening 
formats have been developed to increase scale and reduce costs 
for both count-based165 and information-rich screens166,167. These 
screens leverage multiple perturbations per cell, whose signal can 
be deconvolved during data analysis, to reduce the number of cells 
per experiment or increase the number of perturbations screened 
within a limited number of cells.
For count-based high MOI screens, the introduction of multiple 
differentially barcoded constructs for each gRNA sequence allows 
the gRNA fold change to be compared across all associated barcodes, 
which should behave similarly as they all cause identical perturbations. 
Such protocols increase statistical power and decrease the detection 
of false positive effects arising from multiple transductions, whereby 
a perturbation phenotype is assigned to ‘free rider’ gRNAs present in 
the same cell as the gRNA responsible for the phenotype165. For high 
MOI scCRISPR screens with transcriptomic read-outs, computational 
approaches have been developed to deconvolve the effect of individual 
perturbations from the composite effects measured in cells receiving 
random combinations of multiple gRNAs, provided that assumptions 
about sparse perturbation effects and the extent of higher order 
interactions are met166,167. Although these high MOI approaches have not 
yet been widely applied, they represent an intriguing avenue to reduce 
the size and cost of screens that aim to measure the phenotype of vast 
lists of perturbations and, potentially, their interactions.
Scale of gRNA libraries
Libraries used for direct in vivo screens have ranged in size from 10 
to ~130,000 gRNAs (Table 1 and Supplementary Table 1). The design 
of a gRNA library involves balancing experimental goals with tech-
nical and financial constraints112, but three variables common to all 
screen types constrain library size. First, enough cells per perturbation 
must be analysed to ensure sufficient statistical power. As a general 
reference, count-based enrichment screens require 200–500 cells per 
perturbation and count-based dropout screens require 500–1,000 cells. 
As information-rich screens are emerging methods, the number 
of cells per perturbation required to extract meaningful information 
is currently being explored but they tend to require fewer cells than 
count-based screens; scCRISPR screens can be performed with as few 
as 10 cells when perturbations are expected to drive a strong transcrip-
tional phenotype112. However, subtle effects might require approxi-
mately 100–200 cells per perturbation168, with some studies using up 
to 500 cells to deeply explore molecular pathways112,169, whereas both 
published and preprint studies demonstrate that the values for spatial 
screens are not standardized because they heavily depend on the phe-
notype being investigated130,131,163. Second, libraries need to be redun-
dant (that is, each gene must be targeted by multiple gRNAs) to account 
for variations in gRNA efficiency and include intergenic-targeting and 
non-targeting controls170. Although count-based screens have been 
performed with up to ten gRNAs per target gene and 10% control gRNAs, 
information-rich screens are more constrained (largely owing to finan-
cial considerations) and therefore typically include fewer gRNAs per 
gene (two to three) and controls (5%) to maximize the number of targets 
within the library. Third, experimental costs must be considered, espe-
cially for scCRISPR screens that require the use of costly single-cell and 
deep sequencing methods. The total number of cells needed rapidly 
increases with additional targets and is directly proportional to the 
number of cell types under study. For example, a scCRISPR screen of 
35 perturbations aiming for 500 cells per perturbation for each cell 
type would require 17,500 cells when performed in an in vitro mono-
culture, whereas the same experiment in vivo including six major cell 
types within the brain cortex would need 105,000 cells. It is expected 
that new developments in single-cell library preparation protocols 
and deep sequencing platforms will lower the cost and increase the 
scale of fut

Clinical use of polygenic risk 
scores: current status, barriers 
and future directions
Iftikhar J. Kullo 
Abstract
Genome-wide association studies have identified thousands of 
single-nucleotide variants that are associated with complex traits, 
including cardiometabolic diseases, cancers and neurological 
disorders. Polygenic risk scores (PRSs), which aggregate the effects 
of these variants, can help to identify individuals who are at increased 
risk of developing such diseases. As PRSs are typically only weakly 
associated with conventional risk factors for these diseases, they have 
incremental predictive value and are beginning to be incorporated into 
clinical practice to guide early detection and preventive strategies. 
However, challenges to their use — such as suboptimal precision, poor 
transferability across diverse populations and low familiarity among 
patients and providers with the concept of polygenic risk — must be 
addressed before their broader clinical adoption. This Review explores 
the current state of the field, highlights key challenges and outlines 
future directions for the use of PRSs to improve risk prediction and 
to advance personalized prevention in clinical care.

Background
Mathematically, a PRS is the sum of risk alleles at disease-associated 
loci weighted by the strength of association of each risk allele with the 
trait or disease (which can, for example, be expressed as the log odds 
ratio for binary traits or as the slope of the linear regression between 
allele count and trait for continuous traits)13 (Box 1). Initial PRSs were 
constructed from loci identified in GWAS that met the threshold of 
statistical significance. However, for many highly polygenic traits, PRSs 
perform better when they also include a much larger number of vari-
ants below the threshold14–16. The source GWAS data (either individual 
level or summary statistics) are called the training dataset, and the 
parameters (for example, the P-value threshold for statistical signifi-
cance below which SNVs are included) are selected in an independent 
tuning dataset. The final step of testing is performed in an independent, 
out-of-sample cohort to avoid generating inflated prediction metrics13.
The assessment of polygenic disease risk in this manner is the focus 
of intense research, with increasing reports of the clinical validation and 
implementation of PRSs. For example, PRSs for CHD, type 2 diabetes, 
Alzheimer disease and breast and prostate cancers are available for clini-
cal application and are being used in clinical settings in several countries 
including the USA. In addition, PRSs for immune-mediated inflamma-
tory diseases (such as type 1 diabetes and ankylosing spondylitis)17, eye 
disorders such as glaucoma18 and respiratory diseases (such as chronic 
obstructive pulmonary disease)19 are being evaluated for clinical use. 
Although no guidelines have yet been established for the clinical use of 
PRSs, as the field awaits additional studies demonstrating their clinical 
utility, there is recognition of the potential to improve health outcomes 
and the need for further research.
Research consortia studying PRSs include Electronic Medical 
Records and Genomics (eMERGE)20 and Polygenic Risk Methods in 
Diverse Populations (PRIMED)21 in the USA, the former focusing on 
clinical implementation of PRSs and the latter on reducing the perfor-
mance gap in PRSs between population groups. The All of Us22 cohort, 
established in the USA with an emphasis on diversity, and the FinnGen23 
and UK Biobank24 cohorts from Europe are valuable resources for 
validating PRSs. Several additional global genomic data sharing ini-
tiatives are attempting to develop PRSs for diverse groups25,26. The 
ClinGen consortium in the USA includes PRS working groups that have 
developed a PRS reporting standard27 and are establishing a framework 
for curating evidence for the clinical utility of PRSs. Several speciality 
societies, such as the American Heart Association28, European Society of 
Cardiology29 and American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics 
(ACMG)30, as well as a Task Force of the International Common Disease 
Alliance17, have commented on the clinical use of PRSs.
Although enthusiasm for using PRSs is increasing — as reflected in 
the emergence of PRS-focused companies, direct-to-consumer (DTC) 
genetic testing services31 and academic centre-based genomic initia-
tives — the transition to routine clinical use faces several hurdles. These 
include the limited familiarity of patients and clinical service providers 
with the probabilistic nature of polygenic risk, the lack of integration 
of PRSs into electronic health record (EHR) systems and the paucity 
of clinical decision support (CDS) tools to guide the interpretation of 
PRSs and the clinical management of patients. There is a need to estab-
lish clinical standards for PRSs and regulatory and policy guidelines, 
given the different methods for constructing PRSs and their applica-
tion to different diseases. Moreover, outcome studies are needed to 
establish whether the return of a PRS to an individual improves clinical 
decision-making and health outcomes, thereby informing practice 
guidelines and supporting the cost–effectiveness of PRS testing.
Introduction
Most common human diseases, such as cardiometabolic diseases, 
cancers and neurological disorders, result from multiple aetiological 
factors, including both genetic and environmental factors. These condi-
tions are leading causes of morbidity and mortality worldwide, and risk 
assessment has a crucial role in devising screening strategies and guid-
ing preventive or therapeutic interventions. Traditionally, risk estima-
tion has relied on risk factors identified in large cohort studies (such 
as age, male sex, smoking, hypertension, diabetes and hypercholes-
terolaemia for coronary heart disease (CHD)), and for some diseases, 
validated algorithms are available to estimate absolute risk over defined 
time periods based on these factors. However, the accuracy of risk 
prediction for common diseases is modest, partly owing to the limited 
availability of sufficiently predictive biomarkers. In this context, the 
development of polygenic risk scores (PRSs), based on genetic variants 
identified in genome-wide association studies (GWAS)1,2, represents an 
important advance in disease risk assessment3.
A historical perspective
The origin of PRSs can be traced back to the principles of complex trait 
genetics and statistical genetic prediction, first proposed in the early 
twentieth century4. At that time, the scientific divide between biometri-
cians, who analysed continuous variation in traits, and ‘Mendelians’, 
who focused on discrete patterns of inheritance, was reconciled by 
Ronald Fisher5 in a seminal paper published in 1918. Fisher proposed 
that complex traits are influenced by the additive effects of many 
genetic variants of small effect and that these traits could be studied 
using quantitative statistical approaches4. He proposed analysis of 
variance as a statistical method to partition phenotypic variation into 
genetic and environmental components, introducing the concept 
of heritability. Importantly, these early models of genetic architecture 
were based on the analysis of phenotypes among related individuals, 
primarily in the context of animal or plant breeding programmes, with-
out knowledge of genotypes. Traits such as milk yield in cattle or oil 
content in maize became the focus of selection experiments, which 
provided further insights into quantitative genetics6.
In the mid-twentieth century, population geneticists including 
Fisher, JBS Haldane and Sewall Wright advanced theoretical models 
to describe how genetic variation is shaped by forces such as drift, 
mutation, migration and selection7 (see Fig. 1 for a population genetics 
background for PRSs). However, it was not until later in the twentieth 
century — when genetic markers across the genome became available — 
that the field of disease genetics emerged8. Although linkage analysis 
had been successful in identifying loci for rare Mendelian diseases, 
it was largely ineffective for complex traits characterized by poly-
genicity and small effect sizes9. In a 1996 commentary, Neil Risch and 
Kathleen Merikangas10 proposed a shift in strategy: the genotyping 
of common single-nucleotide variants (SNVs) across the genome to 
identify associations with complex traits. This vision came to fruition 
with the advent of GWAS, catalysed by the availability of the human 
genome sequence, Haplotype Map (HapMap) data and genotyp-
ing arrays. Subsequent GWAS, including the landmark study by the 
Wellcome Trust Case Control Consortium2, validated this approach, 
leading to the discovery of thousands of loci associated with a wide 
range of diseases and traits, often implicating many variants for a 
single condition11. A logical next step was to aggregate the effects of 
multiple trait-associated variants into a single PRS for that trait — that 
is, quantifying an individual’s inherited susceptibility to disease based 
on the cumulative contribution of many common variants1,2,12.

Review article
This Review focuses on the translational aspects of polygenic risk 
assessment; it summarizes the potential use of PRSs in the clinic, with 
an emphasis on practical challenges and the evidence that is needed for 
their responsible implementation. Although other recent reviews have 
covered PRS methodology and reporting standards14,27,32, the author 
focuses here on the next steps required for their clinical adoption, 
particularly in the context of improving risk prediction for common 
diseases (see Table 1 for potential clinical applications of PRSs). The 
current status of PRS testing is discussed within the four domains — 
analytical validity, clinical validity, clinical utility and ethical, legal and 
social implications — of the ACCE framework33, which is a standard 
analytical process adopted by various entities worldwide for evaluating 
scientific data on emerging clinical genetic tests. Barriers to PRS use, 
including scientific and infrastructure gaps, are highlighted. Future 
directions in data harmonization and regulatory frameworks to bridge 
the translational divide between genetic discovery and personalized 
medicine and to promote the successful clinical implementation of 
PRSs are discussed.
Analytical validity of PRSs
Polygenic risk assessment can be considered an ‘omic’ technology that 
uses genome-wide genetic variation to construct a PRS. Here, the author

discusses aspects related to the analytic validity of PRSs, including iden-
tifying genetic variants by genotyping arrays or whole-genome sequenc-
ing (WGS), imputation of non-genotyped variants and methods for 
constructing PRSs and adjusting for genetic ancestry and admixture.
Measuring genetic variation
An initial step in calculating a PRS is the accurate capture of com-
monly occurring genetic variation across the genome of the individual. 
Genotyping on arrays, followed by statistical imputation of non- 
genotyped variants using patterns of linkage disequilibrium, is a 
cost-effective way to calculate PRSs. For example, the Global Diversity 
Array34 includes more than 1.8 million SNVs and is optimized for under-
studied groups, such as those of African ancestries or Latino ethnicities. 
Array-based genotyping is highly reproducible for common variants, 
especially when using the same genotyping platform, rigorous quality 
control pipelines and high-quality reference panels for imputation35. 
Reproducibility is lower for rare variants, when different genotyping 
arrays are used, and in cohorts of diverse genetic ancestries. By contrast, 
WGS can capture both common and rare variants without reliance on 
imputation, which could potentially provide more robust input data for 
calculating a PRS. However, the analytical validity of WGS data used in PRS 
calculations is sensitive to coverage depth, variant calling algorithms and 
sequencing error rates36,37. Insufficient coverage or suboptimal variant 
calling pipelines can lead to the misclassification of genotypes, which 
in turn may reduce the performance of PRSs that are calculated from 
WGS data. At present, genotyping arrays remain the pragmatic standard 
in most research settings owing to their scalability and affordability 
whereas, for clinical use, low-pass WGS is emerging as an alternative.
Imputing non-genotyped variants
Genotype imputation — and, by extension, PRS accuracy — is influ-
enced by both genotyping array design and the choice of reference 
panel38. The differences in genotype imputation quality across differ-
ent reference panels can be substantial and can affect PRS calculation. 
The quality of imputation depends on several factors, including refer-
ence panel size, sequencing coverage of the reference panel, minor 
allele frequency (in the reference panel) of the variant being imputed, 
haplotype accuracy in reference and study samples, density of geno-
typing array, match between the study and reference populations 
and the imputation algorithm used39. Although the 1000 Genomes 
Project reference panel has been widely used for genotype imputation, 
larger and more diverse panels such as the Trans-Omics for Precision 
Medicine (TOPMed) reference panel40 identify a greater number of 
variants. However, linear reference panels derived from short-read 
sequences will miss a proportion of the genomic variation in under-
studied populations, which could reduce the performance of PRSs in 
these groups41. Recognizing this limitation, the Human Pangenome 
Project42 has completed telomere-to-telomere sequencing of 350 indi-
viduals from diverse groups to develop comprehensive reference 
panels that capture most of the genetic variation worldwide. This 
will enable a more complete ascertainment of genetic variation in 
non-European genetic ancestry groups, such as individuals of African

Constructing PRSs
PRSs are constructed using two broad categories of method that differ 
in variant selection strategy: pruning and thresholding or genome-wide 
methods (for example, LDpred, PRS-CS or SBayesR)13. The pruning and 
thresholding method chooses a P-value threshold for disease-associated 
variants that produces the highest prediction accuracy in a tuning 
cohort. Correlated SNVs within an arbitrarily chosen window size for 
linkage disequilibrium are removed to select those SNVs that are nearly 
independent from each other and thus can be fit additively. By contrast, 
genome-wide methods include all SNVs simultaneously, accounting 
for linkage disequilibrium between SNVs, using a reference panel to 
reduce the risk of overfitting43. Statistical techniques are used to apply 
shrinkage or regularization to the GWAS effect sizes, such as penalized 
regression (for example, LASSO regression using Lassosum, an R pack-
age that adapts penalized regression to GWAS summary statistics44) 
as well as Bayesian approaches (for example, SbayesR or PRS-CS) that 
implement shrinkage by specifying a prior distribution of SNV effect 
sizes45,46. An independent validation dataset is typically used to assess 
the predictive power and generalizability of SNV weights. The optimal 
method (pruning and thresholding or genome-wide) depends on the 
genetic architecture of a trait47,48. Genome-wide methods can adapt to 
different genetic architectures and tend to perform better than pruning 
and thresholding49 but are computationally burdensome, motivating 
efforts to develop methods that improve both prediction accuracy and 
computational efficiency, particularly in large biobank-scale datasets50,51.
Adjusting for genetic ancestry
For clinical application, PRSs must be adjusted to the ancestral 
background of the tested individual52. This requires both inference 
of the genetic ancestry of the test subject and alignment to appro-
priate reference distributions. One strategy uses principal compo-
nent analysis (PCA) to place an individual within a global ancestry 
space52,53. The adjustment of PRSs based on PCA should ideally model 
both the variance and means of PRSs in an ancestry-dependent 
manner52,53. Alternative methods to adjust for ancestry quantify 
genetic distance — for example, using Euclidean metrics — to identify 
reference individuals with similar ancestry, such as by a k-nearest-
neighbour algorithm54 or interpolation weights that are based on the 
Euclidean distance from ancestry groups in the global PCA space55. 
These approaches can improve PRS adjustment to avoid systematic 
misclassification of risk, particularly in individuals of admixed or 
under-represented backgrounds.
Clinical validity of PRSs
The clinical validity of a PRS depends on how strongly it is associated 
with the trait of interest. Metrics for reporting the clinical validity of 
a PRS27 include the hazard ratio associated with a 1 standard devia-
tion increase in PRS or with having a high PRS (for example, in the top 
5th percentile), the proportion of disease liability56 explained by a PRS 
and discrimination as assessed by the area under the receiver operat-
ing curve, which is a composite metric of sensitivity and specificity57. 
Additional metrics include reclassification indices and net benefit58. 
Being in the highest range of the distribution of a PRS for certain 
diseases may be associated with risk equivalent to that posed by the

The clinical validity of PRSs in certain settings may be reduced by the 
modest performance and variable transferability across genetic ances-
