long telomeres29,30. Both short and long telomere syndromes are associ-
ated with increased risk of clonal haematopoiesis and haematological 
and non-haematological cancers. Short telomeres may create selec-
tive pressure for mutations that rescue cellular fitness and confer an 
advantage over other HSCs31. By contrast, long telomeres may increase 
HSC self-renewal capacity, creating more opportunities to acquire onco-
genic mutations and allowing mutations that promote proliferation to 
persist for more cell divisions. As such clones expand, the likelihood of 
secondary driver mutations also increases31. Collectively, these findings 
suggest that telomeres are dynamically regulated in a tight equilibrium 
to preserve genome integrity and cellular homeostasis, establishing 
telomere biology as a critical determinant of HSC fitness32.
Like the telomere disorders, Fanconi anaemia demonstrates the 
dependence of HSC function on genome integrity. First described 
by Guido Fanconi in 1927, Fanconi anaemia is a predominantly auto-
somal recessive disorder that typically presents in childhood with 
low blood cell counts and progressive bone marrow failure across all 
haematopoietic lineages, accompanied by characteristic develop-
mental abnormalities33. Long before the molecular basis of Fanconi 
anaemia was understood, cells from patients with Fanconi anaemia 
were known to exhibit hypersensitivity to DNA cross-linking agents 
such as mitomycin C, revealing a core defect in interstrand lesion 
repair. Systematic genetic dissection of Fanconi anaemia exemplified 
the use of complementation analysis to systematically map disease 
genes. By fusing cells from different patients and testing whether the 
cross-linking hypersensitivity phenotype could be rescued, genetically 
distinct complementation groups were defined from which causal 
genes could be cloned and functionally characterized34–36.
This approach initially revealed the core Fanconi anaemia genes, 
which assemble into a nuclear E3 ubiquitin ligase complex that 
triggers ubiquitylation of FANCD2–FANCI and recruitment of effec-
tor proteins36. A transformative advance came with the identifica-
tion of BRCA2 mutations in patients with Fanconi anaemia, linking the 
BRCA/homologous recombination pathway to the Fanconi anaemia 
core complex, and eventually implicating other cancer predisposi-
tion genes including BRCA1, PALB2 and BRIP1 in an expanded Fanconi 
anaemia/BRCA pathway, positioning Fanconi anaemia proteins as 
master guardians of genome integrity that coordinate the function of 
multiple overlapping repair pathways36,37 (Fig. 1). Subsequent targeted 
and WES studies have identified additional rare mutations in scaffolding 
proteins and nucleases such as SLX4 and ERCC4, demonstrating how 
Fanconi anaemia proteins interface with effectors of DNA cross-link 
repair, safeguarding stem cells from mutagenesis and malignant 
transformation38,39. Expanding beyond the Fanconi anaemia pathway, 
mutations in ERCC6L2, encoding a helicase involved in double-strand 
break repair, cause a distinct bone marrow failure syndrome with 
increased risk of myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) and acute myeloid 
leukaemia (AML)40. Germline variants in DDX41, an RNA helicase, have 
emerged as among the most frequently identified inherited predisposi-
tion variants in adult MDS and AML and are associated with impaired 
resolution of transcription–replication conflicts, DNA damage and 
consequent inflammation41,42. Together, these findings have established 
DNA repair as a fundamental requirement for HSC maintenance, reveal-
ing how defects across different aspects of genome integrity converge 
on phenotypes of marrow failure and cancer predisposition.
Ribosome biology and proteostasis in haematopoietic

The ribosomal disorders or ribosomopathies, including Diamond– 
Blackfan anaemia (DBA) and Shwachman–Diamond syndrome 
Box 1 | Tools for genetic discovery
 
Genetic variation provides a powerful lens for understanding mech­
anisms of human disease biology and for stratifying risk. Before 
the advent of genome-wide association studies (GWAS), linkage 
analysis was the primary method for human genetic mapping of 
phenotypes239. Linkage analysis tracks co-segregation of genetic 
markers and disease phenotypes within families, identifying 
chromosomal regions likely to harbour disease genes240. The 
development of genome-wide maps of naturally occurring poly­
morphisms enabled systematic linkage scans and positional cloning 
of disease genes241. However, linkage analysis requires recruitment 
of large families and has limited power to detect common, small-
effect variants, restricting its utility for complex traits with polygenic 
architectures239.
Completion of the Human Genome Project and characterization 
of common haplotype structure through the HapMap Project revealed 
patterns of linkage disequilibrium across the human population. 
This result enabled the use of GWAS, initially through the design 
of microarrays that efficiently genotype hundreds of thousands of 
single-nucleotide polymorphisms and more recently via sequencing 
approaches242. In GWAS, individual variants across the genome are 
tested for association with a phenotype of interest, with statistical 
methods to account for population stratification and the large 
number of statistical tests performed243,244. As population biobanks 
have grown to hundreds of thousands of participants, GWAS have 
identified reproducible associations for common diseases and traits, 
with common variants capturing a substantial fraction of heritability 
(the phenotypic variance attributable to genotypic variance)101.
Beyond common variants, rare, large-effect variants contribute 
to trait architecture. Whole-exome sequencing efficiently captures 
protein-coding regions (~1–2% of the genome), enabling discovery 
of rare variants underlying Mendelian disorders and contributing 
to complex traits245. At population scale, rare variant association 
studies test variants individually or aggregate them using gene- 
based burden tests to identify disease-associated genes246. 
As sequencing costs have continued to decrease, whole-genome 
sequencing at population scale is revealing contributions of non- 
coding rare variants, structural variants and other types of variation 
overlooked by genotyping arrays and whole-exome sequencing247 
and is increasingly replacing arrays as the genotyping platform for 
GWAS.
The scale of modern population biobanks, which include many 
related individuals, has also enabled within-family association 
studies, combining early family-based designs with population-scale 
data244,248. These frameworks leverage family structure to partition 
genetic effects into direct effects acting within individuals and 
indirect effects mediated through relatives248. Collectively, these 
approaches have illuminated the genetic basis of human phenotypes 
across the spectrum of rare and common variation.

(SDS), reveal how disruption in core cellular functions can produce 
lineage-restricted haematopoietic disease. DBA is characterized by 
striking and selective reduction in erythroid progenitors or precur-
sors in the bone marrow with ostensibly normal production of other 
blood lineages, typically manifesting in infancy43. Early gene mapping 
identified heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in RPS19, and sub-
sequent targeted and WES identified haploinsufficient variants across 
at least 23 other ribosomal protein genes43–46. Some studies of ribo-
somal protein mutants have implicated aberrant p53 activation trig-
gered by imbalance in ribosomal subunits or excessive free ribosomal 
proteins47,48. However, it remained unclear how loss-of-function muta-
tions in ribosomal proteins selectively impaired production of eryth-
roid cells. WES in individuals affected by DBA without known ribosomal 
protein mutations revealed splice site-altering variants in GATA1, a key 
erythroid transcription factor, that resulted in reduced production of its 
full length form49. Mechanistic interrogation of DBA-causing ribosomal 
protein variants revealed that ribosomal protein haploinsufficiency 
reduces overall ribosome levels and decreases GATA1 mRNA translation, 
unifying these seemingly disparate observations50,51 (Fig. 1). Broadly, 
this work clarified the role of GATA1 in specifying development of the 
human erythroid lineage and provided insights into how haploinsuffi-
cient mutations in ribosomal proteins (which occur in other rare disease 
contexts52) can cause disease by selectively impairing translation of 
functionally central transcripts with intrinsic vulnerable properties, 
such as GATA1, whose relatively short 5′-untranslated region renders it 
sensitive to reduced ribosome availability50. The establishment of GATA1 
as a unifying mechanism for disparate DBA mutations has motivated 
therapeutic development of gene therapy approaches for DBA53.
The example of DBA highlights ribosomal defects as a more general 
mechanism underlying bone marrow failure. SDS is an autosomal reces-
sive bone marrow failure syndrome most prominently characterized 
by neutropenia and accompanied by exocrine pancreatic insufficiency 
as well as skeletal and cardiac abnormalities. Positional cloning and 
targeted sequencing identified the causal gene for SDS to be SBDS, with 
subsequent mechanistic studies revealing its key role in maturation of 
the large (60S) ribosomal subunit54–57. Exome sequencing has more 
recently revealed mutations in several other genes, including DNAJC21, 
SRP54 and EFL1, each linked to ribosome biology and associated with 
Shwachman–Diamond-like presentations58–61. Additionally, rare muta-
tions in the histone deubiquitinase MYSM1 that cause bone marrow fail-
ure have been shown to impair ribosomal protein gene transcription in 
HSCs, causing loss of HSCs62,63. Collectively, these discoveries established 
the group of ribosomopathies while raising fundamental questions 
regarding the relative importance of global dysregulation of ribosomal 
assembly versus translation of specific lineage-defining mRNAs and 
how these two non-exclusive mechanisms ultimately lead to bone mar-
row failure47. Broadly, the rare ribosomopathies reveal an unexpected 
connection between ribosome assembly and specific haematopoietic 
lineage or HSC defects, highlighting the broader principle that protein 
synthesis is tightly regulated at distinct stages of haematopoiesis64.
The ribosomopathies also intersect with dyskeratosis congenita 
and the telomere biology disorders (discussed above): some genes that 
cause telomere biology disorders, including DKC1, NHP2 and NOP10, 
are also implicated in ribosomal RNA processing, suggesting that, for 
a subset of telomere biology disorder patients, impaired ribosomal 
function may contribute to bone marrow failure24. Disruption of pro-
teostasis downstream of translation can also cause lineage-restricted 
defects. In severe congenital neutropenia, germline variants in ELANE 
result in accumulation of misfolded neutrophil elastase in granulocyte 
progenitors, triggering endoplasmic reticulum stress, activation of the 
unfolded protein response and apoptosis of neutrophil precursors65.
Haematopoietic transcription factors
GATA1 (discussed above in the context of ribosome biology) also 
provides a key example of a haematopoietic transcription factor as a 
critical node in which genetic variation can disrupt lineage specifica-
tion. Similarly, mutations in other transcription factors have provided 
fundamental insights into blood cell development (Fig. 1). For example, 
what were initially thought to be distinct clinical syndromes — including 
MonoMAC syndrome (monocytopenia and bacterial infection), 
Emberger syndrome (primary lymphoedema with leukaemia pre-
disposition) and certain cases of familial MDS/AML — were unified in 
2011 by the discovery that heterozygous loss-of-function mutations 
in one transcription factor, GATA2, underlie this remarkably broad 
clinical spectrum66–69. The resulting condition, now termed GATA2 defi-
ciency, exhibits striking phenotypic variability both between affected 
individuals and within the same patient over time, highlighting the 
complex temporal and context-dependent requirements for GATA2 
in haematopoietic stem and progenitor cell function70.
As exemplified by GATA2, transcription factors essential for lineage 
specification represent key nodes: germline loss-of-function variants 
cause lineage-specific defects and predispose to leukaemia, whereas 
somatic mutations drive malignant transformation. For example, 
variants in MECOM identified in a rare bone marrow failure syndrome 
revealed MECOM as a key transcription factor node in an HSC regulatory 
network that has also been found to be co-opted in some high-risk acute 
myeloid leukaemias71,72. This pattern is evident in multiple early-onset 
leukaemias, in which several critical transcription factors associated 
with germline predisposition syndromes harbour recurrent somatic 
driver alterations. Mutations in RUNX1, first identified in the 1990s as 
the cause of familial platelet disorder with predisposition to myeloid 
leukaemia, have revealed essential functions in megakaryopoiesis and 
leukaemogenesis73,74. Notably, RUNX1-deficient patients are at mark-
edly elevated risk of clonal haematopoiesis and AML; mechanistic 
studies have suggested that inflammatory pathways might play a role 
in driving this risk, contributing to an emerging paradigm of clonal hae-
matopoiesis as an inflammatory disease75,76. Similarly, mutations in the 
ETV6 transcription factor disrupting its nuclear localization and bind-
ing result in a syndrome of thrombocytopenia and predisposition to 
haematological (particularly lymphoid) malignancies77. IKZF1, encod-
ing the lymphoid transcription factor IKAROS, further illustrates how 
germline and somatic variation converge on malignant risk: germline 
IKZF1 mutations cause immunodeficiency with B cell lymphopenia and 
predisposition to ALL, whereas somatic IKZF1 deletions are a hallmark 
of high-risk paediatric B-ALL, emphasizing the requirement for tightly 
regulated IKAROS dosage in early lymphoid development78,79. Similarly, 
germline mutations in PAX5 and TCF3 impair B cell development and 
predispose to ALL, and somatic alterations in these genes are among the 
most common B-ALL drivers80,81. Together, these findings demonstrate 
how even subtle perturbations in transcriptional regulators can disrupt 
the precise temporal and dose-dependent control of transcription in 
haematopoiesis, with variable clinical consequences that reflect the 
complex interplay between stem cell exhaustion, disruption of normal 
differentiation and malignant transformation.
Open challenges for rare blood diseases
Whereas family-based analyses and sequencing studies identified rare 
variants and highlighted core disease pathways in many haematopoietic

609
Review article
diseases, population-scale studies have profoundly expanded and 
complicated understanding of the role of rare variants in disease. 
In particular, incomplete penetrance (when a variant may or may not 
cause disease) and variable expressivity (when the same variant causes 
clinical symptoms that vary widely in severity or presentation) repre-
sent key challenges in clinical genetics. Variants originally thought to 
cause disease with complete or high penetrance based on studies of 
cohorts of rare disease patients and families have increasingly been 
observed in apparently healthy individuals in population biobanks. 
This finding has prompted downward revision of penetrance estimates 
across diverse conditions, including the thalassaemias, telomere biol-
ogy disorders and inherited bleeding disorders82–84. Regarding variable 
expressivity, in many rare blood disorders, affected individuals can vary 
greatly in presentation, even among carriers of the same pathogenic 
variant, limiting the ability to predict clinical trajectories for individual 
rare mutation carriers. For example, in the telomere biology disorders, 
identical mutations in TERT or PARN can manifest as bone marrow 
failure in childhood, idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis in adulthood, or 
remain clinically silent until late life24. Notably, carriers of pathogenic 
variants may exhibit subclinical biological effects, even when they 
do not develop overt disease. Furthermore, heterozygous carriers 
of recessive disease-causing variants can exhibit phenotypic effects, 
with important implications for purifying selection and, consequently, 
population frequencies of these variants85,86.

interactions between genetic variants and each of these factors (Fig. 3). 
Combinatorial effects of genetic variants also contribute. Polygenic 
background has been shown to modify the penetrance and expressiv-
ity of rare variants in multiple contexts, including bleeding disorders 
and telomere biology disorders87,88. In addition, somatic mutations 
can affect expressivity of blood disease mutations by restoring fitness 
to HSCs carrying rare pathogenic variants, either by direct reversion 
mutations or secondary compensatory alterations89 (Fig. 3). These 
phenomena highlight the need for quantitative frameworks that model 
inherited mutations, gene–gene interactions and somatic evolution 
within relevant environmental contexts to refine estimates of pen-
etrance and expressivity. Development of such frameworks and inte-
gration of larger patient cohorts with germline genetics, clinical and 
multi-omic patient data will enable improved clinical prediction.
Relatedly, for many rare syndromes including the telomere biology 
disorders and DBA, a subset of patients have no identified rare causa-
tive variants even with state-of-the-art sequencing, reflecting several 
challenges24,46,90. Some pathogenic variants remain technically difficult 
to detect, including repeat expansions, structural variants and variants 
in highly repetitive or poorly captured genomic regions91. Long-read 
sequencing approaches have catalogued more than 20,000 struc-
tural variants (greater than 50 base pairs) per individual on average92. 
Telomere-to-telomere and pangenome references, as well as careful 
integration of complex types of variation into association studies, 
will enable more complete capture of genomic variation, increasing 
diagnostic yield and identifying new associations with disease92,93. 
In other cases, the causal gene or genes remain unidentified, or vari-
ants of uncertain significance cannot be confidently interpreted. As 
one example, in a cohort of familial AML/MDS families, 43% of fami-
lies did not have a known disease-causal variant identified by WES, 
although many had variants of uncertain significance. Interrogation 
of these cases revealed new candidate genes, some of which have been 
supported by subsequent mechanistic work94,95.
As gene discovery progresses, new disease loci are likely to be 
associated with smaller effect sizes and increasingly variable presenta-
tions, making further discovery and confident causal association with 
disease increasingly difficult. Additional challenges include patho-
genic non-coding variants, oligogenic inheritance involving multiple 
low-penetrance alleles, complex gene–gene and gene–environment 
interactions, and epigenetic alterations such as parent-of-origin 
effects96 or locus-specific methylation changes that will be missed 
by standard diagnostic pipelines. Addressing these gaps will require 
both technical advances to enable the use of long-read sequencing 
technologies at population scale and analytical advances for variant 
interpretation. Integration of multimodal data, functional assays and 
improved variant effect prediction models, including machine learning 
approaches84,97, together with the continued growth of large, deeply 
phenotyped cohorts, are poised to expand discovery and clinical utility 
of rare variant interpretation for blood diseases in the years ahead.
Population variation affecting blood phenotypes
Whereas studies of rare haematopoietic diseases have mapped critical 
nodes in important pathways in haematopoiesis, population studies 
have revealed broader impacts of common and rare genetic variation 
on blood cell development. Phenotypes including blood cell counts 
and haemoglobin levels are routinely measured clinically and are 
highly heritable, meaning that a substantial fraction of population 
variation is attributable to genetic variation83,98. At the extremes, these 
traits can reflect disease phenotypes such as polycythaemia, anaemia, 
neutropenia and thrombocytopenia; variation in blood cell traits also 
represents independent risk factors for non-haematological diseases, 
including cardiovascular and autoimmune diseases98,99. Increasingly 
large genome-wide association studies (GWAS) over the past 15 years 
have nominated tens of thousands of genetic variants associated 
with blood phenotypes83,98,100, which can be incorporated into poly-
genic prediction of disease and leveraged for a deeper mechanistic 
understanding through variant-to-function studies.
Genetic architecture of blood traits
GWAS have revealed the contribution of common and rare variants 
to the genetic architecture of blood traits. As with other complex 
traits, protein-coding regions are enriched for heritability, but the 
vast majority of common variant signals are in non-coding intronic 
and regulatory regions83,101. Fine-mapped association signals for 
blood traits are strongly enriched for accessible chromatin regions 
in lineage-committed haematopoietic cells, and likely causal vari-
ants map to specific stages in the differentiation cascade from HSCs 
to lineage-committed precursors, supporting functional roles in 
regulating blood cell development83,102.
Although common variants explain most overall heritability, 
many rare variants have been identified with large effect sizes, and 
rare variants affecting blood traits are strongly enriched in genes that 
cause Mendelian blood disorders83. Rare variants collectively explain 
a smaller fraction of phenotypic variance than common variants101,103. 
For example, for platelet counts, heritability attributable to common 
variants is about fourfold greater than for rare variants, and for red 
blood cell counts, about 5.5-fold greater101. Rare coding variants, which 
tend to contribute about one-fifth to a quarter of overall rare variant 
heritability, have also been examined in detail101,103.
Common and rare variants largely implicate the same pathways 
and cell types for blood traits, but common variants are spread across 
many more genes, whereas rare coding variants are highly concen-
trated in a smaller set of genes and pathways. For example, variation 
in a single gene, JAK2, explains a significant fraction of the rare variant 
burden for platelet count. Biologically, the divergence in architecture 
between rare and common variants may reflect evolutionary con-
straint, in which high-impact variants in core genes are kept rare by 
purifying selection, whereas common variation is distributed among 
many loci with smaller effects104. It is also consistent with an omnigenic 
model in which core biological genes have large, interpretable effects, 
but highly interconnected cellular networks propagate regulatory 
perturbations such that variants at many loci have small effects105. 
Overall, these findings reveal a complex architecture in which both 
rare and common variants make significant contributions to blood trait 
variation. Understanding this architecture is critical for informing the 
design of future genetic studies and for enabling mechanistic insights 
and therapeutic translation.
As biobanks continue to expand in size, recent population studies 
with whole-genome sequencing data have explained nearly all herit-
ability for some blood traits by identified common and rare variant 
associations101. Looking ahead, population studies of blood phenotypes 
will need to shift from finding additional loci towards uncovering the 
causal variants at known loci and the underlying molecular mecha-
nisms. At the same time, biobanks continue to comprise mostly indi-
viduals of European and East Asian ancestry, in which genetic discovery 
is more saturated. In other populations, discovery remains limited, 
underscoring a critical need for diverse cohort recruitment to improve 
variant discovery, interpretation and phenotype prediction106–108. 

Nature Reviews Genetics | Volume 27 | August 2026 | 603–621
611
Review article
Additionally, future population studies might benefit from creative uses 
of existing data that leverage cryptic or derived phenotypes. For exam-
ple, past work has used somatic mutations detected in sequencing 
reads to identify clonal expansions109,110, searched for genetic vari-
ants associated with phenotypic variability rather than directional 
effects on traits111 and creatively used phenotype data to characterize 
gene–gene and gene–environment interactions112,113. These approaches 
highlight that deep interrogation of existing biobank data can yield 
new biological insight. Finally, whereas most studies at present have 
focused on cell-intrinsic genetic mechanisms acting within HSPCs, an 
important frontier is understanding genetic effects mediated by the 
bone marrow microenvironment. HSCs reside within perivascular 
niches supported by endothelial cells, mesenchymal stromal cells and 
osteolineage cells, as well as neural and immune components114–117. For 
example, GWAS identified CXCR4, the HSC receptor for the key niche 
chemokine CXCL12, as a central regulator of circulating CD34+ hae-
matopoietic stem and progenitor cell levels, linking genetic variation 
in niche–HSC signalling to blood phenotypes118. Additionally, changes 
to the niche have been implicated in HSC ageing119, yet the role of 
genetic variation acting through the niche remains relatively unex-
plored. This gap may reflect the relative importance of cell-intrinsic 
genetic effects on HSC function, HSC resilience to microenvironmen-
tal changes, or requirements for cells in the microenvironment in 
other physiological contexts. It may also reflect the technical chal-
lenges of isolating and profiling niche cells and studying HSCs in situ. 
Emerging approaches, including spatial transcriptomics and efforts 
to create in vitro bone marrow microenvironments, provide plat-
forms to interrogate cell-extrinsic genetic effects alongside intrinsic 
regulation120,121.
Variant-to-function for population genetic traits
To identify causal variants and biological mechanisms, variant-to-
function approaches aim to move beyond statistical associations from 
GWAS to pinpoint causal variants, link them to target genes, and place 
those genes within cellular and regulatory contexts in haematopoiesis 
(Fig. 4). To this end, recent work has used diverse approaches, includ-
ing fine-mapping complemented with functional genomics, as well 
as predictive modelling and high-throughput functional validation.
Fine-mapping methods leverage population linkage disequilib-
rium patterns and functional annotations to assign probabilities of 
causality to variants, reducing a large set of linked statistically signifi-
cant variants to a more tractable set of high-confidence candidates122. 
Complementing fine-mapping efforts, systematic approaches to 
incorporate functional genomics data — including transcriptomics, 
chromatin accessibility profiles, histone modification patterns and 
three-dimensional chromatin interaction maps — aim to predict which 
variants are most likely to disrupt regulatory elements and identify 
their target genes across haematopoietic cell types. Whereas these 
integrative models represent a major step forward, applying these 
approaches to non-coding variants remains challenging, pointing 
to the need for better modelling of the effects of variation on gene 
regulation123–126. Molecular quantitative trait loci (QTL), including 
expression, splicing and chromatin QTLs, provide a framework to 
interpret regulatory variants by linking them to intermediate molecular 
phenotypes that may mediate genetic effects on phenotypes127–130. 
One limitation of these traditional functional genomics approaches is 
that they rely on bulk-level phenotypic measurements, typically from 
peripheral blood, but haematopoietic cell production is a dynamically 
regulated and continuous process of differentiation that largely occurs 
within the bone marrow. As such, variants acting transiently or within 
specific progenitor cells may thus be overlooked131, which may in part 
explain why GWAS hits do not strongly overlap with expression QTLs in 
peripheral blood (in which predominantly mature blood cells reside) 
and other tissues132. Using samples of primary bone marrow haema-
topoietic progenitors and using single-cell approaches that capture 
heterogeneous cell types and dynamic cell states may better elucidate 
the effects of variants, which act at specific stages of haematopoietic 
differentiation133–137.
Alternatively, the combination of predictive modelling and 
high-throughput functional validation presents an increasingly pow-
erful approach to variant interpretation. For coding variants, machine 
learning tools can accurately predict true loss-of-function variants, 
splicing variants and deleterious missense variants138–142; for non-coding 
regions, in which most GWAS signals fall, deep learning models are 
increasingly capturing regulatory logic and cell-type specificity138,143,144. 
These predictions can be both informed by and validated using meth-
ods such as pooled CRISPR knockout and CRISPRi/CRISPRa screens 
that enable unbiased discovery of genes and regulatory elements 
impacting diverse cellular phenotypes, enhanced by single-cell tran-
scriptomic, epigenomic and imaging-based readouts145. In haema-
topoiesis, CRISPR-based approaches have been used to illuminate 
the role of specific enhancers during erythroid differentiation, map 
gene regulatory networks in primary haematopoietic progenitors and 
systematically perturb haematopoietic transcription factors to assess 
effects on chromatin and gene expression profiles146–148. Notably, as 
pooled CRISPR–Cas9 screens generate heterogeneous indels, they 
are not optimal to resolve single-base effects at high throughput149. 
Base editors and prime editors extend this framework by enabling 
precise variant-level substitutions in primary HSPCs. With these 
modalities, large-scale perturbation screens of specific candidate 
single-nucleotide variants can be used to precisely map regulation of 
fetal haemoglobin and systematically mutagenize GATA1 and identify 
effects on haematopoietic differentiation150. As the toolkit of base 
and prime editor screens continues to improve and diversify, so will 
insights from connecting variant-to-function in haematopoiesis151,152. 
Alongside perturbational strategies, massively parallel reporter assays 
enable coupling of thousands of synthetic regulatory sequences to bar-
coded reporters to quantify regulatory effects. This approach has been 
used to systematically map the logic of cell-state-specific enhancers 
and their interactions with transcription factors during haematopoietic 
differentiation153 and dissect variant effects impacting erythropoiesis 
and other phenotypes154–156. Together, these experimental strategies 
generate rich, high-dimensional datasets that can then be used to refine 
computational predictions, creating a positive feedback loop. Integra-
tion of these approaches will be critical for closing the gap between

Evolutionary genetics of ageing
Handan Melike Dönertaş 
  1,2 
 & Linda Partridge 
  3 
Abstract
Modern humans now routinely survive to advanced ages, in far 
greater proportions than ancestral populations, and thus experience 
the consequences of molecular pathways optimized for youth yet 
still active in old age. Natural selection weakens over the course of 
adulthood, creating a selection ‘shadow’ in which deleterious late- 
acting mutations accumulate and alleles with early-life benefits persist 
despite late-life costs. An evolutionary lens helps us to understand 
puzzling patterns — from conserved longevity pathways spanning 
the tree of life to a 100-fold variation in maximum lifespan across 
vertebrates — and explains why age-related diseases share genetic 
architectures. Advances in comparative genomics, large-scale human 
genetic studies and multi-omics ageing biomarkers now enable 
rigorous testing of evolutionary predictions. This Review integrates 
evolutionary genetics with molecular mechanisms to clarify why 
ageing evolves, how it varies across species and individuals, and how 
these insights can guide healthspan extension.

are considered hallmarks of ageing, manifest primarily in industrial-
ized populations, with Indigenous populations showing markedly 
different age-related profiles24. Similarly, alleles selected for early-life 
metabolic efficiency now confer late-life disease risk in nutrient-rich 
environments25, illustrating how environmental mismatch can unmask 
antagonistic pleiotropy at cardiometabolic loci.
This Review synthesizes the evolutionary genetics of ageing 
around three interconnected themes. First, we examine how mutation 
accumulation and antagonistic pleiotropy shape the genetic landscape 
of ageing, creating architectures vulnerable to late-life decline. Second, 
we analyse conserved genetic pathways and cross-species genomic 
signatures that reveal both shared and lineage-specific solutions 
to longevity. Third, we explore how genetic variation within human 
populations underlies individual differences in ageing trajectories 
and disease susceptibility.
Evolutionary genetic theories of ageing
Ageing arises as a consequence of weakened natural selection with 
age, creating a so-called ‘shadow’ that obscures deleterious late-life 
phenotypes from selection (Fig. 1a). Selection intensity decreases 
progressively with adult age across human populations, both those 
in the pre-demographic-transition phase (characterized by high 
fertility and high mortality) and those in the post-demographic-
transition phase (marked by low fertility and low mortality) (Fig. 1b). 
In post-demographic-transition populations, increased adult survival 
extends the selection window, yet lower fertility results in overall lower 
selection intensity26. Today, modern humans routinely survive far 
beyond the ages at which selection operated with appreciable force, 
be it in contemporary or ancestral demographic scenarios8,27. Whereas 
deleterious mutations affecting early-life phenotypes, when selection 
is strong, are efficiently purged (Fig. 1a, mutation A), within the selec-
tion shadow, ageing emerges not as a programme but as a ‘side effect’ 
of genetic processes that selection either actively favours for early-life 
benefits3,28 or cannot prevent because effects manifest too late (Box 1).
Antagonistic pleiotropy
The antagonistic pleiotropy theory proposes that alleles conferring 
early-life benefits can be favoured despite late-life costs, because selec-
tion weights early effects more heavily3,14,28 (Fig. 1a, mutation B). The 
theory predicts negative genetic correlations between early fitness and 
late-life performance. Experimental evolution studies demonstrate 
that lifespan-extending manipulations incur early-life costs, includ-
ing reduced fecundity, delayed development or compromised stress 
resistance29,30. Direct selection on lifespan in Drosophila revealed that 
long-lived lines produced half the lifetime progeny of short-lived lines, 
with this difference present across all ages31. In humans, Mendelian 
randomization demonstrated that genetic variants driving earlier 
menarche or childbirth accelerate ageing outcomes and increase the 
risk of multiple age-related diseases17. At the population level, polygenic 
scores — which aggregate the effects of many genetic variants into a 
single metric of genetic liability — for reproductive traits increased 
across successive UK Biobank birth cohorts (1940 to 1969), consistent 
with ongoing positive selection for reproduction. The same scores cor-
related negatively with survival to age 76 years, with antagonistically 
pleiotropic variants outnumbering concordant ones by nearly four to 
one16. These trade-offs might operate through age-dependent regula-
tory changes, whereby variants drive beneficial expression patterns in 
youth, but harmful patterns in old age. Widespread genetic pleiotropy 
among age-related diseases highlights shared architectures through 
Introduction
Ageing, the progressive decline in biological function with age, emerges 
from weakening natural selection during adulthood1. Despite its del-
eterious effects2,3, ageing evolves and persists across many species. 
Mechanistic analyses alone cannot explain ageing, whereas an evolu-
tionary perspective can clarify why patterns of longevity and late-life 
disease differ across individuals, populations and species4–6. Modern 
humans survive more frequently to advanced ages than individuals 
in ancestral populations7. Natural selection has not had the opportu-
nity to mould survival and fecundity at these late ages, which exposes 
late-acting genetic variants and reveals molecular pathways that have 
been selected to function well in youth but not at later ages8. By integrat-
ing evolutionary and biomedical research we can clarify the genetic 
architecture underlying ageing and age-related diseases. These evolu-
tionary foundations benefit precision medicine approaches, because 
human disease risk reflects deep evolutionary histories combined with 
recent lineage-specific variants and contemporary environments6,9. 
Geroscience builds on this logic, positing that ageing represents the 
major risk factor for common chronic diseases and that targeting 
shared genetic mechanisms can improve healthspan10,11.
Classic evolutionary genetic theories provide the organizing 
framework for understanding how genetic architectures underlying 
ageing evolve. Natural selection acts with full force until the onset of 
reproduction, because death before this stage results in the loss of all 
potential progeny. Natural selection weakens progressively during 
adulthood, so that late-acting deleterious mutations undergo weak 
purging, whereas alleles enhancing early-life fitness can be favoured 
despite late-life costs12. The mutation accumulation theory proposes 
that germline mutations with late-acting harmful effects can reach 
appreciable frequency under mutation–selection balance13. Antago-
nistic pleiotropy posits genetic trade-offs between early and late life14,15, 
with human genomic studies demonstrating strong negative genetic 
correlations between reproductive traits and lifespan16,17.
Although ageing seems to be widespread, it is not universal, and 
its rate varies across species. Maximum lifespan differs over 100-fold 
among vertebrates, and the underlying genetic mechanisms remain 
incompletely understood18. This diversity coexists with striking con-
servation of longevity-regulating pathways. Genetic manipulations of 
insulin/insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1) signalling, mTOR and stress- 
response pathways can extend lifespan across invertebrates and mam-
mals, suggesting conserved mechanisms modulating longevity19,20. 
Recent frameworks distinguish ‘public’ mechanisms (conserved path-
ways) from ‘private’ mechanisms (lineage-specific adaptations), clarifying 
how longevity evolves through both shared and unique solutions5,6.
Methodological advances now enable the genome-wide genetic 
interrogation of ageing. Comparative genomics across mammals 
has uncovered amino acid changes and evolutionary rate shifts in 
longevity-linked genes, including genes involved in immune func-
tion, blood clotting and vascular repair21. Genome-wide association 
studies (GWAS) of human longevity, parental lifespan and healthspan 
have revealed highly polygenic architectures with small individual 
effects but substantial aggregate impact. Multi-omics approaches 
have uncovered age-related changes in gene expression, epigenetic 
modifications and protein abundance across tissues and individuals22. 
These developments are transforming the evolutionary genetics of age-
ing into a data-rich field, where models generate testable predictions 
about molecular mechanisms and intervention targets23.
Environmental contexts modulate these genetic architectures in 
important ways. Inflammatory circulating cytokine patterns, which 

Nature Reviews Genetics | Volume 27 | September 2026 | 708–723

which these trade-offs manifest in late-life pathology32,33. A large-scale 
analysis of 62 complex diseases found that 87% of those with significant 
genetic correlations showed positive associations with fertility34. Sev-
eral influential theories, including disposable soma and hyperfunction, 
represent specific mechanistic accounts of how antagonistic pleiotropy 
operates at the physiological level (Box 1).
Mutation accumulation
The mutation accumulation theory posits that germline alleles with 
late-acting deleterious effects achieve higher frequency under 
mutation–selection balance, because selection declines with adult age13 
(Fig. 1a, mutation C). The theory predicts that genetic variance in fitness 
components and inbreeding depression — the reduced survival and 
fertility of offspring of related individuals — should increase with age as 
late-acting deleterious variants escape removal35. In Drosophila, inbreed-
ing depression severity increases systematically across the lifespan, with 
the mortality difference between inbred and outbred flies widening 
progressively with age36,37. Molecular studies extend these findings across 
diverse taxa. Comparative analyses spanning mammals and insects show 
that genes expressed late in life show weaker purifying selection and 
faster amino acid evolution at both single-cell and tissue levels38–40. These 
multilevel signatures, from population genetics to molecular evolution 
across phylogenetically diverse species, provide compelling evidence 
that mutation accumulation shapes the genetic architecture of ageing.
The relative contribution of antagonistic pleiotropy versus muta-
tion accumulation varies with ecological and demographic context. 
Mathematical models suggest that mutation accumulation dominates 
when extrinsic mortality (death risk from environmental causes) is high 
and populations are small, whereas antagonistic pleiotropy becomes 
more important in larger populations with lower extrinsic mortality41. 
Contemporary syntheses emphasize that their relative contributions 
depend on population context4,42. Table 1 maps the distinct genomic 
signatures predicted by each theory to the study designs, evidence and 
limitations that currently inform their roles.
Special cases and exceptions
Special cases emphasize the boundaries of the classic theories. Ham-
ilton concluded that selection pressure must always decline with age2, 
but this conclusion depends on whether mutations have additive or 
proportional effects43. In some organisms, the selection force increases 
over part of adulthood3,44. Many fish species continue growing after 
reproduction commences, increasing survival and fecundity with body 
size, although selection force eventually declines. The classic predic-
tion that higher extrinsic mortality accelerates senescence evolution 
assumes that extrinsic mortality acts randomly with respect to indi-
vidual condition4. When mortality is instead condition-dependent 
(for example, if predators preferentially capture slower or less vigilant 
individuals), higher extrinsic mortality can strengthen selection to 
maintain survival-relevant traits, and senescence evolves to be slower45. 
This hypothesis has been confirmed experimentally in Caenorhabditis 
remanei; populations under condition-dependent mortality (heat 
shock killing weaker individuals) evolved longer lifespans, whereas 
those under random mortality evolved shorter lifespans46. Guppies 
under high predation in Trinidadian streams similarly evolved longer 
reproductive lifespans47,48. Formal models demonstrate that the 
outcome depends on density regulation, age structure and whether 
­mortality is additive or condition-dependent49–52.
Extreme life histories further challenge classic predictions. Semel-
parity (a single reproductive episode followed by death), exemplified 
by Pacific salmon, which die shortly after spawning, represents the 
extreme end point of reproduction–ageing trade-offs, evolving under 
high adult mortality or extreme breeding costs53. In Caenorhabditis 
elegans, a self-destructive reproductive programme repurposes

gies and extending lifespan54,55. This apparent programmed death 
might be explained by high relatedness in this self-fertilizing inbreeder, 
where selection could favour resource transfer to offspring56.
Hamilton’s inclusive fitness theory predicts that post-reproductive 
individuals can persist through selection if they enhance the fitness of 
relatives. In killer whales, post-reproductive females provide ecologi-
cal knowledge and leadership, improving grandoffspring survival57,58. 
Comparative analysis across toothed whales revealed that menopause 
evolved convergently in at least five lineages through extended lifespan 
rather than shortened reproductive span59. Such grandmother effects, 
combined with intergenerational reproductive conflict, might also 
explain the evolution of menopause in humans60. Post-reproductive 
women can increase grandchild survival through provisioning, child-
care and knowledge transfer, as shown in historical demographic 
data61,62, while reproductive conflict models propose that ceasing 
reproduction in older age raises inclusive fitness by avoiding overlap 
with younger co-resident females competing for the same non-parental 
help in raising offspring63.
Conserved features of ageing
Despite the vast diversity in ageing rates, the underlying molecular 
processes show remarkable conservation. This conservation was not 
anticipated by classic evolutionary genetics, because mutation accu-
mulation predicts that distinct late-acting alleles would accumulate 
independently in each lineage5,64, generating largely species-specific 
(‘private’) mechanisms. The discovery of conserved longevity-regulating 
pathways represented a conceptual turning point that antagonistic 
pleiotropy helps to explain (Box 1). Where similar fitness trade-offs 
recur across taxa, selection shapes similar pathway architectures, pro-
ducing ‘public’ ageing mechanisms. Rather than implying an ageing 
programme, this conservation reflects evolution repeatedly acting 
on ancient, pleiotropic pathways coordinating growth, development 
and reproduction.
Hallmarks of ageing
The hallmarks framework summarizes cellular and molecular processes 
that accompany and drive ageing; originally consisting of 9 hallmarks, 
this framework has since been expanded to 12 (Fig. 2a), adding disabled 
Box 1 | Evolutionary theories of ageing
 
Ageing evolves because the force of natural selection declines with 
adult age, creating a ‘selection shadow’ over late-life phenotypes2,203. 
Two foundational population genetics theories explain how 
deleterious late-life effects accumulate under weakened selection, 
and several mechanistic theories describe the physiological 
processes through which these effects manifest.
Mutation accumulation
Germline alleles with exclusively late-acting deleterious effects can 
drift to higher frequencies because purifying selection against them 
weakens with age13. The theory predicts increasing genetic variance 
in fitness components at later ages and largely species-specific 
(private) ageing mechanisms, because distinct mutations accumulate 
independently in different lineages3.
Antagonistic pleiotropy
Alleles conferring benefits in early life can be maintained by selection 
despite causing harm in late life, because selection weights early-life 
effects more heavily3,14. The theory predicts negative genetic 
correlations between early-life fitness and late-life performance, 
and conserved (public) ageing pathways in which similar trade-offs 
recur across species. Two complementary mechanistic theories 
describe specific physiological routes through which antagonistically 
pleiotropic alleles exert their late-life costs: disposable soma 
proposes insufficient investment in maintenance, and hyperfunction 
emphasizes excessive continued activity of youth-optimized 
programmes.
Disposable soma The cost of reproduction can manifest as reduced 
investment in somatic maintenance1. Organisms preferentially 
allocate metabolic resources towards reproduction at the expense 
of somatic repair. Disposable soma represents a special case of 
antagonistic pleiotropy, because genes promoting reproductive 
investment at the cost of somatic maintenance are, by definition, 
antagonistically pleiotropic204.
Hyperfunction Under this theory, ageing results not from 
accumulated damage but from the continued, inappropriate activity 
of developmental and growth-promoting programmes beyond 
their selected context185. These ‘quasi-programmes’, exemplified 
by the mTOR pathway, drive cellular senescence, hypertrophy and 
age-related pathology when they persist into late life.
Biological constraints
Complex organisms must balance many competing physiological 
priorities simultaneously, and the resulting high-dimensional trade-off 
structures may contribute to ageing independently of the selection 
shadow205,206. Under this view, optimizing one physiological function 
(for example, an immune response) can unavoidably compromise 
others (for example, tissue integrity). Senescence may therefore 
emerge even without any individual allele being antagonistically 
pleiotropic in the classical sense. If ageing substantially reflects such 
constraints, its genetic basis may be highly polygenic and diffuse 
rather than concentrated in discrete trade-off loci. This architecture 
would affect both the detectability of antagonistic pleiotropy 
signatures and the feasibility of targeted interventions4.
Group selection and programmed ageing
Programmed ageing theories propose that ageing is adaptive, 
maintained by group-level selection to benefit populations, and 
invoke conserved longevity-regulating pathways as evidence for an 
ageing ‘programme’207. However, the conditions required for group 
selection to override individual-level selection (small, structured 
populations with limited migration and strong between-group 
competition) rarely apply in nature. Systematic evaluation finds 
that the theoretical arguments for programmed ageing lack robust 
support208. One exception may be organisms with colonial ecology 
and high relatedness, where kin selection could favour adaptive 
death56. For most taxa, individual-level selection operating through 
mutation accumulation and antagonistic pleiotropy provides a more 
parsimonious explanation for the evolution of ageing.

manipulations and experimental interventions have demonstrated that

reflects strong purifying selection on genes with essential develop-
mental and housekeeping roles, rather than selection for longevity 
itself. These gene lists are subject to ascertainment bias, because well 
studied pathways are over-represented in curated databases, and the

observed patterns should be interpreted as indicative of evolutionary 
constraint rather than precise quantitative estimates. The hallmarks 
with the deepest evolutionary roots (proteostasis, genomic instabil-
ity, mitochondrial dysfunction, nutrient sensing) trace to unicellular 
organisms, whereas cellular senescence emerged more recently in 
metazoans68. The hallmarks framework itself continues to expand, 
with extracellular matrix changes and psychosocial isolation recently 
proposed69, yet the core picture of hallmarks as conserved, pleiotropic 
mechanisms remains consistent. This conservation extends beyond 
hallmarks. The GenAge70 human longevity gene set exhibits consist-
ently higher sequence conservation than matched controls (Fig. 2c), 
supporting the view that evolution has repeatedly tuned a limited set 
of regulatory nodes coordinating growth, reproduction and stress 
responses. These pathways were optimized for early-life functions 
yet continue operating into late life, exemplifying ‘youth-optimized 
features’ functioning beyond their selected contexts.
The geroscience hypothesis, which proposes targeting conserved 
ageing mechanisms to ameliorate multiple age-related diseases simul-
taneously, aligns directly with antagonistic pleiotropy. The pathways 
that geroscience identifies as intervention targets (nutrient sensing, 
proteostasis, inflammatory signalling) are precisely those under strong 
pleiotropic constraint (Box 1). Interventions succeed when they par-
tially relieve the late-life costs of pathways that selection could not 
optimize beyond the reproductive period.
Longevity interventions across species
Successful pro-longevity interventions consistently target a few con-
served nodes rather than species-specific mechanisms, providing strong 
evidence for shared ageing pathways. Dietary restriction extends lifes-
pan in worms, flies and rodents and improves risk markers in humans, 
partly through reduced insulin/IGF-1 and mTOR signalling71–73. High 
physical activity represents the ancestral condition for wild-type rodents 
and pre-industrial humans, and a sedentary lifestyle the derived state.

714

Exercise therefore restores organisms to a state closer to the ancestral 
physiological context, with conserved healthspan benefits74,75. These 
pathways do not merely balance growth against somatic maintenance 
but simultaneously mediate competing causes of mortality, including 
cancer suppression76, immune defence and metabolic homeostasis, cre-
ating high-dimensional trade-off structures (Box 1). Most cross-species 
evidence derives from short-lived laboratory species under ad libitum, 
sedentary, protected conditions, which may not recapitulate the 
trade-off landscapes under which these pathways evolved — although 
such conditions arguably parallel those of modern industrialized human 
populations. Dietary restriction incurs hidden costs, and its benefits vary 
across genetic backgrounds, consistent with life-history trade-offs77.
As antagonistic pleiotropy predicts, intervention effects are geno-
type- and life-stage-dependent. The Intervention Testing Program78 
reveals striking sex- and background-dependent effects in geneti-
cally heterogeneous mice79,80, with genetic background exerting a 
larger influence on lifespan than dietary restriction itself81. The 
Caenorhabditis Intervention Testing Program similarly found that 
most pro-longevity compounds extended lifespan in only a subset of 
genetically diverse strains82, predicting substantial heterogeneity of 
response in human populations. Rapamycin and rapalogues extend 
lifespan in model organisms by modulating autophagy, proteosta-
sis and inflammatory pathways83,84. Low-dose, intermittent mTOR 
inhibition enhanced immune function in older volunteers85,86, and an 
observational study of off-label rapamycin use in 333 adults reported 
improvements in ageing markers87. Clinical trials are now testing 
whether selective mTORC1 inhibition can safely target age-related 
diseases88. Metformin targets AMP-activated protein kinase and mito-
chondrial bioenergetics, affecting nutrient sensing and inflammation, 
including the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP), 
although evidence for direct effects on human ageing rate, as distinct 
from metabolic disease management, remains preliminary89,90. Genetic 
manipulations converge on reduced insulin/IGF-1 or growth hormone 
signalling and increased autophagy, extending lifespan while often 
trading growth for maintenance20,91,92.
Cross-species biomarkers of ageing
Robust biomarkers are essential for evaluating interventions and testing 
evolutionary predictions about ageing. Senescence-associated mark-
ers (p16/p21 activation, SA-β-gal, the SASP) index a conserved cellular 
state across mammalian species93,94. Although chronic inflammation 
has been proposed as a conserved hallmark (inflammageing), recent 
cross-population analyses reveal that this pattern is not universal. 
Age-associated inflammatory signatures seem to be largely confined 
to industrialized contexts24, and comparative biology supports this 
conclusion. Some non-human primates show no inflammageing in 
the wild95, and other long-lived mammals (for example, the blind mole 
rat, Spalax) have evolved to suppress the inflammatory SASP despite 
undergoing senescence96. Inflammageing may therefore represent 
a facultative, environment-dependent response rather than an obli-
gate feature of ageing. By contrast, immunosenescence (the decline of 
adaptive immunity) is more consistently observed across wild animal 
populations97. Omics profiling reveals organ-specific ageing signatures 
in humans, with circulating proteins tracking organ biological age98. 
Organ-specific variation in senescence rates probably reflects differ-
ential selection pressures on tissues. Single-cell analyses have identi-
fied ribosome-to-inflammation balance as a hallmark distinguishing 
super-longevity99, potentially representing a cellular signature of the 
trade-off between growth and damage response.
Epigenetic clocks have emerged as the most robust cross-species 
biomarkers. The original multi-tissue human DNA methylation clock 
accurately predicts age100, and clocks track lifespan dynamics and 
respond to pro-longevity interventions in mice101. Pan-mammalian 
clocks trained on conserved CpG dinucleotides achieve high 
accuracy across species and tissues and respond to pro-longevity 
interventions102,103. Approximately 90% of age-dependent DNA meth-
ylation gain occurs at regions regulated by the Polycomb repressive 
complex 2 (PRC2)104, developmental regulators under strong purify-
ing selection. Cross-species clock performance may therefore reflect 
selection maintaining developmental programmes whose contin-
ued post-maturational activity produces predictable methylation 
changes within the selection shadow105,106. Cross-species transfer-
ability has been demonstrated for DNA methylation clocks but not yet 
for proteomic or transcriptomic signatures. Most epigenetic clocks 
are trained on blood samples from birth onward and may therefore 
conflate developmental programming with ageing signals; restrict-
ing training to post-maturational ages would better isolate ageing 
processes. Causality-enriched clocks that distinguish damage-driven 
from adaptive changes107 could further sharpen mechanistic tests of 
evolutionary predictions.
Variation of ageing features across species
Despite conservation of core ageing pathways, ageing rates and 
maximum lifespan vary over 100-fold among vertebrates and show 
even greater diversity across the tree of life108,109. A phylogenetic 
view of vertebrate lifespans illustrates this variation while also high-
lighting that closely related species often display similar lifespans, 
reflecting shared evolutionary constraints alongside lineage-specific 
adaptations (Fig. 3a). This variation provides natural experiments 
for identifying genetic and molecular mechanisms underlying lon-
gevity differences. However, interpreting cross-species patterns 
requires phylogenetic awareness: most comparative studies lack 
adequate species per taxon for proper phylogenetic correction, 
limiting the ability to distinguish lineage-specific adaptations from 
shared solutions6.
Molecular correlates of lifespan variation
Two complementary approaches identify longevity-associated molecu-
lar features (Fig. 3b). Convergent evolution analysis detects sequence 
variants or molecular features that arise independently in long-lived 
species across a limited number of phylogenetically controlled com-
parisons. Large-scale comparative approaches integrate multi-omics 
data with phylogenetic information, using phylogenetic generalized 
least squares (PGLS) regression to identify molecular traits correlating 
with lifespan while accounting for shared ancestry. Among the molecu-
lar traits identified through these approaches, somatic mutation rates 
show particularly striking scaling with lifespan.
Across 16 mammalian species, per-year mutation rates scale 
inversely with lifespan110. End-of-life mutational burdens vary only 
3-fold despite 30-fold lifespan differences, suggesting selection for 
lower mutation rates in long-lived species. These patterns probably 
reflect selection on cancer risk111, although whether somatic mutation 
accumulation directly drives organismal ageing or primarily con-
strains lifespan through neoplasia remains debated112. More broadly, 
within-individual somatic evolution (clonal expansions, somatic selec-
tion, age-related mosaicism) operates at a different level of selection 
from the germline processes that are the focus of this Review. However, 
declining organismal-level selection with age may create permissive 

Nature Reviews Genetics | Volume 27 | September 2026 | 708–723
715
Review article
conditions for such sub-organismal processes, as the ageing body 
becomes less able to suppress aberrant clonal growth113.
Evolutionary constraint on longevity pathways
Genes in conserved longevity pathways, including genes related to DNA 
repair, cell cycle control, IGF-1 signalling and immunity, show stronger 
purifying selection in larger, longer-lived mammals114. Transcriptomic 
comparisons reinforce these findings. Across 26 mammalian species, 
longevity-associated gene expression organizes around circadian and 
pluripotency networks modulated by conserved nutrient-sensing 
pathways115. A broader analysis across 103 species linked longevity to 
elevated expression of nonsense-mediated decay, translational fidelity 
and methionine restriction pathways116. Primate-specific analyses have 
identified amino acid substitutions in wound healing, blood coagula-
tion and cardiovascular pathways that arose in parallel across lineages 
with increased longevity, many of which exhibit antagonistic pleiotropy 
signatures117. These patterns demonstrate that conserved ageing path-
ways are constrained by their pleiotropic effects on early-life fitness, 
with species-specific longevity emerging from variation in how selec-
tion balances these trade-offs. Even within primates, where lifespan 
varies fivefold, variation in baseline mortality far exceeds variation in 
the rate at which mortality increases with age109. This finding indicates 
that longevity differences across primates arise primarily from changes 
in overall survival rather than altered ageing rates.
Lineage-specific adaptations
Individual lineages show diverse evolutionary trajectories. Rockfishes 
(genus Sebastes) exemplify the repeated evolution of extended lifes-
pan, varying over 100-fold in maximum lifespan (11 to 205 years), with 
long-lived species having evolved multiple times from shorter-lived 
ancestors118. Comparative genomics across 88 rockfish species identified 
137 longevity-associated genes under positive selection, including genes 
in insulin signalling, DNA repair and immune pathways. These pathways 
are the same — showing increased purifying selection — in mammals; 
however, in rockfish, they exhibit signatures of adaptive evolution.
Additional lineages reveal further adaptive diversity. The naked 
mole rat (Heterocephalus glaber), an exceptionally long-lived rodent 
(>37 years), combines multiple tumour-suppressive innovations, 
including an atypical p15/p16 hybrid gene product, high-molecular-
weight hyaluronan119–121, enhanced translational fidelity122, genomic 
signatures of positive selection in DNA repair and protein homeostasis 
genes123 and enhanced DNA repair through a mutant-DNA-sensing 
receptor cyclic GMP–AMP synthase (cGAS)124. Despite their reputation 
for negligible senescence, DNA methylation clocks demonstrate that 
naked mole rats age epigenetically, although breeding queens age more 
slowly than non-breeders125,126. The bowhead whale (Balaena mysticetus), 
the longest-lived mammal at over 200 years, maintains genome integ-
rity through enhanced DNA double-strand break repair mediated by the 
cold-inducible RNA-binding protein CIRBP127. This mechanism differs in 
elephants, which evolved an expanded TP53 copy number128, illustrat-
ing that long-lived lineages achieve genome stability through diverse 
molecular solutions. Bats show transcriptomic profiles distinct from 
other ageing mammals. Longitudinal RNA sequencing data from wild 
Myotis myotis bats revealed that, during ageing, they maintain stable 
expression of DNA repair, autophagy and tumour-suppression genes129. 
Together, these examples illustrate that extended longevity evolves 
through diverse molecular routes, yet convergently targets the same 
conserved pathways (DNA repair, proteostasis, immune regulation, 
nutrient sensing), consistent with antagonistic pleiotropy.

The African turquoise killifish provides an instructive contrast: 
in short-lived annual species, relaxed purifying selection led to 
genome-wide accumulation of deleterious variants, including in genes 
such as mtor, insr, ampk, foxo3 and polg130, consistent with mutation 
accumulation130.
Variation of ageing features within species
Genetic variation within species drives individual differences in age-
ing through segregating alleles, rare-variant burden (the cumula-
tive load of rare deleterious variants across a gene or gene set) and 
gene–environment interactions. In social insects, for example, queen 
and worker castes share a genome yet their lifespans differ by over 
100-fold, thanks to differential gene expression and environmental 
cues131. Dog breeds, shaped by intense recent selection, show a three-
fold lifespan variation that demonstrates a strong trade-off between 
large body size and longevity132. We focus on human populations, where 
twin and genealogical studies estimated lifespan heritability at 15–30%. 
However, these estimates are confounded by assortative mating for 
lifespan-correlated traits133 and by extrinsic mortality. When extrinsic 
mortality is accounted for, heritability rises to approximately 50%134, 
consistent with the substantial role of extrinsic mortality in Hamilton’s 
selection models. Even so, GWAS currently capture only a small frac-
tion of this heritability. Evolutionary theory predicts this gap, because 
mutation accumulation distributes effects across many genes with small 
individual contributions, and antagonistic pleiotropy renders allelic 
effects dependent on life stage, genetic background and environment, 
limiting the variance attributable to individual loci. The value of genet-
ics therefore lies in mapping these distributed effects onto biological 
pathways rather than predicting individual lifespan. Notably, genetic 
influences strengthen markedly at the oldest ages, with familial cluster-
ing of exceptional longevity135,136. Molecular ageing shows increasing 
inter-individual variability with age, consistent with declining selection 
and variable environmental exposures137,138. Healthspan trajectories dif-
fer substantially among individuals, with both heritable and modifiable 
components139,

Comment
Transposable elements as catalysts 
of evolutionary innovation
Cedric Feschotte
Long understudied for dogmatic and technical 
reasons, transposable elements are now 
recognized as major drivers of evolutionary 
innovation. They contribute both as prolific 
sources of cis-regulatory elements that rewire 
gene networks and as donors of protein 
domains that give rise to new host genes.
When Barbara McClintock identified transposable elements (TEs) 
in maize in the late 1940s, she called them ‘controlling elements’ — 
­convinced she had discovered the mechanism by which genes are 
turned on and off during development. Her insight prefigured what 
Jacob and Monod would formalize for the lactose operon: a trans-acting 
factor governing cis-regulatory sequences. Although the Nobel com-
mittee recognized McClintock “for the discovery of mobile genetic 
elements”, her prescient framing of TEs as regulatory agents has made 
a forceful comeback to the foreground of genetics. Heavily inspired 
by McClintock and other visionaries, I argued 18 years ago in this jour-
nal that TEs were central players in the evolution of eukaryotic gene 
regulation1 — contributing both as a source of non-coding cis-regulatory 
elements (CREs) and as raw material for new regulatory proteins. In this 
Comment, I revisit and expand on these ideas in light of work from 
many laboratories worldwide, which has cemented the view that TEs 
are powerful drivers of regulatory innovation, both non-coding and 
coding, and therefore catalysts of biological novelty.
TEs as a source of non-coding regulatory elements
Over the past two decades, technological advances have transformed 
how we interrogate genome activity. Earlier functional genomics studies 
frequently overlooked TEs for both dogmatic and technical reasons. Most 
researchers operated under the assumption that TEs were ‘selfish’ or ‘junk’ 
DNA — abundant remnants of past genomic invasions, immobilized, inert 
and silenced by host control mechanisms. On the technical side, as repet-
itive sequences (some families, such as Alu in humans, number over one 
million copies per haploid genome), TEs were plagued by multi-mapping 
reads routinely discarded from analysis pipelines. Longer sequencing 
reads have now made this evasion impossible, and an explosion of studies 
have documented TE contributions to non-coding regulatory activities.
The most systematic catalogue comes from the human genome. 
Recent, conservative estimates indicate that TEs contribute at least 
25% of all candidate CREs annotated in the human genome — that 
is, roughly 500,000 of around 2 million currently predicted CREs2. 
Because TEs have proliferated throughout the course of mammalian 
evolution, most human TE loci are not shared with distant mammals. 
Approximately half of human TEs were inserted in the primate lineage, 
and about 1% are unique to humans, with an even smaller subset of 
insertions (around 1,000 per haploid genome) being polymorphic in 
the human population. TE-derived CREs are drawn from all these evo-
lutionary strata, making TEs a ­continuous source of novel regulatory 
DNA throughout mammalian evolution3.
This phenomenon extends far beyond our lineage. TE-derived CREs 
have been identified across a broad range of eukaryotes, many experi-
mentally validated and some directly linked to adaptive traits. Classic 
examples include a TE insertion in the cortex gene of the peppered moth 
responsible for the industrial melanism phenotype that became a text-
book case of adaptation4, a TE insertion near the ruby gene underlying 
the stress-protective crimson colour of blood oranges5, and a TE insertion 
conferring infection inducibility to the human immune gene AIM26 (Fig. 1).
Despite the growing recognition of TEs as pervasive suppliers of 
CREs, the evolutionary consequences of this influx of regulatory DNA 
remain incompletely understood. Because many TEs carry built-in, 
potent CREs, their insertions can immediately and strongly perturb gene 
expression. Natural selection efficiently removes insertions with strong 
deleterious effects; however, the efficiency with which slightly deleteri-
ous insertions are purged depends on effective population size. Species 
with small effective population sizes, such as vertebrates, must contend 
with greater TE-induced regulatory burden — a dynamic that may have 
driven the evolution of molecular systems to mitigate this burden.
Vertebrates, and probably other metazoans, deploy expandable 
batteries of zinc finger proteins (ZFPs) to recognize newly invading 
TEs in a sequence-specific fashion and silence them at the chromatin 
level. Crucially, because the silencing marks applied through ZFPs 
are generally reversible, and because ZFP expression can vary by cell 
type, developmental stage or environmental stimulus, this system can 
finely modulate TE CRE activity across contexts. Mutations that relieve 
individual TE ­copies from ZFP repression offer a further evolutionary 
path towards CRE activation. Although such systems are portrayed as 
‘defence mechanisms’ against TE invasion, they are more accurately 
understood as ‘taming’ agents — facilitating the co-option of TE-derived 
CREs into regulatory networks7.
TEs as a source of new proteins
Some of the most consequential proteins in vertebrate biology — from 
the RAG recombinase to syncytins — have TE origins. TE-encoded 
proteins, particularly transposases and Gag proteins, are dispro-
portionately prone to evolutionary co-option, probably because 
they offer ready-made DNA- and RNA-binding domains, as well as 
protein-interaction and scaffolding modules. Notably, the fusion of 
a transposase DNA-binding domain to an effector instantly creates a 
new regulatory protein capable of engaging a large pool of pre-existing 
binding sites dispersed throughout the genome. This shortcut to estab-
lishing new regulatory circuits may explain why several transcription 
factors carry transposase-derived DNA-binding domains8.
The evolutionary consequences can be spectacular (Fig. 1). The 
paired DNA-binding domain of the PAX6 transcription factor derives 
 Check for updates

Volume 27 | July 2026 | 501–502 | 502
nature reviews genetics
during development — before being fully domesticated. For example, 
in zebrafish and chickens, active endogenous retroviruses encode Gag 
proteins essential for embryonic development13. The ‘TE addiction’ 
model proposes that certain TE products act redundantly with host fac-
tors, progressively eroding selection on endogenous counterparts and 
creating a functional dependency on the TE and a path to full co-option.
These findings challenge the binary classification in which active 
TEs are inherently selfish whereas co-opted TE sequences are, by defi-
nition, immobilized relics. The line between host gene and TE (or self 
and non-self) is increasingly difficult to draw.
Rehabilitation of parasites
Since McClintock’s discovery nearly 80 years ago, our perception of TEs 
has undergone profound paradigm shifts: from ‘controlling elements’ 
integral to the chromosome, to ‘selfish’ or ‘junk’ DNA threatening genome 
integrity, to what we recognize today — major contributors of genetic 
variation and biochemical novelty. Unbiased interrogation of genome 
function over the past two decades has driven this rehabilitation. TEs 
are now understood not just as abundant genomic passengers but as a 
formidable fuel for evolutionary innovation. As technologies to inter-
rogate and manipulate TEs become applicable beyond traditional model 
organisms, and as the practical barriers to their use continue to fall, this 
recognition is destined to grow through every branch of the tree of life.

paste reaction that diversifies antibodies in jawed vertebrates — is cata-
lysed by RAG1 and RAG2, both derived from an ancestral transposon. 
The discovery of a related active transposon in amphioxus, which lacks 
VDJ recombination, has allowed reconstruction of the stepwise trans-
formation of a mutagenic transposase into an essential recombinase9. 
The domestication of a transposon thus gave rise to adaptive immunity, 
one of the defining innovations of vertebrates.
The placenta, a hallmark organ of eutherian mammals, is 
another beneficiary of TE domestication — and repeatedly so. Several 
Gag-derived proteins, including PEG10, are essential for placenta devel-
opment, possibly through the retained ability of these proteins to form 
viral-like particles that package and traffic RNA10. Multiple mammalian 
lineages independently co-opted endogenous retroviral envelope 
­proteins — syncytins — to drive trophoblast fusion and form the syncy-
tium at the fetal–maternal interface11. Immunity is another recurrent 
theme for the co-option of TE proteins. Notably, Gag and Envelope 
proteins of retroviral origins have been repeatedly domesticated as 
restriction factors against exogenous retroviruses12.
Despite these discoveries, TE contributions to proteome evolu-
tion are probably still underestimated. Long-read RNA sequencing 
is poised to reveal a wealth of TE-containing transcript isoforms with 
novel coding capacity. Structure-prediction tools such as AlphaFold 
are likely to illuminate the TE roots of proteins whose sequences have 
diverged beyond recognition by primary sequence homology.
TE addiction: en route to co-option
The mechanisms by which TE sequences transition to co-option remain 
poorly understood. Genomic context is likely to be a key determinant: 
TEs inserting near existing CREs active in a given cell type are more 
likely to retain or even accrue regulatory activity in that context2, 
partly because redundancy buffers against deleterious effects. At the 
coding level, growing evidence suggests that products of active or 
recently mobile TEs can assume important cellular roles — particularly

offer ready-made DNA- and
